The 1981 IBM-World Bank currency swap — exchanging dollar and Swiss-franc obligations to mutual advantage — creates the modern derivatives market. By the 2000s, the over-the-counter derivatives notional value exceeds the world economy by an order of magnitude.

ticks.name: Scanning tunneling microscope
ticks.constraint: individual atoms as too small to see or position
ticks.detail: IBM researchers spelled 'IBM' in xenon atoms. Nanotechnology begins here.

links.label: PRL: Binnig, Rohrer et al — Surface Studies by STM (1982)
Binnig & Rohrer Nobel Lecture: STM birth to adolescence (PDF)

ticks.because: Woodward's total synthesis (1970) had proven engineering-level control over organic chemistry; QCD (1973) and the GPS satellite constellation (1973) demonstrated comparable precision in physics and engineering at their respective scales. The scanning tunneling microscope at IBM brings the same precision down to single atoms — detecting individual atom positions by quantum-tunneling current. Nanotechnology and atom-by-atom physics begin here.

ticks.name: MIDI protocol
ticks.constraint: electronic instruments as incompatible with each other
ticks.detail: Electronic production, DAWs, and modern pop music are all MIDI-native.
ticks.because: The Walkman (1979) had personalized music consumption. MTV (1981) made music videos central. MIDI is the production-side counterpart — a digital protocol letting synthesizers, sequencers, and computers exchange note and timing data. Electronic production, DAWs, and modern pop music are all MIDI-native; the protocol still runs forty years later.

ticks.name: W and Z bosons discovered (CERN)
ticks.constraint: electroweak unification as theoretical only
ticks.detail: The Standard Model was experimentally validated at its core.

links.label: CERN — The Discovery of the W and Z Particles (PDF)
CERN Timeline — W and Z particles discovered

ticks.because: The scanning tunneling microscope (1981) proved that individual atoms could be imaged and manipulated — physics measurement at the smallest scales. Inflation theory (Guth, 1981) proved the Big Bang's puzzles could be solved with a coherent theoretical framework. CERN's W and Z discoveries combine both — high-precision experiment confirms the electroweak unification at exactly the predicted masses, validating the Standard Model at its core.

ticks.name: GPS (made available to civilians)
ticks.constraint: location requiring landmarks or maps
ticks.detail: Uber, Google Maps, precision agriculture, drone delivery — all GPS-dependent.

links.label: State Dept FRUS: NSDD 102 — US Response to KAL Airliner (1983)
State Dept FRUS: KAL 007 Shootdown ch. 3

ticks.because: The IBM-World Bank currency swap (1981), the Falklands War (1982), and the Club of Rome's Limits to Growth (1972) demonstrated that the era's technical and financial innovation was structurally reordering society. GPS's civilian availability in 1983 — with deliberately degraded accuracy initially, full precision after 2000 — extends military positioning technology to consumers. Uber, Google Maps, precision agriculture, and drone delivery all depend on civilian GPS.

ticks.name: DNS (Domain Name System)
ticks.constraint: internet addresses requiring memorization of numeric IPs
ticks.detail: Made the internet human-navigable. Every web request begins with a DNS lookup.

links.label: IETF — RFC 1034 Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities
Internet Society — A Brief History of the Internet

ticks.because: TCP/IP's 1983 standardization (in two formulations: Flag Day and the protocol-unification tick) had unified the network's transport layer. The W and Z bosons' detection at CERN (1983) marked the era's confidence in unified frameworks. DNS — replacing numeric IP addresses with hierarchical human-readable names — is the same unifying logic for the user-facing layer. Every web request begins with a DNS lookup.

ticks.name: System 1 / System 2 (Kahneman, Thinking Fast and Slow)
ticks.constraint: cognition as one undifferentiated reasoning process
ticks.detail: Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) consolidated decades of dual-process research into a public framework: System 1 is fast, automatic, and pattern-based; System 2 is slow, deliberate, and effortful. The dichotomy let economists, designers, and the general public reason about heuristics, biases, and when to trust intuition. The book made cognitive psychology a strategic vocabulary across industries.

links.label: Kahneman — Two Systems in the Mind (American Academy)

ticks.because: Dual-process theories had circulated in cognitive psychology since the 1970s — Wason and Evans, Stanovich and West. Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) packaged the research for the public: System 1 is fast, intuitive, pattern-based, effortless; System 2 is slow, deliberative, effortful, capacity-limited. The framework's empirical specifics are debated. Its conceptual frame entered behavioral economics, public policy, design, and the way ordinary people talk about their own thinking.

ticks.name: Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine
ticks.constraint: vaccine production requiring live pathogen cultivation
ticks.detail: The first vaccine produced by genetic engineering. Every mRNA vaccine builds on this tick.

links.label: Google Scholar: Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine

ticks.because: HIV's identification with ELISA (1983), the AIDS-crisis response (1983), and Marshall and Warren's identification of Helicobacter pylori as ulcer cause (1983) demonstrated that the early 1980s were a peak biomedical-engineering period. The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine — produced by genetic engineering rather than from blood — is the first vaccine made by inserting a viral gene into yeast. Every later mRNA vaccine builds on this principle.

ticks.name: Laparoscopic surgery
ticks.constraint: surgery requiring large incisions and long recovery
ticks.detail: Recovery time dropped from weeks to days. Laparoscopy now dominates abdominal surgery.

links.label: NCBI PMC — History of laparoscopic surgery

ticks.because: HIV's identification (1983) had created urgent pressure for less invasive procedures. The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine (1986) demonstrated industrial-scale designer biology. Helicobacter pylori's identification as ulcer cause (1983) showed how surgical conditions could turn into pharmaceutical ones. Laparoscopic surgery's emergence — small incisions, video-camera guidance, specialized instruments — is the operative analog. Recovery times collapse; the technique becomes standard for abdominal procedures within a decade.

ticks.name: Fall of the Berlin Wall
ticks.constraint: the globe as divided between two incompatible economic ideologies
ticks.detail: The 1990s boom was partly China and Eastern Europe entering the world economy at once.

links.label: History.com — East Germany opens the Berlin Wall (Nov 9 1989)
AP News — AP Was There: The fall of the Berlin Wall

ticks.because: Big Bang deregulation in London (1986) and the AIDS crisis activism (1981 onwards) had each remade institutional rigidity. GPS becoming civilian (1983) demonstrated US technological openness. The Berlin Wall's fall is the geopolitical pivot — Soviet bloc states open, German reunification follows, and the 1990s economic boom is partly China and Eastern Europe entering the world economy at scale.

ticks.name: World Wide Web (Berners-Lee)
ticks.constraint: documents as isolated files
ticks.detail: The web as a universal surface for publishing and finding things.
ticks.because: DNS (1984), the Macintosh GUI for everyone (1984), and backpropagation (Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams, 1986) had each given the era its addressing, interface, and learning substrates. Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal — using hypertext to link documents across computers via HTTP, HTML, and URLs — gives the internet its publishing layer. The Web as a universal surface for finding things begins.

ticks.name: Human Genome Project (launch)
ticks.constraint: the genome as an unknown text
ticks.detail: Genomic medicine begins here.

links.label: National Human Genome Research Institute — history
Lander et al. — Initial sequencing of the human genome (Nature 2001)

ticks.because: The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine (1986) had demonstrated industrial-scale designer biology. Laparoscopic surgery (1987) extended medicine into minimally-invasive territory. PCR's widespread use (1988) made arbitrary DNA segments amplifiable. The Human Genome Project's launch in 1990 takes those tools to species scale — sequence the entire three-billion-base reference genome of Homo sapiens. Genomic medicine as a field begins.

ticks.name: Linux / open-source software
ticks.constraint: software quality requiring corporate ownership
ticks.detail: Collective non-market production out-competing proprietary development at scale.

links.label: Eric Raymond — The Cathedral and the Bazaar

ticks.because: Big Bang deregulation (1986) had recently restructured how financial markets organized. The Washington Consensus (1989) codified development economics around liberalization. Berners-Lee's Web (1989) proved the internet could host new infrastructure. Linux is the same logic applied to operating systems — collective non-market production outcompeting proprietary development. By the 2000s most servers, smartphones, and supercomputers run Linux derivatives.

ticks.name: Python programming language
ticks.constraint: scripting requiring low-level C expertise
ticks.detail: NumPy, TensorFlow, PyTorch — the entire AI stack runs on Python.

links.label: NYCBUG mirror: Guido van Rossum's Python 0.9 announcement (Feb 1991)

ticks.because: The Hubble launch (1990), Berners-Lee's WWW proposal (1989), and HTML's specification (1990) bracket a moment when scientific and consumer infrastructure were both being rebuilt around accessible programming. Guido van Rossum's Python — designed for readability with significant indentation, batteries-included standard library — gave scientists, sysadmins, and educators a high-level alternative to C and Perl, and became the lingua franca of data science thirty years later.

ticks.name: Mosaic browser
ticks.constraint: the internet as text-only and technical
ticks.detail: The moment the internet became accessible to non-engineers.
ticks.because: Unicode (1991) gave the Web language coverage. The first WWW protocols (1990) and the first website (1991) provided the substrate. Linux (1991) demonstrated that open-source software could compete with commercial systems. Mosaic is the user-facing breakthrough — a graphical browser, easy to install, that turns the Web from a physicist's tool into a public medium within a year.

ticks.name: Dolly the sheep / somatic cell cloning
ticks.constraint: adult cells as permanently differentiated
ticks.detail: Stem cell research and the ethics of genetic identity became urgent questions.

links.label: Roslin Institute — The Life of Dolly
Wilmut et al. — Sheep cloned by nuclear transfer (Nature 1996)
National Museums Scotland — The story of Dolly the sheep

ticks.because: Gene therapy's first clinical trial (1990) had shown that genetic intervention could be therapeutic. BRCA1/2 identification (1994) and the DNA microarray (1995) demonstrated that genome-scale genetic information was becoming routine. Dolly's somatic-cell nuclear transfer in 1996 takes the manipulation a step further — an adult cell's nucleus reprogrammed to create a whole new organism. Stem cell research and questions of genetic identity become urgent.

ticks.name: Deep brain stimulation (FDA approved)
ticks.constraint: Parkinson's tremor as pharmacologically resistant
ticks.detail: The first programmable neural intervention. Now used for OCD, depression, and epilepsy.

links.label: FDA: Medtronic Activa Tremor Control PMA P960009 (1997)
De Gruyter: From the FDA — Brain implant to control tremors approved (1997)

ticks.because: The Human Genome Project's launch (1990), laparoscopic cholecystectomy (1990), and the first gene therapy trial (1990) had each opened a previously inaccessible biological territory to engineered intervention. Deep brain stimulation is the same engineering applied to the brain — programmable electrodes implanted in specific nuclei, treating Parkinson's tremor. The first programmable neural intervention; later expanded to OCD, depression, epilepsy.

ticks.name: PageRank (Google)
ticks.constraint: relevance as a keyword-matching problem
ticks.detail: The web's mess became navigable. Unlocked search as infrastructure.
ticks.because: The Mosaic browser (1993) had made the Web accessible. JavaScript (1995) made it programmable. The PalmPilot (1996) demonstrated that personal computing was rapidly mobile. PageRank — Brin and Page's algorithm using the Web's hyperlink structure as a authority signal — solves the relevance problem that Mosaic's growth had created. Search becomes infrastructure; Google becomes the dominant interface to written knowledge.

ticks.name: da Vinci robotic surgery system
ticks.constraint: surgical precision limited by the human hand's tremor
ticks.detail: The beginning of the question: can surgery eventually be fully automated?

links.label: Wikipedia: da Vinci robotic surgery system
Google Scholar: da Vinci robotic surgery system

ticks.because: Deep brain stimulation (FDA, 1997) had demonstrated that fine-grained neural intervention could be delivered through implanted hardware. Viagra (1998) and RNAi (1998) showed that pharmaceutical and molecular precision were both rapidly improving. The da Vinci system applies the same engineering precision to surgery — a console-controlled robotic platform with three to four arms, scaling-down hand tremor and extending visualization. Surgery becomes partly mechanized, raising the question whether it can eventually be fully automated.

ticks.name: Statistical machine translation breakthrough
ticks.constraint: machine translation as requiring linguistic rules
ticks.detail: Statistical patterns in billions of translated sentence pairs outperformed rule-based systems.

links.label: Brown 1993 — Mathematics of statistical MT (ACL Anthology)
Och 2003 — Minimum error rate training for SMT (ACL)

ticks.because: Unicode (1991) had made digital text language-agnostic. Mosaic (1993) and the Web (1993) had created the first global text corpus exceeding any single language's. The CD-ROM electronic dictionary (1985) had proven that lexical knowledge could be stored cheaply at scale. IBM's statistical machine translation closes the loop — instead of hand-coded rules, learn translation probabilities from parallel corpora. The seed of modern neural translation is here.

ticks.name: CRISPR discovery (Doudna/Charpentier)
ticks.constraint: gene editing as expensive and imprecise
ticks.detail: A bacterial immune system repurposed as a molecular scalpel.

links.label: Jinek et al. — A Programmable Dual-RNA–Guided DNA Endonuclease (Science 2012)

ticks.because: RNA interference (Fire and Mello, 1998) had shown that small RNA fragments could silence specific genes. The first complete human chromosome sequence (chromosome 22, 1999) demonstrated genome-scale work was tractable. The RNA world hypothesis support (2001) reinforced the centrality of RNA in early biology. CRISPR's discovery — bacterial immune systems recognizing viral DNA via guide RNAs — extends the same insight: a programmable molecular scalpel that becomes the dominant gene-editing technology of the 2010s.

ticks.name: Facebook / the Like button era
ticks.constraint: social approval as unquantifiable
ticks.detail: Approval legible at scale. The entire attention economy follows.

links.label: Shoshana Zuboff — The Age of Surveillance Capitalism

ticks.because: Napster (1999) had demonstrated that personal sharing could scale globally. Microsoft's Tablet PC (2002) and SETI@home (1999) showed that computing was distributing in new forms. Facebook's Like button is the social-graph engine — making approval legible at scale, turning every user into a signal source. The attention economy becomes a measurable, optimizable system.

ticks.name: AWS S3 / EC2 (cloud computing dawn)
ticks.constraint: compute as requiring hardware ownership
ticks.detail: Netflix, Airbnb, Uber — virtually every startup since 2008 was built on AWS infrastructure they never owned.
ticks.because: Gmail's free 1GB inbox (2004), YouTube's launch (2005), and Google Maps (2005) demonstrated that consumer-scale services could be delivered as utilities rather than products. AWS S3 and EC2 took the same utility-pricing logic and pointed it at developers themselves: storage and compute by the gigabyte-month and CPU-hour, eliminating hardware ownership as a precondition for building software at scale.

ticks.name: iPhone / touchscreen computing
ticks.constraint: computing requiring keyboard and mouse
ticks.detail: Apps, mobile-first, always-connected computing — all unlocked by this form factor.
ticks.because: AWS S3 and EC2 (2006) had created the cloud-computing substrate. Jeff Han's multi-touch demo at TED (2006) demonstrated that direct manipulation of pixel content was technically feasible at consumer scale. The iPhone in 2007 packages all of it — capacitive touch, app store, always-connected, pocket form factor. Mobile-first computing, the app economy, and the always-on attention environment all follow.

ticks.name: App Store model (iPhone SDK)
ticks.constraint: software distribution requiring physical media or complex installation
ticks.detail: The mobile app economy — $500B/year by 2023 — was created by this distribution model.

links.label: Reuters: Apple unveils iPhone software creation tools (Mar 2008)

ticks.because: YouTube (2005) had proved that user-generated content at global scale could displace media gatekeepers, and the iPhone (2007) put a touchscreen-first computer in every pocket. The App Store fused the two: a curated, frictionless distribution channel that turned every developer into a global publisher and built the $500B/year mobile economy on top.

ticks.name: Bitcoin / blockchain
ticks.constraint: trust requiring human institutions
ticks.detail: Replace trust with math and incentives.

links.label: Nakamoto — Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (whitepaper)

ticks.because: The 2008 financial crisis was a fresh case study in counterparty trust failure. Public-key cryptography (1976) and Merkle trees (1979) had given the primitives. Satoshi Nakamoto's October 2008 paper combined them into a working trustless ledger: a chain of blocks, each cryptographically linked, each block confirmed by costly proof-of-work. The first system that replaced institutional trust with computation. Whatever Bitcoin becomes, the design is now infrastructure.

ticks.name: Quantitative easing (post-financial crisis)
ticks.constraint: central bank intervention limited to interest rate adjustment
ticks.detail: The zero-lower-bound on interest rates wasn't a hard constraint on monetary policy.

links.label: Federal Reserve Board: Bernanke — The Crisis and the Policy Response (Jan 2009)
St. Louis Fed: What is Quantitative Easing, and How Has It Been Used?
St. Louis Fed: Quantitative Easing Explained (PDF)

ticks.because: The 2008 financial crisis broke the central-bank toolkit: rates couldn't go below zero, and the credit channel was frozen. Bernanke's Fed expanded its balance sheet from $900B to $4.5T by purchasing Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities — quantitative easing. The ECB and BOJ followed. Asset prices recovered before wages did, accelerating the inequality that defined the next decade. The unconventional became conventional; central banks are still unwinding.

ticks.name: AWS commoditization of cloud infrastructure
ticks.constraint: server capacity as a capital investment
ticks.detail: The cost of starting a software company dropped by orders of magnitude.

links.label: Wikipedia: Timeline of Amazon Web Services

ticks.because: Google's IPO (2004) demonstrated that ad-supported software businesses could reach tens of billions in market cap without owning physical retail or distribution. AWS extended that lesson to infrastructure itself — server capacity sold by the hour — and dropped the cost of starting a software company from millions to hundreds, restructuring venture capital and the cost basis of every later platform.

ticks.name: AlexNet / ImageNet breakthrough
ticks.constraint: image recognition as requiring hand-engineered features
ticks.detail: Top-5 error dropped from 26% to 15%. The AI research community collectively realized deep learning was the path forward.
ticks.because: The iPad (2010) and Watson's Jeopardy win (2011) mark when consumer computing and AI were both producing breakthrough demonstrations. AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet result — top-5 error of 15% versus the 26% best previous — used a deep convolutional network trained on GPUs and triggered the deep-learning revolution: every major AI lab pivoted to deep learning within 18 months.

ticks.name: Higgs boson discovered (CERN/LHC)
ticks.constraint: the Standard Model as lacking experimental confirmation of its final piece
ticks.detail: 48 years after Higgs proposed it. The Standard Model is now experimentally complete.

links.label: ATLAS & CMS — Observation of a new boson (PLB 2012)

ticks.because: Dark energy (1998) had revealed unknowns at the cosmic scale; graphene's isolation (2004) demonstrated experimental ingenuity at the atomic. The LHC's first collisions (2010) put the experimental machinery in place. The Higgs boson detection in 2012 — forty-eight years after Higgs's prediction — completes the Standard Model's particle inventory. The mass-giving mechanism for elementary particles is observed.

ticks.name: Generative Adversarial Networks (Goodfellow)
ticks.constraint: generative AI as requiring explicit probabilistic models
ticks.detail: Two networks trained in opposition. Deepfakes, AI art, and drug discovery synthesis all use GANs or their descendants.

links.label: Goodfellow et al. 2014 — Generative Adversarial Nets (arXiv)

ticks.because: AlexNet (2012) showed that deep learning crushed prior image recognition systems, and Watson's Jeopardy win (2011) plus the Higgs discovery (2012) bracket a period when AI and physics were both reaching their long-promised milestones. Goodfellow's GAN paired two networks in adversarial training — generator versus discriminator — and opened the path to deepfakes, AI-generated art, and most modern generative models.

ticks.name: ResNet / skip connections (He et al.)
ticks.constraint: very deep neural networks as unable to train
ticks.detail: Enabled the depth that makes modern vision models powerful. Every subsequent large neural network architecture uses skip connections.

links.label: He et al. — Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (2015)

ticks.because: Goodfellow's Generative Adversarial Networks (2014) and Kubernetes (2014) had each pushed deep learning's substrate forward. ResNet's skip connections solve the vanishing-gradient problem at depth — networks of one hundred fifty layers train smoothly. Computer-vision benchmarks fall by large margins; every later large neural network uses skip connections.

ticks.name: Gravitational waves detected (LIGO)
ticks.constraint: gravitational waves as theoretically predicted but inaccessible
ticks.detail: A new form of astronomy — listening to the universe rather than seeing it.

links.label: Abbott et al. — Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger (PRL 2016)
Wikipedia: First observation of gravitational waves

ticks.because: The Higgs boson discovery (2012, both at CERN/LHC and as Standard Model completion) had proven the Standard Model with experimental finality. LIGO's gravitational wave detection in 2015 is the corresponding cosmological proof — Einstein's general-relativity prediction confirmed a century later by detecting the spacetime ripple from a black-hole merger 1.3 billion light-years away. Multi-messenger astronomy begins.

ticks.name: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol
ticks.constraint: Go as a game beyond AI's computational reach
ticks.detail: Shifted expert consensus on AI timelines. AlphaFold and AlphaCode are its direct successors.

links.label: Nature 2016 — Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks
BBC News — AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol (2016)

ticks.because: LIGO's gravitational wave detection (2015), the broader gravitational-wave-astronomy opening (2015), and Kubernetes (2014) demonstrated that the era's technical infrastructure was rapidly maturing. AlphaGo's defeat of Lee Sedol in 2016 — a four-to-one match for a game thought intractable for decades — shifts expert consensus on AI timelines. AlphaFold and AlphaCode are the same lab's later applications.

ticks.name: Neural machine translation (Google NMT)
ticks.constraint: machine translation as producing awkward, unidiomatic text
ticks.detail: Translation became a commodity.

links.label: Wu et al. — Google's NMT System (arXiv 2016)

ticks.because: Statistical machine translation (1993) had been the dominant approach for two decades. Twitter (2006) and Google Translate's launch (2006) had each scaled multilingual real-time text. Google NMT's neural sequence-to-sequence approach drops error rates by sixty percent overnight in 2016 — translation becomes a commodity, available across hundreds of language pairs at near-human quality for major pairs.

ticks.name: Attention Is All You Need (Transformer paper)
ticks.constraint: sequence models requiring recurrent computation
ticks.detail: GPT, BERT, T5, and every modern language model is a transformer variant.

links.label: Vaswani et al. — Attention Is All You Need (2017) — original paper

ticks.because: TensorFlow open-sourcing (2015) had democratized large-scale ML infrastructure, and AlphaGo Zero (2017) plus federated learning (2016) showed that self-supervised and decentralized training were viable. The Transformer paper replaced recurrence with self-attention — a parallelizable architecture — and enabled language models, vision, and protein folding once anyone could scale it.

ticks.name: BERT / transfer learning for NLP
ticks.constraint: NLP models as task-specific and trained from scratch
ticks.detail: Fine-tuning rather than training became the paradigm.

links.label: Google AI Blog — Open Sourcing BERT

ticks.because: TensorFlow's open-sourcing (2015), the Transformer paper Attention Is All You Need (2017), and Hinton's capsule networks (2017) had each pushed deep-learning's substrate forward. BERT's bidirectional Transformer — pre-trained on a massive corpus, fine-tuned for specific tasks — establishes transfer learning as the dominant NLP paradigm. The seed for GPT, the contemporary LLM era, and most production NLP since.

ticks.name: Quantum supremacy (Google Sycamore)
ticks.constraint: quantum computation as theoretically promising but practically undemonstrated
ticks.detail: The race to practical quantum computing began in earnest.

links.label: Arute et al. — Quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor (Nature 2019)
IBM's response: quantum advantage, not supremacy

ticks.because: LIGO's gravitational-wave detection (2015–2016) had shown that exquisitely sensitive measurement could observe phenomena classical physics could not, and BERT (2018) plus the Transformer (2017) demonstrated that the bottleneck in computation was now algorithmic and architectural. Google's 53-qubit Sycamore chip executed a sampling task in 200 seconds that they argued would take a classical supercomputer 10,000 years — the first claimed quantum advantage.

ticks.name: GPT-3 (175B parameters)
ticks.constraint: language models as narrow task specialists
ticks.detail: Zero-shot and few-shot performance across tasks the model was never trained on.

links.label: Brown et al. — Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (2020)
Gary Marcus & Ernest Davis — GPT-3 and its discontents

ticks.because: GPT-2 (2019) crossed the coherence threshold for short-form text, and BERT (2018) plus Google's quantum supremacy (2019) showed both that transformers scaled and that compute infrastructure was reaching the levels needed to push them. GPT-3 simply made the transformer larger — 175B parameters — and demonstrated few-shot learning across hundreds of tasks without any fine-tuning, ending the era of narrow language models.

ticks.name: AlphaFold 2 (protein structure prediction)
ticks.constraint: protein structure determination as requiring years of experimental work
ticks.detail: Released the structure of virtually every known protein (200 million+). Drug discovery transformed overnight.

links.label: Nature 2021 — Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold

ticks.because: The mRNA vaccine push (2020) demonstrated that biology had become a programmable system at species scale, and continuous-glucose monitoring (2018) showed routine real-time molecular sensing. AlphaFold 2 collapsed protein-structure determination — previously years of crystallography per protein — to minutes of inference, and made structural biology a query-driven science.

ticks.name: ChatGPT / RLHF alignment
ticks.constraint: powerful language models as too unpredictable for mass deployment
ticks.detail: 100 million users in 2 months — the fastest product adoption in history.

links.label: Ouyang et al. — Training language models to follow instructions (InstructGPT, 2022)

ticks.because: GPT-3 (2020), AlphaFold 2 (2021), GitHub Copilot (2021), and Whisper (2022) bracket a two-year period when AI capabilities crossed multiple thresholds in language, biology, code, and speech. ChatGPT — GPT-3.5 fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from human feedback — gave the public a usable conversational interface to a frontier language model, hit 100M users in two months, and reset every assumption about AI deployment timelines.

ticks.name: Brain-computer interface (Neuralink / BrainGate)
ticks.constraint: paralysis as permanently severing communication between brain and world
ticks.detail: Paralyzed patients could control computers using only neural signals.

links.label: NCBI/PMC: Long-term performance of intracortical arrays in 14 BrainGate participants
Reuters Investigates: US regulators rejected Musk's bid for human trials

ticks.because: BrainGate (early 2000s) had shown that paralyzed patients could control a cursor using motor-cortex implants. Neuralink (founded 2016) made the surgical procedure semi-automated and increased channel density. By 2023, paralyzed patients could control computers directly with neural signals — typing, emailing, browsing. The communication channel between brain and world reopened for people who had lost it. The medical-device frontier with the deepest implications for what counts as a person.

ticks.name: GPT-4 multimodality / frontier model capabilities
ticks.constraint: AI assistance as text-only and limited to known information
ticks.detail: The question shifted from 'can AI do this?' to 'how do we integrate AI that can?'
ticks.because: GPT-3 (2020) had been text-only. GPT-4 (March 2023) accepted images as input — interpreting graphs, screenshots, math problems, and physical scenes. Capability across professional benchmarks crossed graduate-student level in many domains. The conversation in industry shifted from 'can AI do this?' to 'how do we integrate AI that already can?' API access at consumer prices made the question practical. The frontier model became infrastructure within months.

ticks.name: Reasoning models (o1/o3, chain-of-thought at inference)
ticks.constraint: AI reasoning as limited to patterns in training data
ticks.detail: Spending more compute at inference time — reasoning step by step — dramatically improved performance on hard problems. The model was solving, not just recalling.
ticks.because: GPT-3 (2020) and the Transformer (2017) had shown that scale produced capability. Chain-of-thought prompting (2022) showed that asking the model to think step-by-step improved hard-task performance. OpenAI's o1 (2024) and o3 (2024) made step-by-step reasoning a built-in inference mode: the model spends additional compute reasoning before answering. The model was solving, not just recalling. The frontier moved from training to test-time compute.

ticks.name: Organized warfare (first armies)
ticks.constraint: conflict as individual or small-group raids
ticks.detail: Permanent settlements created something worth defending — and conquering. The first organized armies emerged alongside the first cities. War became a state function, not just a feature of human aggression. Every military institution, alliance, and strategic doctrine begins here.

links.label: Ex Oriente Neo-Lithics: Warfare in Levantine Early Neolithic (Bar-Yosef et al.)
Guinness World Records: First depiction of organised armed forces (Sumerian)

ticks.because: City-state governance (3000 BC) gave communities something centralized worth defending or attacking. Mesopotamian clay-tablet record-keeping (3000 BC) made it possible to track conscripts, supplies, and tribute. Irrigation canals (3500 BC) created the surplus that could feed standing soldiers. The Narmer Palette (3100 BC) shows the unified outcome — a single authority commanding violence across a geographic territory. Organized warfare is the institutional consequence.

ticks.name: Fortification walls (Uruk, Jericho)
ticks.constraint: settlement defense requiring abandonment or flight
ticks.detail: Jericho's walls predate farming by some accounts. Uruk's walls, built under Gilgamesh, were 9km long. Permanent fortification meant you could hold ground. The city as a military unit — the origin of siege warfare, garrison strategy, and the relationship between urban density and defensibility.

links.label: Met Museum — Uruk: The First City

ticks.because: Organized warfare (3000 BC) had created the first standing armies; the Narmer Palette (3100 BC) showed that conquest could be a unifying political event. Fortification walls — Jericho's, then Uruk's nine kilometers under Gilgamesh — are the defensive answer. Permanent settlement means there is something worth defending, and walled cities mean territory can be held against organized aggression. Urban civilization becomes durable.

ticks.name: Composite bow
ticks.constraint: archery range limited by single-material bow
ticks.detail: Layers of horn, sinew, and wood laminated together produced a bow far more powerful than any single material could achieve. The composite bow gave mounted archers range and penetration that changed the battlefield for 4,000 years. Every steppe nomad empire — Scythian, Mongol, Hunnic — was built on this technology.

links.label: Bowden — Archery in Sumerian and Canaanite Contexts (Academia)
Origins and Performance of the Composite Bow (thesis)
Bow International — History of the composite bow

ticks.because: Organized warfare (3000 BC) had created standing armies. Fortification walls (3000 BC) demanded longer-range answers to siege. The phalanx (2500 BC) and the khopesh (2500 BC) had specialized close combat. The composite bow — wood, horn, and sinew bonded under tension — is the long-range answer: more power than a self-bow, short enough to fire from horseback. Steppe warfare and the Bronze Age power balance reorder together.

ticks.name: Chariot warfare
ticks.constraint: cavalry speed advantage requiring a mounted warrior
ticks.detail: The chariot combined mobility, elevation, and a stable platform for archers. Egypt vs the Hittites at Kadesh (1274 BC) was the first recorded large-scale chariot battle. The Bronze Age military balance of power hinged on who could afford and field the most chariots.

links.label: Fordham IHSP: Battle of Kadesh primary sources

ticks.because: The composite bow (2400 BC) had introduced powerful but short-portable ranged weapons. Thutmose III's sole rule (1458 BC) consolidated Egyptian military doctrine; the fall of Jericho (1400 BC) demonstrated that fortified cities could fall to mobile attackers. Chariot warfare combines mobility, elevation, and a stable platform for archers — the dominant Bronze Age battlefield system, used at Kadesh and across the Near East.

ticks.name: The phalanx (Greek hoplite formation)
ticks.constraint: infantry effectiveness depending on individual warrior skill
ticks.detail: Interlocking shields and coordinated spear thrusts turned individual soldiers into a collective machine. The phalanx democratized warfare — a disciplined citizen army could defeat elite warriors. Alexander's Macedonia extended it into the combined-arms syntagma. The first truly systematic infantry tactic.
ticks.because: Bronze weapons and military metallurgy (3000 BC) had established the materials. Assyrian siege warfare (700 BC) had codified offensive practice. Indian iron swords (600 BC) demonstrated the era's spreading metallurgy. The Greek phalanx — interlocking shields, coordinated spear thrusts, citizen-soldiers in disciplined ranks — turns infantry into a formation rather than a collection of individuals. Marathon and Plataea prove its decisive power.

ticks.name: The Art of War (Sun Tzu)
ticks.constraint: military strategy as purely improvisational and commander-dependent
ticks.detail: The first systematic treatise on strategy as a discipline. Sun Tzu's principles — deception, information asymmetry, the importance of logistics, adapting to terrain — remain the foundation of military theory and business strategy. The idea that war is won before it's fought.

links.label: World History Encyclopedia — The Art of War
Project Gutenberg — The Art of War (Giles translation)

ticks.because: The Battle of Marathon (490 BC) had proven that disciplined infantry could decide a war. Marathon's wider effect — Athenian confidence and the citizen-soldier model — reordered Greek statecraft. Sun Tzu's Art of War is the contemporaneous Chinese codification — strategy, deception, terrain, supply, and morale as systematic objects of analysis, with maxims that still appear in military and business curricula 2,400 years later.

ticks.name: Combined arms warfare (Alexander/Philip)
ticks.constraint: battlefield effectiveness requiring dominance in a single arm
ticks.detail: Philip II and Alexander the Great coordinated cavalry, heavy infantry, light infantry, and siege engines as a unified system. Each arm created conditions for the others. The Companion cavalry's hammer-and-anvil with the phalanx was essentially undefeated. Combined arms doctrine still governs modern military thinking.
ticks.because: Marathon (490 BC) had proven that disciplined infantry could defeat numerical superiority. Sun Tzu's Art of War (400 BC) had codified the strategic logic of force coordination. The Chinese repeating crossbow (400 BC) had introduced ranged firepower at scale. Philip and Alexander combine all three lessons — pikemen, cavalry, archers, and engineering arms operating as one system. Combined arms is now the template for every successful army since.

ticks.name: Roman manipular legion
ticks.constraint: phalanx rigidity on broken terrain
ticks.detail: Rome replaced the Greek phalanx with a flexible formation of maniples — smaller units that could operate independently, adapt to terrain, and rotate frontline soldiers. The legion's articulation gave Rome tactical adaptability its enemies couldn't match. The organizational template for every Western army until gunpowder.
ticks.because: Alexander's siege of Tyre (332 BC) and the Pyrrhic victory at Asculum (280 BC) demonstrated that rigid formations could be defeated by tactical flexibility. Roman lorica hamata (300 BC) provided the era's reliable body armor. The manipular legion — small flexible units that can fight independently — replaces the Greek phalanx as Rome's dominant formation. Roman expansion through the third and second centuries BC runs on this tactical innovation.

ticks.name: Archimedes' war machines (Syracuse)
ticks.constraint: fortification defense as passive
ticks.detail: Archimedes designed catapults, cranes, and grappling devices that held off a Roman fleet for three years. The application of mathematics to warfare — range calculation, mechanical advantage, projectile physics. The first documented military engineering in service of systematic defense.

links.label: NYU/Rorres — Polybius on Siege of Syracuse
NYU/Rorres — Plutarch on Siege of Syracuse
Perseus — Polybius Histories Book 8: Inventions of Archimedes

ticks.because: Roman roads (312 BC), Hannibal's strategic surprise crossing the Alps (218 BC), and the double envelopment at Cannae (216 BC) demonstrated that the era's military operations were becoming systematically planned. Archimedes's Syracuse defenses — catapults, cranes, grappling hooks — are the engineering counterpart, holding off Roman siege for two years. Engineering as military force-multiplier becomes a permanent strategic category.

ticks.name: Roman military logistics (castra, supply lines)
ticks.constraint: army campaign range limited by foraging
ticks.detail: The Roman legion built a fortified camp (castra) every night — a standard layout troops could construct in hours. Combined with organized supply lines and engineering capability, this extended campaign range and sustained army size far beyond what any previous force could maintain. Logistics as the actual determinant of military power.
ticks.because: Hannibal's Alpine crossing (218 BC), Archimedes's Syracuse defense (214 BC), Zama (202 BC), and Marius's army reforms (107 BC) bracket the Republic's transition from citizen militia to professional standing army. Roman military logistics — standardized castra (marching camps), grain magazines along supply lines, road networks tied to fortifications — extended campaign range from a season's foraging to year-round occupation, and made the Empire administratively possible.

ticks.name: Greek fire (Byzantine incendiary weapon)
ticks.constraint: naval fire attack requiring close contact
ticks.detail: The Byzantine Empire's secret incendiary weapon — likely naphtha-based — could burn on water and resisted extinguishing. Used to destroy Arab fleets attacking Constantinople in 672-678 and 717-718 AD. The first area-denial naval weapon. Also the first documented use of chemistry as a military system.
ticks.because: Chariot warfare (1300 BC), the Battle of Teutoburg Forest (9 AD), and the Battle of the Milvian Bridge (312 AD) demonstrated that ancient warfare was constantly evolving its decisive technologies. Greek fire — the Byzantine Empire's secret naphtha-based incendiary that could burn on water — saves Constantinople from Arab and other naval assaults for centuries. Chemical warfare as a strategic asset begins with this seventh-century weapon.

ticks.name: Gunpowder weaponized (China, then West)
ticks.constraint: projectile weapons limited by muscle-powered range and force
ticks.detail: Chinese chemists discovered gunpowder in the 9th century seeking immortality elixirs. Fire arrows, bombs, and early guns followed within 200 years. When gunpowder reached Europe via the Islamic world in the 13th century, it began dismantling feudal military hierarchy — castle walls and armored knights both became obsolete.

links.label: History of War — Fire-lance (li hua ch'iang)
Wikipedia — Siege of De'an (first recorded fire lance use, 1132)
Columbia Asia for Educators — Gunpowder in Song China

ticks.because: The Battle of Teutoburg Forest (9 AD) had earlier demonstrated that frontier resistance could halt imperial expansion. Greek fire's Byzantine deployment (673) showed that chemical incendiaries could be strategic weapons. Furusiyya's codification (892) had organized cavalry warfare. Chinese gunpowder weapons by 1000 — fire arrows, bombs, eventually firearms — and Western adoption two centuries later transform warfare permanently.

ticks.name: Crusades / military religious orders
ticks.constraint: long-distance military campaigns requiring national armies
ticks.detail: The Crusades created a new institutional form: the military religious order (Templars, Hospitallers, Teutonic Knights) — standing professional armies funded by donations, exempt from feudal obligations, with a transnational identity. The first multinational military institutions. Also: the logistical and financial systems developed to fund them seeded European banking.

links.label: Library of Congress: Speech of Pope Urban II at Clermont 1095
Fordham IHSP Medieval: Urban II at Clermont (Robert the Monk)

ticks.because: Greek fire (673) and gunpowder weaponized (1000) established that medieval warfare was acquiring increasingly sophisticated technologies. Crossbow proliferation in Europe (1000) demonstrated infantry firepower's spread. The Crusades create a new institutional form — the military religious order, like the Knights Templar and Hospitaller — that combines monastic discipline with knightly violence. The model influences every later religious-military formation.

ticks.name: Longbow at Crécy / missile dominance
ticks.constraint: armored cavalry as the decisive military arm
ticks.detail: English longbowmen at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415) destroyed French cavalry at range. The longbow could penetrate plate armor at 200 yards. The age of the mounted knight — and the feudal military system built around it — began its end. Missile weapons defeating shock weapons reshaped social hierarchy, not just tactics.

links.label: Wikipedia: Longbow at Crécy / missile dominance

ticks.because: The Mongol communications network (Yam, 1200), Mongol mobile-warfare doctrine (1241), and the sack of Baghdad (1258) had already broken the European assumption that armored cavalry was the decisive arm. The English longbow at Crécy applied the same lesson with a different weapon: massed missile fire from disciplined yeomen archers cutting down French knights — and signaled that armored cavalry's dominance was over.

ticks.name: Fall of Constantinople / cannon vs. walls
ticks.constraint: fortified city walls as defensible against conventional siege
ticks.detail: Mehmed II's massive Ottoman cannons breached Constantinople's 1,000-year-old walls in 53 days. The same cannon technology that ended the Byzantine Empire made every medieval castle in Europe vulnerable. The Hundred Years' War's last phase was simultaneously a demonstration that gunpowder siege artillery had made the feudal fortification obsolete.

links.label: Oxford Reference — Constantinople, Siege and Fall of (Reinert)

ticks.because: The longbow at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt (1415) had demonstrated that infantry missile fire could defeat armored cavalry. The Compagnie d'ordonnance (1445) established Europe's first standing army. Mehmed II's massive Ottoman cannons in 1453 take the same logic to medieval fortification — a thousand-year-old wall breached in weeks. Gunpowder warfare's dominance is established; the Byzantine Empire's fall completes the transition from medieval to early-modern.

ticks.name: Pike and shot formation
ticks.constraint: infantry requiring either missile or shock — not both simultaneously
ticks.detail: Swiss pikemen and Spanish arquebusiers learned to operate as combined units: musketeers fired while pikemen protected them from cavalry. The tercio formation dominated European battlefields for 150 years. The first systematic doctrine for integrating firearms into infantry tactics.

links.label: Erenow: Italian Wars and Rise of the Spanish Tercio

ticks.because: The fall of Constantinople by cannon (1453), the line-of-battle naval tactic (1500), and the galleon ship design (1501) bracket the late-medieval transition from medieval to early-modern warfare. Pike-and-shot — combining pikemen for defense against cavalry with arquebusiers and later musketeers for offensive fire — became the dominant European infantry formation from the Italian Wars through the Thirty Years' War, until the bayonet collapsed it.

ticks.name: Battle of Lepanto / broadside naval warfare
ticks.constraint: naval combat as galley ramming and boarding
ticks.detail: Lepanto demonstrated the dominance of gunpowder artillery aboard sailing ships over oar-powered galleys. The sailing warship with broadside cannons became the decisive naval instrument. This shift gave Atlantic-facing European powers — Portugal, Spain, England, Netherlands — inherent strategic advantages over Mediterranean powers.

links.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Lepanto / broadside naval warfare
Google Scholar: Battle of Lepanto / broadside naval warfare

ticks.because: The fall of Constantinople by cannon (1453), the galleon ship design (1501), and pike-and-shot formation (1534) demonstrated that gunpowder warfare was reordering early-modern combat. Lepanto's massed broadside artillery aboard sailing galleys — and the Holy League's victory over Ottoman galleys — confirms that artillery on ships now decides naval engagements. The age of broadside naval warfare runs three centuries.

ticks.name: Gustavus Adolphus military reforms
ticks.constraint: army effectiveness requiring numerical superiority
ticks.detail: The Swedish king introduced lighter, more mobile artillery; standardized drill; linear tactics; and combined-arms integration that produced a smaller, faster, more effective army. The Military Revolution of the 17th century — armies became professional, drilled, and state-funded. The conscript national army follows from these reforms.

links.label: Britannica — Gustavus Adolphus, Entry into Thirty Years War

ticks.because: The Battle of Lepanto (1571) and pike-and-shot formation (1534) demonstrated gunpowder warfare's evolution. Galileo's Two New Sciences (1589) showed that quantitative thinking could organize practical engineering. Gustavus Adolphus's reforms — lighter mobile artillery, standardized regimental units, drilled volley fire — combine all of it into coherent doctrine. The Swedish army becomes early-modern Europe's most effective; modern combined-arms doctrine traces here.

ticks.name: Levée en masse (French Revolutionary Army)
ticks.constraint: army size limited by professional recruitment and pay
ticks.detail: France mobilized 300,000 citizen-soldiers in a single decree. The nation-in-arms concept transformed war's scale. Napoleon's armies were its product. Mass conscription, national service, and the idea that war is fought by entire societies — not just professional militaries — all begin with this moment.

links.label: Gallica/BnF: Arrêté du 23 septembre 1793 sur la levée en masse
Persée: Minute du projet de décret 23 août 1793 (Carnot/Barère)

ticks.because: Frederick the Great's oblique order (1757), the Battle of Quebec's amphibious operational art (1759), and Lavoisier's conservation of mass (1773) demonstrated that the late eighteenth century was acquiring systematizing capacity in different domains. The French Revolutionary government's levée en masse — three hundred thousand citizen-soldiers conscripted by decree — invents modern total mobilization. The first nation-in-arms; every later mass-conscription war runs on this template.

ticks.name: Napoleon's corps system
ticks.constraint: army command requiring the general to directly oversee all units
ticks.detail: Napoleon organized armies into self-sufficient corps — each with infantry, cavalry, and artillery — that could operate independently but concentrate quickly. A corps could fight an entire enemy army long enough for others to arrive. The operational level of war as a distinct layer between strategy and tactics.
ticks.because: The Battle of Quebec's amphibious operational art (1759), the Levée en Masse (1793), and the Turtle submarine attack (1776) demonstrated that the late eighteenth century was reordering military organization. Napoleon's corps system — self-sufficient combined-arms units that can fight independently for days — is the synthesis. Modern army organization derives directly from Napoleonic corps structure.

ticks.name: Colt revolver / repeating firearms
ticks.constraint: firearm advantage negated by slow reloading
ticks.detail: The revolver's rotating cylinder allowed six shots before reloading. Combined with the later rifle and cartridge ammunition, repeating firearms fundamentally changed the lethality calculus of war. The American Civil War was the first major conflict to demonstrate industrial-era firepower — and its casualties shocked the world.

links.label: Texas State Historical Association — Colt Revolvers

ticks.because: Napoleon's Egyptian campaign (1798) and his eventual defeat (1813) demonstrated that nineteenth-century warfare was reordering around industrial logistics. Oersted's electromagnetism (1820) marked the era's broader technical confidence. Colt's revolver — a rotating cylinder allowing six shots before reloading — gives individual soldiers and civilians unprecedented sustained firepower. Personal-armament dynamics in the American West and beyond reorder around the revolver.

ticks.name: Railroad warfare (American Civil War)
ticks.constraint: army strategic mobility limited by marching speed
ticks.detail: The Civil War was the first major conflict where railroads moved armies strategically. The side that controlled railroads controlled the campaign. Sherman's March was fundamentally a railroad destruction campaign. Every subsequent industrial war — WWI, WWII — was primarily a contest of logistics networks, not just battle lines.

links.label: Perseus: E.P. Alexander, Military Memoirs of a Confederate (Ch. 3)
AHR: The Confederate Government and the Railroads (1861)

ticks.because: The Colt revolver (1836), the rifled musket (1855), and Kirchhoff-Bunsen spectroscopy (1859) demonstrated that nineteenth-century engineering and science compounded fast. Railroad warfare in the American Civil War is the strategic application — moving mass armies across hundreds of miles in days, supplying them along iron rails. Industrial logistics decides outcomes; the side with more tracks wins.

ticks.name: Ironclad warships (Monitor vs. Virginia)
ticks.constraint: wooden warships as the basis of naval power
ticks.detail: The battle of the USS Monitor and CSS Virginia (1862) made every wooden warship on Earth obsolete overnight. Iron (then steel) hulls, steam propulsion, and rotating gun turrets defined naval warfare for the next century. The naval arms race that followed — especially Britain vs. Germany — shaped the path to WWI.

links.label: Britannica — Battle of the Monitor and Merrimack

ticks.because: The rifled musket (1855) and rifled cannon (1855) gave infantry and artillery vastly increased range and accuracy. Railroad warfare (1861) demonstrated that industrial logistics could decide campaigns. The Monitor-Virginia engagement is the corresponding move at sea — wooden warships made obsolete in a single afternoon, naval power rewrote as industrial output.

ticks.name: Maxim gun / machine gun
ticks.constraint: automatic fire requiring multiple shooters
ticks.detail: Hiram Maxim's recoil-operated machine gun could fire 600 rounds per minute with a single operator. The colonial implications were immediate: small European forces could hold off thousands of African or Asian warriors. WWI's static trench warfare was the direct product — machine guns made offensive infantry movement suicidal.

links.label: Library of Congress — The Machine Gun: History, Development and Use

ticks.because: Ironclad warships (1862), the telegraph in warfare (1862), and Maxwell's equations (1865) demonstrated that mid-to-late-nineteenth-century military technology was rapidly industrializing. Maxim's recoil-operated machine gun — six hundred rounds per minute — automates infantry firepower. Colonial conquests in Africa run on Maxim guns; WWI's industrial slaughter is partly a consequence.

ticks.name: WWI chemical weapons (chlorine/mustard gas)
ticks.constraint: area denial requiring physical fortification
ticks.detail: Germany's 1915 chlorine attack at Ypres was the first large-scale use of chemical weapons in war. Mustard gas followed. The psychological impact outlasted the tactical: the specter of chemical attack shaped 20th-century warfare and arms control. The Chemical Weapons Convention (1993) is still responding to 1915.

links.label: Adam Matthew/UK National Archives: Gas Attacks on Western Front (CAB 45/289)
Wilfrid Laurier: Humphries, First Use of Poison Gas at Ypres 1915

ticks.because: The Maxim gun (1884) and trench warfare's emergence by 1915 had made traditional infantry advance suicidal. Germany's chlorine attack at Ypres in April 1915 was the first large-scale battlefield use of poison gas; mustard gas followed in 1917. Tactically, neither side gained ground. Strategically, every arms-control regime since — the 1925 Geneva Protocol, the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention — is still responding to it.

ticks.name: Tank (Battle of the Somme)
ticks.constraint: machine gun dominance over offensive infantry
ticks.detail: British tanks first appeared at the Somme in 1916. Mechanically unreliable and tactically misused, they nevertheless demonstrated the concept: armored, mobile fire support could cross no-man's land. German shock tactics and Allied armor doctrine converged by 1918. WWII's blitzkrieg was the theory fully realized.

links.label: Imperial War Museums — Tanks and the Battle of the Somme

ticks.because: Submarine warfare (1915), poison gas at Ypres (1915), and Einstein's general relativity (1915) bracket the wartime moment when industrial chemistry, machinery, and theory were all converging. The British Mark I tank's debut at Flers-Courcelette during the Somme offensive — armored, tracked, machine-gun-armed — broke the tactical stalemate of trench warfare for the first time, even as mechanical unreliability limited its operational impact in 1916.

ticks.name: Submarine warfare (unrestricted)
ticks.constraint: naval blockade requiring surface fleet superiority
ticks.detail: Germany's U-boat campaign proved that submarines could conduct strategic economic warfare independently of surface fleet control. Unrestricted submarine warfare nearly starved Britain and brought the US into WWI. The submarine became the capital weapon of naval strategy, culminating in WWII's Battle of the Atlantic.

links.label: Imperial War Museums — Why Germany sank Lusitania

ticks.because: The Schlieffen Plan's failure had locked WWI into trench warfare (1914), and the diesel-electric submarine (1914) gave navies a stealthy underwater striking platform. Germany's declaration of unrestricted submarine warfare (1915 and 1917) — sinking neutral merchant ships in war zones without warning — gave naval blockade a new doctrine that did not require surface fleet superiority, and triggered both US entry into WWI and decades of debate about commerce raiding's legitimacy.

ticks.name: Air power doctrine emerges (WWI)
ticks.constraint: military reconnaissance requiring ground observation
ticks.detail: WWI produced reconnaissance aircraft, then fighters to shoot them down, then bombers. By 1918, strategic bombing theory was being articulated: attack the enemy's industrial and civilian base directly. The interwar period saw this formalized by Douhet, Mitchell, and the RAF. WWII tested and largely validated strategic air power as an independent military instrument.

links.label: USAF/GPO: Douhet, The Command of the Air (PDF)

ticks.because: The tank's debut at the Somme (1916) and the Battle of the Somme's industrial slaughter (1916) demonstrated that WWI was a laboratory for new combat technology. General relativity's emergence (1916) is among the era's broader markers of confidence in engineered systems. WWI's progression — reconnaissance aircraft, then fighters to shoot them down, then bombers, then strategic targeting — develops air power as a doctrinal category that the next century elaborates without changing in substance.

ticks.name: Blitzkrieg doctrine (Poland/France)
ticks.constraint: armored advance requiring infantry consolidation before proceeding
ticks.detail: Germany's Panzer divisions bypassed fortified positions, drove deep into enemy rear areas, and collapsed command structures before defenders could react. Blitzkrieg wasn't a new technology — it was a new doctrine using existing tanks and aircraft. Speed as the decisive variable, not firepower. The concept reshaped every subsequent armored doctrine.

links.label: Holocaust Encyclopedia (USHMM) — World War II in Europe

ticks.because: WWI air power doctrine (1917) and German stormtrooper infiltration tactics (1918) had already demonstrated that armored advance plus aerial coordination could break linear defense — but only as point breakthroughs. The interwar physics of the day (Eddington's relativity confirmation 1919, de Broglie 1924) sat outside this thread. The Wehrmacht's 1939–1940 doctrine combined tanks, dive bombers, and radio in coordinated deep advance — the first time mechanized war achieved operational, not just tactical, surprise.

ticks.name: Carrier warfare (Coral Sea/Midway)
ticks.constraint: naval battles requiring surface ships to exchange gunfire
ticks.detail: Coral Sea (May 1942) was the first naval battle where the opposing surface fleets never saw each other — fought entirely by carrier aircraft. Midway (June 1942) decided the Pacific war with dive bombers. The aircraft carrier replaced the battleship as the capital ship of naval power. Naval doctrine worldwide realigned around this in months.

links.label: Naval History and Heritage Command — Battle of the Coral Sea
Australian War Memorial — Coral Sea, Midway and After
Australian War Memorial — Battle of the Coral Sea, 4-8 May 1942

ticks.because: Blitzkrieg (1939) had shown that combined-arms operational tempo could break linear defense, the Battle of Britain (1940) confirmed air power was decisive, and the Norden bombsight (1941) made precision attack from altitude possible. Coral Sea (May 1942) was the first naval battle fought entirely by aircraft launched from carriers — surface ships never sighted each other — and Midway a month later turned that fact into the war-defining battle.

ticks.name: D-Day amphibious doctrine
ticks.constraint: seaborne landings on defended beaches as prohibitively costly
ticks.detail: Operation Overlord was the largest amphibious operation in history — 156,000 troops on day one. It required purpose-built landing craft, artificial harbors, specialized armor, and coordinated deception operations. The doctrine developed for D-Day codified joint operations (air, sea, land) as the standard approach for contested landings.

links.label: National Archives: Records Relating to D-Day
Eisenhower Library: D-Day, The Invasion of Normandy

ticks.because: The Battle of Britain (1940), carrier warfare at Coral Sea and Midway (1942), and Fermi's first controlled nuclear chain reaction (1942) demonstrated WWII's industrial scale. D-Day on June 6, 1944 is amphibious doctrine at its operational peak — 156,000 troops landed across five beaches with airborne support. Combined-arms amphibious assault becomes the canonical doctrine for every later major landing.

ticks.name: Strategic bombing doctrine validated and questioned
ticks.constraint: industrial society as resilient to air attack
ticks.detail: WWII's strategic bombing campaigns destroyed German and Japanese industrial capacity — but required far more resources and caused far more civilian casualties than pre-war theorists predicted. The post-war assessments created the precision bombing doctrine that guided air power through Vietnam, Gulf War, and into the era of GPS-guided munitions.

links.label: Wikipedia: Strategic bombing doctrine validated and questioned

ticks.because: D-Day (1944) demonstrated that amphibious operational art was working at scale, and the V-1 (1944) plus the atomic bomb (1945) framed a year when air power's ceiling kept rising. The strategic bombing campaigns over Germany and Japan validated the doctrine — industrial output crippled, civilian morale tested — but also showed that area bombing's ethical and operational costs were enormous, a debate the post-war RAND analyses would prosecute for decades.

ticks.name: Nuclear deterrence theory (MAD)
ticks.constraint: military superiority as a guarantee of strategic dominance
ticks.detail: The Soviet atomic test (1949) and the H-bomb race produced Mutually Assured Destruction — the doctrine that nuclear war is unwinnable, and therefore rational actors won't start one. MAD replaced victory with stability. Every Cold War crisis — Cuba, Berlin — was navigated within this framework. The most consequential strategic concept in history.

links.label: Sokolski (ed.) — Getting MAD: Nuclear Mutual Assured Destruction (PDF)

ticks.because: Hiroshima and Nagasaki (1945) had shown what nuclear weapons could do. The Soviet test (1949) ended the US monopoly. The H-bomb (1952) made warheads city-killers. Mutually Assured Destruction emerged not as policy but as the only logical equilibrium: a first strike could not prevent retaliation, so neither side could rationally start. Cuba (1962) tested it. The Cold War's failure to escalate is MAD's main piece of evidence.

ticks.name: Intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM)
ticks.constraint: nuclear weapons delivery requiring aircraft penetrating defended airspace
ticks.detail: The Soviet R-7 (1957) and US Atlas (1958) could deliver nuclear warheads across continents in 30 minutes, flying above the atmosphere where they couldn't be intercepted. ICBMs made every point on Earth a potential target. They also drove the second-strike capability that stabilized MAD — and made missile defense an arms control crisis.

links.label: NASA: Korolev proposals on R-7 and Sputnik (1957)
CIA: SNIE 11-10-57 The Soviet ICBM Program

ticks.because: The Korean War's lessons in limited war (1950), the practical solar cell (1954), and the Suez Crisis (1956) bracket the 1950s moment when nuclear strategy and great-power decline were being recalculated. The first ICBMs — Soviet R-7 (1957) and US Atlas (1959) — gave both superpowers the ability to deliver nuclear weapons across continents in 30 minutes, and made the strategic-bombing penetration of defended airspace obsolete as the primary delivery mode.

ticks.name: Counterinsurgency doctrine (Malaya/Vietnam)
ticks.constraint: guerrilla warfare as solvable by conventional military superiority
ticks.detail: The British success in Malaya (1948-1960) against Communist insurgents — using 'hearts and minds' population-centric tactics, intelligence, and isolation of insurgents from their base — was codified as counterinsurgency doctrine. Its mixed results in Vietnam and later Iraq and Afghanistan showed its limits when political conditions weren't right.
ticks.because: ICBMs and Sputnik (both 1957) had moved great-power conflict into deterrence, leaving below-the-threshold conflicts as the practical battlefield. The British in Malaya and the Americans in Vietnam wrote the doctrine that emerged: population-centric operations, intelligence-led targeting, hearts-and-minds — the framework every later counterinsurgency manual extended.

ticks.name: Precision-guided munitions (Yom Kippur War)
ticks.constraint: air-to-ground accuracy requiring low-altitude attack runs
ticks.detail: Egyptian and Syrian SAM missiles and wire-guided anti-tank weapons in the 1973 war shocked Western military observers. Meanwhile, US laser-guided bombs ('smart bombs') demonstrated accuracy previously impossible. Precision strike changed the cost-benefit calculus of air power — you needed fewer sorties, fewer aircraft, and fewer aircraft losses to achieve the same effect.

links.label: FAS — The First Crisis: Yom Kippur War 1973 (Sparks)

ticks.because: The Tet Offensive (1968) had taught that information warfare could be strategically decisive. Apollo 11 (1969) demonstrated extreme-precision aerospace engineering. Synthetic organic chemistry's total synthesis (1970) showed precision in chemistry. The 1973 Yom Kippur War's deployment of Egyptian and Syrian SAM missiles and wire-guided anti-tank weapons demonstrates that consumer-grade precision has reached the battlefield. Modern guided-munition warfare's first major use.

ticks.name: Gulf War / network-centric warfare
ticks.constraint: battlefield awareness requiring physical reconnaissance and slow intelligence cycles
ticks.detail: Operation Desert Storm demonstrated satellite communications, GPS navigation, stealth aircraft, precision guided munitions, and real-time intelligence integration. The 100-hour ground war with minimal coalition casualties validated a new paradigm: information dominance as a force multiplier. Network-centric warfare doctrine followed.

links.label: USNI Proceedings: Cebrowski & Garstka, Network-Centric Warfare (1998)

ticks.because: Precision-guided munitions in the Yom Kippur War (1973) and the Falklands War (1982) had proved that single-shot kills against high-value targets were now standard, and the Hubble launch (1990) plus W/Z boson confirmation (1983) showed how routine the underlying physics had become. The Gulf War used satellite imagery, GPS, and AWACS to dissolve the fog of war for one side — a coalition that fought a networked battle against a 1980s-doctrine opponent.

ticks.name: Ukraine war / commercial drones and OSINT
ticks.constraint: military intelligence requiring classified infrastructure
ticks.detail: The Russia-Ukraine war demonstrated that commercial drones ($500 quadcopters) could locate and destroy multi-million-dollar tanks, that social media posts could track army movements, and that satellite imagery services open to the public could document war crimes in real time. The democratization of battlefield intelligence and aerial attack.

links.label: CSIS — Commercial Tech Flexing Military Muscle in Ukraine
C4ISRNET — How Ukraine cloaked its drones from Russian surveillance
Modern War Institute — Will the Drone War Come Home? (Fogel)

ticks.because: DJI's consumer quadcopter (2013) had put aerial filming in everyone's hands. Twitter (2006) and Telegram (2013) made user-generated coverage continuous. The Russia-Ukraine war (2022) was the first major conflict in which a $500 commercial drone could destroy a multi-million-dollar tank, in which OSINT volunteers tracked army movements from public satellite imagery, and in which front-line video reached the world without state media. The information environment of war was permanently flattened.

ticks.name: Linnaeus / binomial nomenclature
ticks.constraint: natural history as locally named and regionally incomparable
ticks.detail: Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae gave every species a two-part Latin name — genus and species. For the first time, a botanist in Sweden and one in Brazil could refer to the same plant unambiguously. Taxonomy enabled comparison, accumulation of biological knowledge, and eventually the evolutionary framework that explained the patterns.

links.label: Biodiversity Heritage Library: Linnaeus, Systema Naturae (1735)

ticks.because: Hooke's Micrographia (1665) coined 'cell' as a unit of life. Redi (1668) and Leeuwenhoek (1676) showed that life had hidden organizational layers — controlled experiments, microscopes, animalcules. Hales (1727) and Réaumur (1734) extended quantitative observation into plants and insects. Linnaeus's binomial system is the bookkeeping that makes all that local observation comparable — a botanist in Sweden and one in Brazil now share a vocabulary for the same plant.

ticks.name: Mendel's inheritance rules
ticks.constraint: heredity as a continuous blending of parental traits
ticks.detail: Gregor Mendel's pea plant experiments (1856-1863, published 1866) showed inheritance is particulate — traits come in discrete units that don't blend. Dominant and recessive. Ignored for 35 years, then recognized as the foundation of genetics. The gene as a concept was implicit in Mendel before anyone knew what DNA was.

links.label: Berkeley Evolution — Mendel: Discrete Genes Are Inherited
Nature Scitable — Mendel and the Principles of Inheritance

ticks.because: Crawford Long's first ether anesthesia (1842) and Morton's first public ether surgery (1846) had created surgical conditions where systematic data could be collected. Semmelweis's handwashing intervention (1847) demonstrated that controlled variable changes could transform mortality. Mendel's pea-plant experiments — published 1866, ignored for thirty-four years — apply the same systematic experimental discipline to inheritance. Discrete units transmitted in predictable ratios; modern genetics begins here.

ticks.name: Natural selection (Darwin/Wallace)
ticks.constraint: biological diversity requiring a designer
ticks.detail: Darwin and Wallace independently proposed that variation + selection + time = adaptation without any directing intelligence. Evolution by natural selection is the central organizing principle of all biology. It explained the distribution of species, the structure of anatomy, the fossil record — and eventually behavior, psychology, and medicine.

links.label: Darwin Online: Darwin & Wallace 1858 Linnean Society paper

ticks.because: Mendel's inheritance rules (1856) had quantified discrete biological variation. The Darwin-Wallace joint paper at the Linnean Society (1858) made the public claim. Natural selection as published in On the Origin (1859) is the synthesis — variation plus selection plus time produces adaptation, with no designer required. The theological worldview structuring Western biology collapses.

ticks.name: DNA discovered (Miescher)
ticks.constraint: cell nuclei as structurally uniform and functionally unknown
ticks.detail: Friedrich Miescher isolated an acidic substance from white blood cell nuclei in 1869 — what he called 'nuclein,' now known as DNA. He didn't know its function. It took 84 years (until 1953) to understand that this molecule carries hereditary information. The gap between discovery and understanding is one of science's longest.

links.label: NCBI PMC — Friedrich Miescher and the discovery of DNA

ticks.because: Lister's antiseptic technique (1867) and Pasteur's pasteurization (1864) had established germ theory and the methods to work with biological material safely. Mendel's laws of heredity (1866) showed that traits were inherited as discrete units. Darwin and Wallace's natural selection (1859) framed those units as the substrate of evolution. Miescher's isolation of nuclein from white blood cells is the first physical encounter with the substance that carries those Mendelian units — DNA, named eighty years before its function would be understood.

ticks.name: Germ theory extended to immune response (Metchnikoff)
ticks.constraint: immune defense as chemical and passive
ticks.detail: Élie Metchnikoff discovered phagocytosis — white blood cells actively engulfing and destroying bacteria. The immune system was not a wall but an army. Cellular immunology was born. Every vaccine, immunotherapy, and understanding of autoimmune disease builds on Metchnikoff's observation of a starfish larva eating a rose thorn.

links.label: Rosales & Uribe-Querol — Phagocytosis: A Fundamental Process in Immunity (PMC)

ticks.because: Mendel's laws of heredity (1866) had identified discrete units of biological inheritance; Miescher's discovery of DNA (1869) provided a candidate substance. Metchnikoff's recognition of phagocytic cells extends the biology one level out — the body has its own population of cells that hunt and consume invading microbes. Cellular immunology begins, and the concept of an active immune system replaces the picture of passive infection.

ticks.name: Rediscovery of Mendel / birth of genetics
ticks.constraint: hereditary mechanism as continuous and unknowable
ticks.detail: Three botanists (de Vries, Correns, Tschermak) independently rediscovered Mendel's 1866 paper in 1900. The science of genetics was officially born. Within a decade: chromosomes were identified as the physical carriers of Mendel's 'factors,' and the word 'gene' was coined. Genetics and evolution merged into the Modern Synthesis.

links.label: Natuurtijdschriften: The Hereditary Statistics of Hugo de Vries

ticks.because: Pasteur's rabies vaccine (1885), Röntgen's X-rays (1895), and Kraepelin's psychiatric classification (1899) demonstrated that nineteenth-century biological science was systematizing rapidly. The simultaneous rediscovery of Mendel's 1866 paper by de Vries, Correns, and Tschermak is the moment biology gets its missing inheritance theory — discrete units transmitted in predictable ratios. Genetics as a field starts in 1900.

ticks.name: Chromosomes as carriers of genes (Morgan)
ticks.constraint: genes as abstract units without physical location
ticks.detail: Thomas Hunt Morgan's Drosophila experiments showed that genes are carried on chromosomes and that linked genes are sometimes separated during reproduction (crossing over). The chromosome theory of heredity was established. Gene mapping became possible — you could know not just that a gene existed, but where it lived.

links.label: NCBI PMC — Morgan and the chromosome theory

ticks.because: The rediscovery of Mendel (1900) and ABO blood typing (1900) showed discrete biological inheritance was real and measurable. Cajal's neuron doctrine (1906) demonstrated cellular individuality at the structural level. Morgan's fruit fly experiments take the next step — genes are physical objects, located on specific chromosomes, with measurable distances between them. Genetics becomes a chromosomal science.

ticks.name: Mutation via X-rays (Muller)
ticks.constraint: genetic mutation as a random, uncontrollable event
ticks.detail: Hermann Muller showed that X-ray exposure dramatically increased the mutation rate in Drosophila. Mutations were physical events, caused by physical agents. This opened radiation genetics, the study of mutagens, and eventually the understanding that mutations cause cancer. Also: it alarmed the world about nuclear radiation's biological effects.

links.label: Muller — The Production of Mutations by X-Rays (PNAS 1928)
Encyclopedia.com — Hermann J. Muller and Induction of Genetic Mutations

ticks.because: The Flexner Report (1910), the Spanish flu (1918), and insulin (1921) had each professionalized medical science in different directions. Muller's X-ray-induced mutation work demonstrates that genes are physical objects vulnerable to physical agents — radiation alters heredity. Genetic toxicology and the therapeutic use of radiation both begin from this finding.

ticks.name: DNA as the genetic material (Avery et al.)
ticks.constraint: protein as the presumed carrier of genetic information
ticks.detail: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty showed that the 'transforming principle' — the substance that could permanently alter bacteria — was DNA, not protein. Most scientists didn't believe it. It took nine more years and Watson & Crick's structure to convince the field. The click was definitively identifying the molecule of heredity.

links.label: J Exp Med: Avery, MacLeod, McCarty 1944 paper

ticks.because: Blood banking (1940), the Rh factor (1940), and Muller's X-ray-induced mutations (1927) proved that biological inheritance was physical and molecular. Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty's upheaval experiments — purifying the substance that turns harmless pneumococcus into virulent strains — identify DNA as the genetic material. Hershey-Chase confirms in 1952; Watson-Crick give it structure in 1953.

ticks.name: Genetic code / protein synthesis (Crick's central dogma)
ticks.constraint: the mechanism connecting DNA to protein as unknown
ticks.detail: Crick's 'central dogma' (1958): DNA → RNA → Protein. Information flows one way. Sequences of DNA codons specify sequences of amino acids.
