Christianity's universal-salvation message — Paul's letters extending the Jewish covenant to Gentiles — gave Mediterranean monotheism its first explicitly trans-ethnic theology, and within three centuries became the religion of an empire that had previously been organized around blood and city.

ticks.name: Muhammad's first revelation / Quranic revelation
ticks.constraint: divine revelation as confined to a single people or tradition
ticks.detail: The Quran's claim to be the final, universal revelation — correcting and completing previous scriptures — produced a religion explicitly designed for all humanity. Islam's rapid spread was partly military, but also theological: a simple, memorizable creed (shahada), direct relationship with God (no clergy required), and a practical legal framework applicable anywhere.

links.label: Al-Islam — The Birth of Islam and Proclamation by Muhammad
Alim — Story of Muhammad's First Revelation

ticks.because: The compilation of the Babylonian Talmud (550) had just produced the most extensive rabbinic legal commentary, demonstrating that Abrahamic monotheism was producing rich textual traditions. The first Quranic revelation to Muhammad in 610 — at the cave of Hira — extended that monotheistic textual tradition into Arabic, and started the umma whose Hijra to Medina twelve years later would institutionalize Islam as a polity.

ticks.name: Magna Carta / rule of law over divine right
ticks.constraint: monarch's claim to rule by divine right as unchallenged
ticks.detail: Though Magna Carta is primarily a legal document, its assertion that even the king is subject to law challenged the theological foundation of medieval monarchy: the idea that kings ruled by divine appointment. The long-term implication was the secularization of political authority — legitimacy from law, not God.

links.label: UK National Archives: Magna Carta 1215 translation
Salisbury Cathedral: Magna Carta translation (British Library)

ticks.because: The Great Schism between Eastern and Western Christianity (1054) and the First Crusade's religiously justified war (1095) demonstrated that medieval European political authority operated through religious legitimation. Magna Carta in 1215 introduces the contrary principle — even the king is subject to law, with specific procedural rights for free persons. The constitutional tradition that runs through English common law, the US Constitution, and modern liberal democracy begins.

ticks.name: Luther's 95 Theses / Reformation
ticks.constraint: the Catholic Church's monopoly on Christian religious authority
ticks.detail: Luther's challenge to indulgences quickly became a challenge to papal authority itself — his 'sola scriptura' (scripture alone) principle bypassed the Church's interpretive monopoly entirely. The Reformation didn't just split Christianity; it created the concept of conscience against institution, individual against church, text against tradition.
ticks.because: The Wycliffe Bible (1380) had set the precedent of vernacular scripture defying Church monopoly on textual mediation. Gutenberg's press (1440) and movable type (1440) made mass-produced text reproducibly identical and therefore challengeable in detail. Luther's 95 Theses, posted to Wittenberg's church door and immediately printed across the German states, weaponize all three — vernacular argument, point-by-point dispute, mass distribution. The Reformation is the consequence.

ticks.name: Copernicus / religion confronts cosmology
ticks.constraint: Earth's central position as theological necessity
ticks.detail: De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium moved Earth from the center of creation. This wasn't primarily a religious crisis immediately — Copernicus was a canon of the Church — but Galileo's confirmation using the telescope forced the confrontation. The Galileo affair defined the relationship between religious authority and empirical science for centuries.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Nicolaus Copernicus

ticks.because: Luther's 95 Theses (1517), the Church of England's establishment (1534), and Henry VIII's Witchcraft Act (1541) demonstrated that religious authority was being contested and restructured. Copernicus's De Revolutionibus moves Earth from the center of creation — the cosmological challenge to theological structure. The Galileo affair eighty years later is the predictable consequence; modern cosmology and religious authority must thereafter coexist on different terms.

ticks.name: Galileo's trial / science vs. institutional religion
ticks.constraint: natural philosophy as subordinate to theological authority
ticks.detail: The Inquisition forced Galileo to recant heliocentrism. The trial defined the conflict between empirical inquiry and religious authority that would shape European intellectual history. Voltaire, the philosophes, and the Enlightenment assault on religious authority all referenced Galileo. The tick: institutional religion had staked its authority on a factual claim that was demonstrably wrong.

links.label: Ohio State HTI: Documents in the Case of Galileo (1633 indictment, sentence, abjuration) PDF
ETH Library Zurich: Galileo's trial virtual exhibition

ticks.because: Copernicus's heliocentric model (1543) had been published as 'mathematical hypothesis.' Galileo's telescopic observations of Jupiter's moons (1610) and the phases of Venus made heliocentrism observational. The Counter-Reformation Church, defending its authority over natural philosophy, forced Galileo to recant in 1633. The trial defined the conflict between empirical inquiry and institutional religion that would shape European intellectual history. The Enlightenment used Galileo as exhibit A.

ticks.name: Hobbes' Leviathan / secular political theory
ticks.constraint: political philosophy as requiring theological foundation
ticks.detail: Hobbes derived political authority from a purely secular basis: the social contract to escape the 'state of nature' (war of all against all). The sovereign's legitimacy came from its power to provide security, not from divine appointment. Secular political philosophy — politics analyzable without reference to God's will — begins here.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Thomas Hobbes

ticks.because: European political philosophy since Augustine had grounded political authority in divine appointment. The Wars of Religion (1517-1648) had discredited that grounding by killing a third of central Europe over which version of Christianity was authoritative. Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) derived political authority from a secular contract: people exit the state of nature (war of all against all) by agreeing to a sovereign whose legitimacy is its capacity to provide security. The first sustained secular political theory.

ticks.name: Spinoza's Tractatus / biblical criticism
ticks.constraint: sacred texts as literally true and divinely authored
ticks.detail: Spinoza argued that the Bible was a human document, authored by humans in particular historical contexts, and should be interpreted historically and critically. Higher biblical criticism — treating scripture as literature to be analyzed — begins here. Every subsequent liberal theology, every secular biblical scholarship tradition, follows Spinoza's method.
ticks.because: Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) had argued for a secular political theory. Spinoza's Tractatus Theologico-Politicus (1670) extended the move to scripture itself: the Bible was a human document, written by humans in particular historical contexts, and should be interpreted historically and critically. Higher biblical criticism begins here. Every liberal theology and every secular biblical scholarship since is downstream.

ticks.name: Newton's natural theology / God as first cause
ticks.constraint: science and religion as necessarily opposed
ticks.detail: Newton believed his physics revealed God's rational design of the universe. Natural theology — the attempt to find God through reason and observation — became the dominant mode of 18th-century religious thought. It persisted until Darwin made the argument from design untenable. The dialogue between natural science and religious thought that Newton initiated continues.
ticks.because: Hobbes's Leviathan (1651), Spinoza's Tractatus (1670), and Knorr von Rosenroth's Kabbala Denudata (1677) bracket the late-17th-century moment when European thought was wrestling with how to ground religious authority in an age of scientific revolution. Newton's natural theology — God as first cause, the lawful order of nature as evidence of divine wisdom — gave the Enlightenment a workable theological framework that did not require revelation to authorize science, and shaped Anglo-American religious thought for two centuries.

ticks.name: Kant's Critique of Pure Reason
ticks.constraint: metaphysics as capable of yielding knowledge of God, freedom, and immortality
ticks.detail: Kant argued that pure reason, unaided by experience, cannot establish knowledge of God, the soul, or free will — these lie beyond the bounds of possible experience. But he rescued them as postulates of practical reason (ethics). The critique ended rationalist metaphysics as Descartes and Leibniz had practiced it and defined the limits of human knowledge.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Kant's Critique of Pure Reason

ticks.because: Hume's problem of induction (1748) had thrown the foundations of empirical knowledge into question. Rousseau's social contract (1762) had built political theory on rational agency. Diderot's Encyclopédie (1751) had ambitiously systematized human knowledge. Crompton's spinning mule (1779) demonstrated that mechanical reasoning could industrialize craft. Kant's First Critique answers Hume — establishing the limits of what theoretical reason can know, and the synthetic a priori as the route through.

ticks.name: French Revolution / dechristianization
ticks.constraint: Christianity as Europe's default civic religion
ticks.detail: The Revolution's radical phase attempted to replace Christianity with the Cult of Reason and then the Cult of the Supreme Being — rational, deistic alternatives to Catholicism. It failed, but it established secularism — the separation of religious and civic life — as a political possibility. France's laïcité principle traces directly to 1789.

links.label: A People's History of the French Revolution — Dechristianization
Alpha History — The Cult of the Supreme Being
Encyclopedia.com — Cult of the Goddess of Reason

ticks.because: L'Épée's school for sign language (1755) and Johnson's Dictionary (1755) demonstrated that linguistic and educational authority could be vested in secular institutions. The Revolutionary cult of Reason and the Cult of the Supreme Being — the deliberate replacement of Catholic worship with civic festival — was the first programmatic attempt to remove Christianity as Europe's default civic religion, and seeded modern secularist politics.

ticks.name: Baha'i faith / religious universalism
ticks.constraint: each major religion's claim to exclusive final truth
ticks.detail: The Bab's 1844 declaration began what became the Baha'i faith — the belief that all major religions are successive revelations of one God, that humanity is one, and that their unification is both possible and necessary. A tick in religious evolution: a new religion explicitly premised on the unity of all previous ones.

links.label: U-M Provost: Declaration of the Báb 1844 (PDF)
Baha'i Library: Declaration of the Bab — survey of sources

ticks.because: The Enlightenment had argued that reason was universal. Religious revival movements (Methodism, Mormonism) showed religion could be remade. The Bab's declaration in Persia in 1844 began what became the Baha'i Faith — the belief that all major religions are successive revelations of one God, that humanity is one, and that their unification is both possible and necessary. The first major religion explicitly premised on the unity of all previous ones.

ticks.name: Darwin / evolution and the argument from design
ticks.constraint: biological complexity as requiring an intelligent designer
ticks.detail: Natural selection provided a mechanism for producing complexity without design. The argument from design — Paley's watchmaker — was the most powerful argument for God's existence in the 18th and 19th centuries. Darwin didn't disprove God, but he removed the need for God as an explanation for biological complexity. Theology has been negotiating this ever since.
ticks.because: Roget's Thesaurus (1852), the Baha'i faith (1844), Millerite apocalyptic disappointment (1844), and Mormon migration (1846) bracket a mid-19th-century moment of religious diversification and reorganization. Darwin's Origin of Species — published the same year as the Council of Trent's Catholic doctrinal counter-reform was being re-litigated by Vatican I — challenged the design argument by providing a non-teleological mechanism for biological complexity, and reordered Western theology for the next century.

ticks.name: Nietzsche / death of God
ticks.constraint: Western culture's ability to ground meaning and morality in Christianity
ticks.detail: 'God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him.' Nietzsche's madman announced not atheism but a civilizational crisis: Western culture had built its moral order on Christianity, and now that the intellectual foundations of Christianity had collapsed, what would replace it? His diagnosis: nihilism, and his prescription: the revaluation of all values. Still the central challenge of secular ethics.

links.label: ThoughtCo — What Does Nietzsche Mean: God Is Dead
Buffalo (Acsu) — Nietzsche's Psychology of Morality and Religion

ticks.because: Mill's Subjection of Women (1869) and Cantor's set theory (1874) showed that fundamental categories were open to systematic challenge. Peirce's pragmatic maxim (1878) put truth in terms of consequences. Frege's Begriffsschrift (1879) made logic a formal calculus. Nietzsche extends the dismantling to the deepest cultural infrastructure — God as the metaphysical assumption underwriting Western morality is dead, and the question becomes how to live without that prop.

ticks.name: Weber's Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
ticks.constraint: capitalism as explicable purely by material conditions
ticks.detail: Max Weber argued that Calvinist Protestantism — particularly the doctrine of predestination and the resulting compulsion to demonstrate one's salvation through worldly success — created the psychological conditions for modern capitalism. Ideas, not just economic forces, shape economic systems. The sociology of religion and economic sociology were both transformed.

links.label: Wikisource: Weber, The Protestant Ethic and Spirit of Capitalism
Internet Archive: Protestant Ethic full text (Parsons trans.)

ticks.because: Nietzsche's death of God (1882) had questioned Western metaphysics. Husserl's phenomenology (1900) and James's defense of faith (1896) had each addressed the nature of religious experience. Weber's argument — that Calvinist predestination, by making earthly success a sign of divine election, generated the disciplined work ethic that made capitalism possible — applies sociological reasoning to economic history. Modern sociology of religion begins.

ticks.name: Wittgenstein's Tractatus / limits of language
ticks.constraint: philosophy as capable of answering all meaningful questions through logic
ticks.detail: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.' Wittgenstein argued that most traditional philosophical problems arise from misuse of language — trying to say things that can only be shown. The Tractatus defined the limits of what language can express. It launched logical positivism and the analytic tradition, then Wittgenstein repudiated it in the Investigations.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Ludwig Wittgenstein

ticks.because: Husserl's phenomenology (1900) and Weber's Protestant Ethic (1905) demonstrated that twentieth-century philosophy was capable of systematic, ambitious projects. The Tractatus's limits-of-language argument — meaningful propositions are pictures of facts, ethical and metaphysical claims are nonsensical — is the early Wittgenstein's most ambitious. The limit-finding move shapes analytic philosophy for the next half-century.

ticks.name: Heidegger's Being and Time
ticks.constraint: philosophy as primarily about knowledge and representation
ticks.detail: Heidegger argued that the fundamental question is not 'what can we know?' but 'what is Being?' — and that Dasein (human existence) is characterized by its being-in-the-world, temporality, and being-toward-death. Existentialism, phenomenology, hermeneutics, and poststructuralism all draw from Heidegger. Also: his Nazi involvement remains philosophy's central ethical scandal.

links.label: Project MUSE — Heidegger History of the Concept of Time (Marburg 1925)

ticks.because: Wittgenstein's Tractatus on the limits of language and logical atomism (1921) had pushed analytic philosophy toward formal precision. Heidegger's Being and Time (1927) goes the opposite direction — the fundamental question is not what we can know but what it is to be, with Dasein's structures of care, being-toward-death, and historicity as the philosophical answer. The continental-analytic split crystallizes here.

ticks.name: Sartre's Being and Nothingness / radical freedom
ticks.constraint: human nature as fixed and essence-giving
ticks.detail: 'Existence precedes essence' — humans have no fixed nature; we are what we make ourselves through free choices. Radical freedom, radical responsibility, and the anguish of having to choose without guaranteed foundations. Existentialism's popular explosion in postwar France captured a generation's response to the war's moral catastrophe.

links.label: WorldCat: Being and Nothingness (Sartre 1943, English ed.)
Internet Archive: Being and Nothingness (Sartre, Barnes trans.)

ticks.because: Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) had shown that formal systems could not be both complete and consistent. Logical positivism's Vienna Circle (1936) had insisted that meaningful claims must be empirically testable. Sartre extends both threads existentially — consciousness is condemned to freedom, no essence precedes existence, and meaning must be produced rather than discovered. The cornerstone of postwar existentialism.

ticks.name: Vatican II / Catholic Church's modernization
ticks.constraint: the Catholic Church's stance toward modernity as primarily hostile
ticks.detail: Vatican II's aggiornamento ('bringing up to date') reversed centuries of Catholic suspicion of liberalism, science, and religious pluralism. Mass was said in vernacular languages; the Church acknowledged truth in other religions; ecumenism replaced condemnation. The largest institutional reform in Christian history. Its interpretation continues to divide the Church.

links.label: Vatican — Documents of the Second Vatican Council
Wikipedia: Vatican II / Catholic Church's modernization

ticks.because: The Holocaust (1945) and the decolonization wave (1960) forced every European institution to reckon with its complicity. John XXIII opened Vatican II in 1962 to bring the Catholic Church 'up to date.' Mass switched to vernacular languages. The Church acknowledged truth in other religions. Ecumenism replaced condemnation. The largest institutional reform in Christian history — and the source of nearly every conservative-progressive Catholic argument since.

ticks.name: Rawls' Theory of Justice
ticks.constraint: political philosophy as either utilitarian or natural rights based
ticks.detail: John Rawls revived social contract theory with the 'veil of ignorance' — principles of justice are those we would choose if we didn't know our place in society. The difference principle (inequalities are just only if they benefit the worst-off) provided a rigorous liberal egalitarian framework. Every subsequent political philosophy debate takes Rawls as its starting point.

links.label: De Gruyter — A Theory of Justice (Rawls 1971, front matter)
Harvard University Press — A Theory of Justice
Harvard — A Theory of Justice (sample PDF)

ticks.because: Derrida's deconstruction (1967) had shown that texts contained internal contradictions readable from multiple angles. Davidson's anomalous monism (1970) proved that reasoning could span mental and physical levels without reducing one to the other. Rawls applied both moves to political philosophy — designing the veil of ignorance as a procedural device that resolves contradictions inside justice itself, by selecting principles from a position that cannot favor anyone.

ticks.name: Singer's Animal Liberation / effective altruism roots
ticks.constraint: moral consideration as limited to humans
ticks.detail: Peter Singer's utilitarian argument that suffering capacity, not species membership, determines moral status launched the modern animal rights movement. Also: his later work on effective altruism (give to maximize impact, not to feel good) created a movement that has redirected billions in charitable giving. Both strands trace to the same utilitarian premise.

links.label: Utilitarian.org: Singer, The Animal Liberation Movement

ticks.because: Derrida's deconstruction (1967), Rawls's Theory of Justice (1971), and Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment (1973) had each pushed analytic philosophy in fundamentally challenging directions. Singer's utilitarian argument — that suffering capacity, not species membership, is what matters morally — extends the same questioning to ethics across species. Animal welfare becomes a serious philosophical position; effective altruism's roots are here.

ticks.name: Rice domestication (Yangtze Valley)
ticks.constraint: East Asian food security as dependent on millet and tubers
ticks.detail: Rice domestication in China's Yangtze Valley began around 7000 BC and spread across Asia over millennia. Wet rice agriculture fed densities of population that no other grain could sustain — enabling East Asian civilizational complexity. Today rice feeds half the world's people. The domestication of rice was as consequential for Asia as wheat was for the Near East.

links.label: Fuller et al. — Presumed domestication: wild rice cultivation Lower Yangtze (Cambridge Antiquity)
Multiple indicators of rice remains and rice domestication (PLOS One)
Innes et al. — Exploration of early rice farming in China (ScienceDirect)

ticks.because: Cattle domestication (7500 BC) proved that one species could be selectively bred over generations to multiply its agricultural yield. Rice in the Yangtze applied the same patience to a grass — wet-paddy cultivation feeds densities of population that no other staple can sustain, and Asian civilization's complexity is built on that yield curve.

ticks.name: Plow agriculture
ticks.constraint: soil turning as requiring intensive human or hand labor
ticks.detail: The ard (scratch plow) and later the moldboard plow allowed draft animals to break and turn soil far more efficiently than human hands. Arable land area expanded. Larger fields could be cultivated by fewer people, releasing labor for specialization. The agricultural surplus that built cities depended on the plow.

links.label: ExplainThat: When Was the Plow Invented in Mesopotamia?

ticks.because: Cattle domestication (7500 BC) gave humans muscle for labor; rice domestication (7000 BC) and grain storage pits (3900 BC) showed surplus could be accumulated; sourdough leavening (3700 BC) demonstrated that food technology could be refined. The plow is the use device — drawn by an ox, it turns soil at an order of magnitude greater area. Agricultural surplus per worker explodes, and city civilization becomes possible.

ticks.name: Three-field crop rotation (Medieval Europe)
ticks.constraint: annual soil exhaustion requiring fallow of 50% of arable land
ticks.detail: Medieval European farmers developed the three-field system: one field planted in autumn, one in spring, one left fallow — rotating annually. Fallow dropped from 50% to 33% of land. The additional field produced legumes (beans, peas) that fixed nitrogen. Agricultural output increased 30-50%. Population grew. European civilization's medieval expansion was built on this rotation.
ticks.because: The bronze-tipped plow (2500 BC) and ancient Mediterranean crop rotation (600 BC) gave medieval Europe both the tools and the precedent. The horse collar (900 AD) and the panemone windmill (900 AD) added the energy. Three-field rotation cut fallow from 50% to 33% — winter grain, spring grain, fallow — increasing arable output by ~50% and supporting the population growth that built medieval cities and the High Middle Ages economy.

ticks.name: Potato introduction to Europe
ticks.constraint: European caloric yield per acre as limited by grain crops
ticks.detail: The potato, domesticated in the Andes 8,000 years ago, arrived in Europe in the 1590s. It produces more calories per acre than any grain, grows in poor soil, and resists many diseases. By 1800 it was feeding Ireland, Germany, and much of Northern Europe. The European population explosion of 1750-1850 was substantially a potato story. The 1845 Irish famine shows its vulnerability.

links.label: Library and Archives Canada — Potato Migration to Europe
Hawkes & Francisco-Ortega — Early history of potato in Europe (Springer)
Smithsonian — How the Potato Changed the World

ticks.because: Three-field rotation (1000), the Columbian Exchange (1492), Norfolk four-course rotation (1500), and the Spanish introduction of tomato (1501) bracket the agricultural revolutions framing European food systems before, during, and after the Columbian Exchange. The potato — domesticated in the Andes 7,000 years ago, brought to Europe by Spanish ships — provided 2-4× the calories per acre of European grain, supported the population growth that fueled industrialization, and (when blighted in 1845-49) caused the Irish famine that killed a million.

ticks.name: Maize / corn global spread
ticks.constraint: African, Asian, and Southern European grain options as the only staple choices
ticks.detail: Maize (corn), domesticated in Mexico ~9,000 years ago, spread globally after Columbus. In Africa, it fed populations that sorghum and millet couldn't sustain as densely. In China, it allowed cultivation of hill country previously unusable. The caloric floor of much of sub-Saharan Africa and Southern China was raised by maize. Also: US industrial corn is now a global food system commodity.

links.label: DPLA: The Columbian Exchange primary source set
ebrary: Corn and the Columbian Exchange

ticks.because: Yemeni coffee cultivation (1450) demonstrated that a New World — or in coffee's case, an African — staple crop could rewrite Eurasian commerce. Maize, brought back by Spanish explorers, spread through Africa, southern Europe, and Asia within a century — its triple-crop tolerance and high yields per hectare added a new staple that supported population growth in regions where previous grains had ceiling yields.

ticks.name: Chemical fertilizer (Liebig's mineral theory)
ticks.constraint: soil fertility as a mystical property requiring organic matter
ticks.detail: Justus von Liebig identified nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium as the specific mineral nutrients plants require. Plants don't need 'humus' — they need specific chemicals. This led directly to the synthetic fertilizer industry and the Haber-Bosch process. Liebig's mistake (he undervalued organic matter) created a century of soil degradation, but his insight fed billions.
ticks.because: Pre-Liebig agriculture treated soil as inherited fertility — depletable but not analyzable. Liebig's 1840 mineral theory of plant nutrition identified nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium as the chemical essentials. Wöhler's synthesis of urea (1828) had already shown that organic-seeming molecules could be made inorganically. The combination meant fertilizer could be manufactured. Half the people alive eat because of nitrogen later extracted from air by the Haber-Bosch process.

ticks.name: Refrigeration / cold chain
ticks.constraint: food distribution range limited by spoilage time
ticks.detail: Mechanical refrigeration (Linde's ice machine, 1876) and refrigerated rail cars transformed food geography. Beef from Chicago could reach New York; Argentine beef could reach London. The cold chain decoupled food production from consumption geography. Urban populations could be fed from distant farms. Industrial food systems — and industrial-scale livestock — became possible.

links.label: Smithsonian — Keeping your food cool: ice harvesting to refrigeration
NC State Extension — Review of Refrigeration

ticks.because: The guano trade (1840), Lawes's superphosphate (1843), Mendel's inheritance work (1856), and Darwin's Origin (1859) bracket a mid-19th-century moment when agriculture and biology were both becoming industrialized sciences. Mechanical refrigeration — first commercialized in slaughterhouses and breweries — extended food shelf life from days to weeks, and made the geography of food production independent of the geography of consumption.

ticks.name: Pasteurization of milk
ticks.constraint: milk as a vector for tuberculosis, typhoid, and scarlet fever
ticks.detail: Louis Pasteur's heating method, applied to milk in the 1880s and mandated in New York City in 1908, eliminated milk-borne disease. Infant mortality dropped dramatically. Pasteurization is estimated to have saved more lives than almost any other public health intervention. It also enabled commercial dairy — milk that could be shipped, stored, and sold safely.

links.label: Project Gutenberg: The Story of Milk (Frederiksen, pasteurization chapter)

ticks.because: Pasteur's germ theory (1864) had identified microbes as the cause of disease. Refrigeration (1870s) had made milk transportable. Pasteur's heating method, applied to milk in the 1880s and mandated in New York City in 1908, eliminated milk-borne tuberculosis, typhoid, and scarlet fever. Infant mortality dropped sharply. Pasteurization probably saved more lives than any other public-health intervention. It also enabled commercial dairy at scale.

ticks.name: DNA double helix (Watson, Crick, Franklin)
ticks.constraint: inheritance as a structural mystery
ticks.detail: The 1953 paper by Watson and Crick — built on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography (Photo 51) and Maurice Wilkins's data — proposed the DNA double helix structure. The model immediately revealed how genetic information is stored (sequence of bases), how it can be copied (complementary strands separating), and how it could mutate. The substrate of all subsequent molecular biology, biotechnology, and genomics.

links.label: Watson & Crick — Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids (Nature 1953)
Nature — The structure of DNA (2019 retrospective)

ticks.because: Mendel's pea-plant inheritance (1866) had been rediscovered around 1900. Avery's transforming principle (1944) showed DNA was the genetic material. Watson and Crick's 1953 paper, built on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography (Photo 51) and Maurice Wilkins's data, gave DNA its double-helix structure. The model immediately revealed how genetic information is stored, copied, and varied. Recombinant DNA (1973) and CRISPR (2012) follow.

ticks.name: Recombinant DNA (Cohen-Boyer)
ticks.constraint: genes confined to the species that carries them
ticks.detail: In 1973 Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer demonstrated recombinant DNA: cutting a specific gene from one organism and splicing it into a plasmid that could replicate in another (E. coli). The technique founded the biotechnology industry — within five years, recombinant insulin and human growth hormone were in clinical use; within fifteen, the first transgenic crops; within thirty, CRISPR's predecessors. The first time DNA could be edited as a substrate.

links.label: PNAS: Cohen, Boyer et al, Construction of Biologically Functional Bacterial Plasmids in Vitro (1973)

ticks.because: DDT-era pesticides (1942), the DNA double helix (1953), and Crick's central dogma (1953) gave biology both molecular structure and large-scale agricultural manipulation. The recombinant DNA techniques developed in the 1970s gave plant biologists tools to introduce genes across species barriers — Bt toxin into corn and cotton, herbicide resistance into soy — and started the GM-crops industry that now covers ~190 million hectares globally.

ticks.name: Flavr Savr tomato / first GM food approved
ticks.constraint: crop traits as bounded by sexual compatibility between species
ticks.detail: The Flavr Savr tomato, engineered with a gene silencing the softening enzyme, was the first GM food approved for human consumption (1994). It was a commercial failure but established the regulatory and cultural precedents for all subsequent GM food approvals. The 'frankenfoods' debate it triggered still shapes agricultural policy worldwide.

links.label: Wikipedia: Flavr Savr tomato / first GM food approved
Google Scholar: Flavr Savr tomato / first GM food approved

ticks.because: Cohen-Boyer recombinant DNA (1973), Sanger sequencing (1977), PCR (1983), and monoclonal antibodies (1984) had built the molecular toolkit. Calgene's Flavr Savr — engineered to suppress polygalacturonase and slow softening — was the first whole genetically-modified food approved for consumer sale (FDA 1994), and opened the regulatory and commercial precedent for every later GM crop.

ticks.name: Vertical farming / LED-lit indoor agriculture
ticks.constraint: agriculture as dependent on weather, soil, and geography
ticks.detail: LED technology made artificial lighting economically feasible for crop production. Vertical farms grow leafy greens in controlled indoor environments, using 90% less water, no pesticides, and with 365-day production regardless of climate. While still niche, vertical farming decoupled food production from land and weather for the first time in 10,000 years of agriculture.

links.label: WIRED — First Vertical Farm Opens in Singapore (2012)
New Statesman — First vertical farm opens in Singapore
Impact Lab — Singapore opens world's first commercial vertical farm

ticks.because: Cheap white-light LEDs hit commercial pricing around 2010. Precision agriculture (1994) had shown that farming could be data-driven. Vertical farms put both inside a warehouse: leafy greens grown in stacked trays under tuned spectra, with 90% less water and no pesticides. Agriculture decoupled from weather and soil for the first time in 10,000 years.

ticks.name: Lab-grown meat (first cultured beef burger)
ticks.constraint: meat production as requiring the slaughter of animals
ticks.detail: Mark Post's team grew the first cultured beef burger from bovine stem cells at Maastricht University in 2013. It cost $300,000. By 2023, cultured chicken was approved for sale in the US. If costs continue to fall, lab-grown meat could eliminate the need for industrial livestock farming — currently responsible for ~15% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

links.label: BBC News: World's first lab-grown burger eaten in London (Aug 2013)
Scientific American: Test-Tube Burger taste test

ticks.because: Tissue engineering had been used in medical research since the 1990s. Mark Post's team at Maastricht grew the first cultured beef burger from bovine stem cells in 2013. It cost $300,000. By 2023, cultured chicken was approved for sale in Singapore and the US. If costs fall further, cultured meat could remove the need for industrial livestock farming — currently responsible for roughly 15% of global greenhouse emissions and most of the world's antibiotic use.

ticks.name: AI-optimized precision agriculture
ticks.constraint: fertilizer and pesticide application as uniform across entire fields
ticks.detail: Satellite imagery, soil sensors, drone scouting, and AI analysis now enable application of inputs exactly where needed at the right time. John Deere's See & Spray system applies herbicide to individual weeds rather than entire fields, reducing chemical use by 90%. Precision agriculture makes large-scale farming far more efficient while reducing environmental impact.
ticks.because: Precision agriculture (1994) used GPS to vary input rates within a field. Computer vision (2012-2020) made plant-level identification possible. AI-optimized precision agriculture combines them: drones scout fields, AI identifies individual weeds and diseased plants, sprayers apply herbicide only where needed. John Deere's See & Spray cuts herbicide use by 90%. The first time agricultural inputs are applied at plant resolution rather than field resolution.

ticks.name: Division of labor (Adam Smith's pin factory)
ticks.constraint: manufacturing efficiency as limited by each worker doing the whole task
ticks.detail: Smith's famous pin factory example showed that dividing production into specialized steps — one worker draws wire, another straightens it, another cuts it — raised productivity by a factor of 240. Specialization and the division of labor are the fundamental mechanisms of industrial productivity. Every factory, every supply chain, every gig economy platform implements this insight.

links.label: Adam Smith Works: Of the Division of Labour (Chapter I)
Harvard Classics 365: Pins and Other Points

ticks.because: Cantillon's Essay (1755) had introduced the price mechanism as a coordinating force, and Physiocracy (1756) framed economic activity as natural circulation. Smith's pin-factory illustration in The Wealth of Nations made the productivity dividend of specialization concrete — one worker producing 4,800 pins per day instead of 20 — and gave the Industrial Revolution its theoretical justification.

ticks.name: Ricardo's comparative advantage
ticks.constraint: international trade as beneficial only to the country with absolute cost advantage
ticks.detail: David Ricardo showed that even if one country can produce everything more cheaply, both countries benefit from specializing in what they're relatively better at and trading. Comparative advantage is the theoretical foundation for free trade, globalization, and WTO rules. It's also the most counterintuitive idea in economics — most people still don't believe it.

links.label: Econlib: A Brief History of Comparative Advantage
Econlib: Ricardo — On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817)
Springer: Ricardo's Chapter VII On Foreign Trade (reprint)

ticks.because: The Buttonwood Agreement (1792), the Corn Laws debate (1815), and Luddite machine-breaking (1811) demonstrated that early-nineteenth-century economic life was structurally reorganizing. Ricardo's comparative-advantage theorem proves that international trade benefits both parties even when one is more productive in everything. The intellectual foundation for free-trade economics and globalization arguments to follow.

ticks.name: Marginal revolution (Jevons/Menger/Walras)
ticks.constraint: value as determined by labor input (classical economics)
ticks.detail: Simultaneously in Britain, Austria, and France in 1871, economists independently proposed that value is determined by marginal utility — the value of the last unit consumed, not the average labor embedded. The diamond-water paradox was solved. Microeconomics as we know it — supply and demand, price theory, optimization — begins here.

links.label: Taylor & Francis: First-generation marginalists (Jevons, Walras, Menger)
JSTOR: History of Marginal Utility Theory

ticks.because: Marx's Das Kapital (1867) had crystallized the labor theory of value, and the synthetic dye industry (1856) plus the stock ticker (1867) showed that economies were becoming networks where the marginal unit mattered more than the average. Jevons, Menger, and Walras — independently in three countries in 1871 — replaced labor cost with marginal utility as the source of value, founding modern microeconomics.

ticks.name: Keynes' General Theory / macroeconomics born
ticks.constraint: economics as solely microeconomic, with macro 'the sum of micro'
ticks.detail: Keynes created macroeconomics as a distinct field — the study of aggregate demand, national income, unemployment, and the business cycle. His insight: the economy can get stuck in a bad equilibrium (high unemployment, low output) that market forces alone won't fix. Government fiscal policy is the cure. Macroeconomics, the IMF, and every government's economic policy team are Keynes' legacy.

links.label: Wikipedia: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
CEPR/VoxEU: Macroeconomic paradigm shifts and Keynes's General Theory

ticks.because: The SEC's establishment (1934) had restructured securities markets after the 1929 crash, and the Depression's persistence had broken the classical assumption that markets always clear. Keynes's General Theory argued that aggregate demand — not just supply-side adjustment — drove employment, and that fiscal policy could close output gaps. Macroeconomics emerged as a distinct discipline from this argument.

ticks.name: Hayek's Road to Serfdom / price mechanism
ticks.constraint: central planning as a viable alternative to markets for resource allocation
ticks.detail: Hayek argued that no central authority can aggregate the dispersed, local knowledge needed for efficient resource allocation — prices do this automatically. Central planning inevitably leads to political authoritarianism. The neoliberal movement (Thatcher, Reagan) drew on Hayek. His debate with Keynes defined 20th-century economic policy.

links.label: University of Chicago Press: Publication History of The Road to Serfdom
Duke University: Caldwell — Editor's Intro to Road to Serfdom (PDF)

ticks.because: Keynes's General Theory (1936) had argued that aggregate demand management was the proper macroeconomic lever. The Bretton Woods Agreement (1944) was being negotiated as Hayek wrote — international monetary architecture built on the assumption of activist state coordination. Hayek's Road to Serfdom is the contrary case — central planning, however well-intentioned, leads to authoritarianism, and the price mechanism is irreplaceable as a coordination device.

ticks.name: Arrow-Debreu model / general equilibrium
ticks.constraint: competitive markets' efficiency as an empirical claim rather than proved theorem
ticks.detail: Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu rigorously proved the conditions under which competitive markets reach an efficient equilibrium. The proof was also a diagnosis of when markets fail: public goods, externalities, information asymmetries. Modern market failure theory, and the justification for government intervention in markets, builds on Arrow-Debreu.

links.label: Econometric Society: Arrow & Debreu, Existence of Equilibrium for a Competitive Economy (1954)
JSTOR: Existence of an Equilibrium for a Competitive Economy

ticks.because: By 1954 the postwar economy was a globally-coordinated system: Marshall Plan reconstruction, UN sovereign-equality treaties, the first nuclear electricity, UNIVAC commercial computing, Diners Club consumer credit. Arrow and Debreu's existence proof gave that system its mathematical foundation — a guarantee that competitive markets could clear, and a precise statement of when and how they fail (public goods, externalities, asymmetric information).

ticks.name: Phillips curve / inflation-unemployment tradeoff
ticks.constraint: inflation and unemployment as independent policy variables
ticks.detail: A.W. Phillips found an empirical inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. Policymakers thought they could choose a point on the curve. Friedman and Phelps showed (1968) the long-run curve is vertical — you can't permanently trade inflation for lower unemployment. The stagflation of the 1970s validated Friedman and ended Keynesian consensus.

links.label: Wiley: Phillips, The Relation Between Unemployment and Money Wage Rates UK 1861-1957 (Economica 1958)
NZAE: The History of the Phillips Curve (Gordon, PDF)

ticks.because: First nuclear electricity generation (1951) and the Arrow-Debreu model (1954) gave postwar economics both the energy substrate and the formal general-equilibrium framework. A. W. Phillips's empirical paper plotted UK wage inflation against unemployment over 1861-1957 and found a stable inverse relationship — and policy economics for the next two decades treated the curve as a menu of tradeoffs, until 1970s stagflation broke the assumption.

ticks.name: Modigliani-Miller theorem / capital structure irrelevance
ticks.constraint: corporate capital structure (debt vs. equity mix) as a key value driver
ticks.detail: Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller proved that in perfect markets, a company's value is independent of how it finances itself. Real-world deviations from their assumptions (taxes, bankruptcy costs, information asymmetry) explain actual capital structure choices. Every corporate finance decision since — buybacks, leverage, dividend policy — is analyzed against MM as a benchmark.

links.label: JSTOR: Modigliani & Miller, The Cost of Capital, Corporation Finance and the Theory of Investment (AER 1958)
AEA JEP: The Modigliani-Miller Propositions after Thirty Years (Miller, 1988)

ticks.because: The Phillips curve (1958), the European Economic Community (1958), and the Perceptron (1958) demonstrated that the era's intellectual production was simultaneously sophisticating economics, politics, and computing. The Modigliani-Miller theorem proves that in perfect markets a company's capital structure (debt vs equity ratio) doesn't affect its value. Modern corporate finance begins from this paradoxical result, working backwards from the deviations from MM assumptions.

ticks.name: Market for lemons / information asymmetry (Akerlof)
ticks.constraint: markets as efficiently pricing quality when buyer and seller information differ
ticks.detail: George Akerlof's 'Market for Lemons' showed that when sellers know more than buyers about product quality, markets can collapse — buyers assume average quality, sellers with above-average products withdraw, quality falls, until only lemons remain. This explained used car markets, health insurance, and credit markets. Information economics, signaling theory, and market design all follow.

links.label: Oxford QJE: Akerlof, The Market for Lemons (1970)
UCLA: Akerlof's Market for Lemons original paper
The Economist: Secrets and Agents (Akerlof's 1970 paper)

ticks.because: The European Economic Community (1958) and the Modigliani-Miller theorem (1958) gave economics empirical and theoretical grounding for postwar markets. Kilby and Noyce's integrated circuit (1961) and Spacewar! (1962) demonstrated that information could be embodied at scale. Akerlof's lemons paper formalizes the consequence — when buyers and sellers have different information, markets break in characteristic ways. Information asymmetry becomes a first-class economic concept.

ticks.name: Black-Scholes / financial derivatives explosion
ticks.constraint: options pricing as requiring dealer intuition rather than mathematical formula
ticks.detail: The Black-Scholes-Merton formula priced options using only the current price, strike price, time to expiration, volatility, and interest rate. The derivatives market grew from $1 trillion to $1 quadrillion in notional value in 30 years. Also: the formula's assumption of continuous trading and normally distributed returns contributed to the 2008 financial crisis.

links.label: JSTOR: Black & Scholes, The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities (JPE 1973)
EconPapers: The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities

ticks.because: The Nixon shock (1971) and OPEC oil embargo (1973) had introduced systemic market volatility unimaginable under Bretton Woods. Email (1971) and the Intel 4004 microprocessor (1971) gave finance the communication and compute substrate. Black-Scholes is the formula that makes options pricing tractable — the derivative markets that grow on this equation now exceed the underlying world economy by an order of magnitude.

ticks.name: Amazon.com / e-commerce and platform economics
ticks.constraint: retail transactions as requiring physical co-presence of buyer and seller
ticks.detail: Jeff Bezos started Amazon as an online bookstore in 1994. Within a decade it was everything. The click: e-commerce eliminated physical retail's geographic constraint. Long-tail economics (Chris Anderson) — the ability to stock and sell items that no physical store could afford to carry — restructured retail, publishing, music, and eventually every industry.

links.label: History.com: Amazon is founded by Jeff Bezos (July 5, 1994)

ticks.because: The Web (1993) had created the substrate for direct-to-consumer commerce. Akerlof's market for lemons (1970) had identified information asymmetry as the central market problem. The Washington Consensus (1989) had pushed economic liberalization globally. Linux (1991) demonstrated that open-source platforms could outcompete proprietary alternatives. Amazon combines all four — online catalog, reputation systems addressing lemons, global reach, and a platform business model that extends beyond books.

ticks.name: 2008 financial crisis / too-big-to-fail
ticks.constraint: systemic financial risk as manageable through market discipline alone
ticks.detail: The collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered a global financial crisis that required unprecedented government bailouts. The tick: financial institutions had become so interconnected and large that their failure threatened the entire system — moral hazard at civilizational scale. Dodd-Frank, Basel III, and the entire post-crisis regulatory architecture responded to this.

links.label: Yale: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission report excerpt

ticks.because: Glass-Steagall's 1999 repeal had let commercial banks combine with investment banks. Securitization had moved mortgage risk off balance sheets, then back on. Lehman's collapse (September 2008) revealed counterparty interconnection: any major bank's failure could pull down the system. Bailouts kept the financial system intact and exposed its political economy: the largest firms were too big to fail, and that knowledge made future risk-taking cheaper for them. The Dodd-Frank Act (2010) and global Basel III rules followed.

ticks.name: First illustrated book (printed woodcuts)
ticks.constraint: illustrations in books as requiring individual hand copying
ticks.detail: The first books with printed woodcut illustrations (the Pfister Bible, ~1462) demonstrated that images could be mass-produced alongside text. Illustrated books transformed the transmission of scientific, botanical, anatomical, and geographical knowledge. Without printed images, Vesalius's anatomy, Fuchs's herbals, and Dürer's art prints couldn't have spread.

links.label: Library of Congress — Gutenberg Bible Resource Guide
University of Manchester — Early European Print

ticks.because: Gutenberg's printing press (1440) and movable type (1440) had made text reproducible and identical. The Gutenberg Bible (1455) demonstrated mass production at scale. Printed woodcuts integrated into the Pfister Bible mark the next visual leap — typography and illustration on the same press, in the same edition. Modern book design begins.

ticks.name: Michelangelo's David / figural perfection
ticks.constraint: sculpture as constrained by available stone and religious subject
ticks.detail: David was carved from a single block of marble that had been considered unusable since 1463. Michelangelo's technical achievement — and his choice of the moment before action rather than the moment of triumph — redefined what sculpture could do. The nude male figure as an expression of humanist ideals rather than divine subject was the tick.

links.label: Britannica Story: How a Rejected Block of Marble Became David
Ringling Docents: Vasari on Michelangelo's David (1550)

ticks.because: Brunelleschi's Florentine dome (1420) had set the architectural standard. The first illustrated printed book (1461) made visual representation reproducible. The first printed Vitruvius (1486) gave Renaissance artists ancient architectural theory in modern circulation. Michelangelo's David — carved from a block deemed unusable, completed in 1504 — synthesizes anatomical study, classical proportion, and political symbolism. Renaissance figurative sculpture reaches its peak.

ticks.name: Dürer's woodcuts / printed art mass distribution
ticks.constraint: fine art as available only to those who could visit it
ticks.detail: Albrecht Dürer's mastery of woodcut and engraving printing allowed his works to circulate across Europe in editions of hundreds. The same image could be owned by a merchant in Antwerp and a scholar in Nuremberg. Printed art created an audience for visual culture that stretched far beyond the wealthy patron class. The art market as we know it begins here.

links.label: National Gallery of Art — Dürer's woodcuts

ticks.because: Piero della Francesca's De prospectiva pingendi (1474) had codified Renaissance perspective mathematically. The first printed Vitruvius (1486) made architectural theory mass-distributable. Dürer's woodcuts and engravings turn fine art into reproducible commodities — the Apocalypse series, the Knight Death and the Devil, sold across Europe. The artist as printed-image celebrity becomes possible.

ticks.name: Baroque music / emotional expression in form
ticks.constraint: music as primarily liturgical or danced
ticks.detail: Claudio Monteverdi's L'Orfeo (1607) — arguably the first opera — demonstrated that music could tell stories, convey psychological complexity, and express emotion as its primary purpose. The affetti (emotional states) became music's subject matter. From Baroque's emotional architecture to Classical's formal balance to Romantic's subjective intensity, Western art music developed from this shift.

links.label: Britannica — Western music: The tonal era and after 1600

ticks.because: Shakespeare's Globe Theatre (1599) had demonstrated that commercial drama could sustain sophisticated emotional content. The Cumberland graphite deposit (1565) gave the era its precision drawing tool, the modern pencil. Monteverdi's L'Orfeo (1607) and the surrounding Baroque musical practice harness intense emotional expression within tightly controlled formal structures. Western music's primary expressive grammar runs three centuries.

ticks.name: First public opera house (Venice)
ticks.constraint: opera as entertainment limited to aristocratic courts
ticks.detail: The Teatro San Cassiano in Venice (1637) was the first opera house open to paying public audiences. Opera became a commercial art form for the first time. The economic model — tickets, star singers, impresarios — that financed Western classical music for 300 years was established here.

links.label: Teatro San Cassiano 1637: The Birth of Public Opera
Teatro San Cassiano 1637: Birth of the Italian Opera House

ticks.because: The King James Bible (1611) had set a high public standard for vernacular performance text. Bonet's sign-language alphabet (1620) and the Académie Française (1635) showed that institutions could deliberately shape communicative form. The Teatro San Cassiano in 1637 is the same engineering for opera — the first opera house open to paying audiences rather than restricted to courts. The commercial-spectacle institutional form runs four centuries.

ticks.name: Antonio Stradivari / violin craft peak
ticks.constraint: string instrument quality as bounded by existing workshop knowledge
ticks.detail: Stradivari's violins (made 1666-1737) are still considered the finest ever made. His achievement codified what a violin could be — the geometry, thickness gradients, varnish, and wood selection that produce the instrument's characteristic tone. The instrument itself became a tick: it defined the sound that shaped Western music for 350 years.
ticks.because: Monteverdi's L'Orfeo (1607) had established opera. The Royal Society's plain English (1667) demonstrated that institutions could deliberately shape craft standards. The first public opera house in Venice (1637) created the institutional frame for performance music. Stradivari's violin construction, refined over decades, becomes the standard for the next three centuries — instruments still considered the finest ever made.

ticks.name: Impressionism / painting en plein air
ticks.constraint: painting as a studio practice requiring stable conditions
ticks.detail: Monet, Renoir, and Sisley painted outdoors (en plein air) to capture light and atmosphere as they changed. The invention of portable tube paint (1841) made this possible. Impressionism shifted painting's subject from historical narrative and portraiture to perception itself — how light falls on a haystack at different times of day. Every subsequent modern art movement responds to Impressionism.

links.label: Met Museum — Impressionism: Art and Modernity

ticks.because: Melville's Moby-Dick (1851) had demonstrated that prose could absorb encyclopedic knowledge while sustaining ambitious literary form. Impressionism's en-plein-air painting — Monet, Renoir, Sisley working outdoors with portable tube paint — does the parallel for visual art. Light and atmosphere become the subject; perception itself replaces narrative as painting's primary content.

ticks.name: First film screening (Lumière, Paris)
ticks.constraint: photography as capturing a single moment
ticks.detail: The Lumières' first public screening at the Grand Café (December 28, 1895) showed L'Arrivée d'un train and workers leaving a factory. Moving pictures were a new medium. Within 20 years they had developed narrative grammar (editing, close-ups, camera movement), a global distribution system, and a star system. Cinema is the art form of the 20th century.
ticks.because: The Eiffel Tower (1889) had demonstrated industrial-scale steel engineering as public spectacle. Cinema (Lumière brothers, 1895) was the technical demonstration. The first paid Paris screening (December 28, 1895) is the social fact — moving images as paid public entertainment, repeatable nightly, profitable. Mass cinema as a cultural form starts at this Boulevard des Capucines screening.

ticks.name: Armory Show / modernism arrives in America
ticks.constraint: American art as provincial relative to European tradition
ticks.detail: The 1913 International Exhibition of Modern Art in New York (the Armory Show) introduced American audiences to Cubism, Fauvism, and Post-Impressionism. Marcel Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase caused a scandal. American artists and collectors were changed. The US art world's trajectory from provincial to globally central began here.

links.label: Smithsonian Archives of American Art — The Armory Show at 100

ticks.because: Cubism's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907), the Futurist Manifesto (1909), and Picasso's Still Life with Chair Caning (1912) demonstrated that European modernist art was advancing rapidly. The 1913 Armory Show in New York exposes American audiences to that work — Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase as the scandal. American modernism enters its formative phase; the Whitney, MoMA, and the New York School trace to this exhibition's reception.

ticks.name: Joyce's Ulysses / stream of consciousness novel
ticks.constraint: the novel as constrained to linear narrative and external description
ticks.detail: Ulysses mapped a single Dublin day through interior monologue, stream of consciousness, and a dozen different styles. The novel's subject became consciousness itself — its associative, fragmented, private quality. Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury, and the entire tradition of modernist fiction follow from Joyce's formal experiment.

links.label: Cambridge — The Cambridge Ulysses: 1922 Text with Essays
Project Gutenberg — Ulysses by James Joyce

ticks.because: De Stijl's geometric abstraction (1917) and Berlin Dada photomontage (1920) demonstrated that art could be assembled from heterogeneous fragments. Radio broadcasting (1920) made multiple voices and contexts simultaneously available. Joyce's Ulysses applies the same logic to prose — interior monologue, multiple registers, a dozen literary styles in a single Dublin day. The modernist novel as form is established.

ticks.name: Surrealism manifesto (Breton)
ticks.constraint: art as subject to rational control and conscious intention
ticks.detail: André Breton's Surrealist Manifesto declared that art should access the unconscious directly — automatic writing, dreamwork, and the irrational. Surrealism's imagery (Dalí's melting clocks, Magritte's impossible juxtapositions) created a visual language for the unconscious. Advertising, cinema, and political propaganda all learned from surrealism's techniques.

links.label: Internet Archive: Breton, Manifestes du surréalisme

ticks.because: Joyce's Ulysses (1922) had pushed prose into stream-of-consciousness territory. Eliot's Waste Land (1922) had collaged literature from fragments. Breton's 1924 Surrealist Manifesto applies the same logic to visual art and writing — automatic technique, dream imagery, the unconscious as raw material. Dali, Magritte, and the entire Surrealist movement run on Breton's framing.

ticks.name: Abstract Expressionism / New York becomes art capital
ticks.constraint: European cities as the exclusive centers of contemporary art
ticks.detail: Pollock, de Kooning, Rothko, and Kline created a gestural, large-scale painting tradition that shifted the art world's center from Paris to New York. Abstract Expressionism was also shaped by CIA cultural diplomacy during the Cold War — it was promoted internationally as the art of a free society. The American art market's global dominance began here.
ticks.because: Nuremberg's simultaneous interpretation (1945) and Citizen Kane (1941) demonstrated American institutional and cultural ambition at war scale. Brecht's epic theater (1928) had earlier provided the political-art frame. Abstract Expressionism in New York — Pollock, Rothko, de Kooning — gives America its first internationally dominant art movement. The art world's center of gravity shifts from Paris to New York.

ticks.name: Pop Art / Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
ticks.constraint: the distinction between high art and commercial imagery
ticks.detail: Warhol's 1962 Campbell's Soup Cans exhibition made mass-produced consumer imagery the explicit subject of fine art. Pop Art erased the boundary between commerce and culture, between unique artworks and reproduction, between irony and celebration. The appropriation art, media criticism, and ironic sensibility of subsequent decades all begin with Warhol's silk-screens.

links.label: MoMA — Andy Warhol Campbell's Soup Cans 1962
History.com — Warhol's Soup Can Paintings: Meaning and Reaction
Origins (OSU) — Andy Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans 1962

ticks.because: Stokoe's proof that ASL is a full language (1960) and Chomsky's transformational grammar (1957) showed that what looked unstructured could be governed by deep formal rules. Esperanto (1887) had earlier proven that cultural artifacts could be deliberately engineered. Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans applies the same systematizing instinct to consumer imagery — mass-produced, repeatable, elevated to gallery status. Pop Art collapses the boundary between commerce and art.

ticks.name: Conceptual art / dematerialization
ticks.constraint: art as requiring a physical object
ticks.detail: Joseph Kosuth's 'One and Three Chairs' (a chair, a photograph of the chair, and a dictionary definition of 'chair') and Sol LeWitt's instructions-based works proposed that the concept is the art — the physical object is incidental. Conceptual art dematerialized the artwork. Performance art, installation art, and net art all follow from the tick that the idea is enough.

links.label: Smithsonian AAA: Lucy Lippard manuscript Six Years

ticks.because: Pop art made consumer imagery into art. Minimalism stripped away representation, leaving only the object. Conceptualism completed the move: the physical object stops being needed at all. Each step removed one layer of what was thought to be art's essence; what remained at the end was the idea.

ticks.name: Punk rock / DIY cultural production
ticks.constraint: popular music production as requiring record label infrastructure
ticks.detail: The Ramones (1976) and the Sex Pistols (1977) demonstrated that you didn't need technical polish, extensive training, or a major label to record and perform music that connected. The 'anyone can do it' ethos of punk created the independent music ecosystem — indie labels, zines, DIY touring — that still exists as an alternative to the mainstream industry.
ticks.because: Atari's Pong (1972) had demonstrated that mass entertainment could be produced cheaply for home consumption. Hip-hop (1973) had proven that culture could be invented from poverty using available materials. Punk applies the same logic to rock — three chords, no production polish, no major label — and creates the independent music ecosystem (indie labels, zines, DIY touring) that still exists as the alternative.

ticks.name: Hip hop / sampling as composition
ticks.constraint: music composition as requiring trained musicians playing original parts
ticks.detail: Grandmaster Flash's 'The Message' (1982) and Afrika Bambaataa's 'Planet Rock' established sampling — using fragments of existing recordings as the raw material for new compositions — as a legitimate musical practice. Sampling radically democratized music production and created a new compositional aesthetic built on quotation, reference, and recontextualization.

links.label: Business Insider — The Evolution of Music Sampling in Hip-Hop

ticks.because: MTV's launch (1981) had made music videos a commercial necessity, putting visual quotation and editing front and center. Sampling extends the cut-and-paste aesthetic into the audio itself — Grandmaster Flash and Bambaataa make sampled fragments the structural raw material. A quotation-based compositional practice is now legitimate, and the next forty years of pop music depend on it.

ticks.name: Mosaic browser / internet as publishing medium
ticks.constraint: publishing as requiring physical infrastructure (presses, distribution)
ticks.detail: The Web's graphical interface made self-publishing trivially easy. Blogs, webcomics, online journalism, and digital art emerged without gatekeepers. The long-tail economics of online distribution allowed niche creative work to find its audience globally. Every creator economy platform (YouTube, Substack, Bandcamp, Patreon) is a consequence of the Web's open publishing.

links.label: Living Internet: Mosaic Web Browser History

ticks.because: Unicode let the Web carry every language; CD-ROM proved that digital copies could be perfect; hip-hop's sampling normalized the idea that creative work was assembled from pieces of other work. Mosaic gave all three a graphical surface — anyone could publish, anyone could link, anyone could remix.

ticks.name: YouTube / video democratized
ticks.constraint: video production and distribution as requiring broadcast infrastructure
ticks.detail: YouTube's 'Broadcast Yourself' (2005) made video publishing free and global. Within years, YouTube creators had audiences larger than network television. The entire creator economy — tutorials, vlogs, independent journalism, music videos, long-form documentary — migrated online. Traditional broadcast's gatekeeping role effectively ended for a generation of creators.

links.label: YouTube Official Blog — A history of YouTube

ticks.because: Statistical machine translation (1993), Mosaic (1993), and the Web (1993) had assembled the substrate — searchable, multilingual, indexed text and image content. Graphene (2004) showed that single-shot innovations could open entire new material classes. YouTube applies the same logic to video — single upload turns into universal access, and the production of moving images is decoupled from broadcast infrastructure for the first time.

ticks.name: Ada Lovelace / first algorithm
ticks.constraint: computation as purely numerical — not capable of manipulating symbols
ticks.detail: Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine include what is recognized as the first algorithm intended for machine execution — instructions for computing Bernoulli numbers. She also articulated the possibility that the Engine could manipulate symbols beyond numbers. The first vision of general-purpose computing as symbol manipulation, not just arithmetic.

links.label: Wikisource: Lovelace's Notes on Sketch of the Analytical Engine
Fourmilab: Sketch of the Analytical Engine (Menabrea & Lovelace)

ticks.because: Babbage's Difference Engine (1822) and Analytical Engine (1837) had specified mechanical computers in detail. Faraday's electrolysis laws (1833) demonstrated that physical systems could be precisely controlled by quantitative input. Lovelace's notes on the Analytical Engine include explicit step-by-step procedures for calculating Bernoulli numbers — the first algorithm written for a computer, with explicit recognition that machines could manipulate symbols beyond mere arithmetic.

ticks.name: Hollerith tabulating machine / US Census
ticks.constraint: census data processing as requiring years of manual calculation
ticks.detail: Herman Hollerith's punch-card tabulating machine completed the 1890 US Census in one year (vs. eight years for 1880). The machine became the foundation of IBM. Punch-card data processing dominated computing until the 1970s. The idea that data could be mechanically sorted and counted — not just stored — was the tick.
ticks.because: The second law of thermodynamics (1850) and Kelvin's absolute temperature (1848) demonstrated nineteenth-century engineering's quantitative depth. Kirchhoff-Bunsen spectroscopy (1859) showed that abstract instruments could yield concrete data. Hollerith's punch-card tabulating machine completes the 1890 US Census in one year instead of eight — the first major commercial application of mechanical computing, founding what becomes IBM.

ticks.name: Turing's computability / halting problem
ticks.constraint: the limits of what machines can compute as unknown
ticks.detail: Alongside proposing the universal machine, Turing proved the halting problem undecidable — no algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary program will ever stop running. This established fundamental limits on what computation can achieve. Computer science's theory of computability — what problems are algorithmically solvable — is built on this proof.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Church-Turing Thesis: Entscheidungsproblem

ticks.because: The differential analyser (1931) had demonstrated that mechanical computation could solve real engineering problems. Turing's universal machine paper proves both the affirmative result — anything computable can be computed by a Turing machine — and the negative result, the halting problem's undecidability. Computer science's foundational duality is set in one paper.

ticks.name: ENIAC / first general-purpose electronic computer
ticks.constraint: programmable computation as requiring mechanical or electromechanical components
ticks.detail: ENIAC used 18,000 vacuum tubes and could perform 5,000 additions per second — 1,000x faster than existing electromechanical computers. It was programmed by physically rewiring the machine. The first electronic computer demonstrated the paradigm that electronic switching could compute at speeds no mechanical device could approach.

links.label: UPenn Online Books: Report on the ENIAC (1946)

ticks.because: Enigma cryptanalysis at Bletchley (1940) had demonstrated that electronic computing could break cipher systems faster than any electromechanical alternative, and the Yalta Conference (1945) framed the post-war scientific reorganization. ENIAC — Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, completed at Penn in 1945 — gave the United States its first general-purpose electronic computer, with 17,468 vacuum tubes and full reprogrammability, and became the template for the von Neumann architecture.

ticks.name: Transistor (Bell Labs, Shockley/Bardeen/Brattain)
ticks.constraint: electronic switching requiring fragile, hot, power-hungry vacuum tubes
ticks.detail: The transistor replaced the vacuum tube as the basic electronic switching element. It was smaller, cooler, more reliable, and faster. The integrated circuit, the microprocessor, and modern computing are all transistors at varying scales. Shockley's subsequent founding of Fairchild Semiconductor launched Silicon Valley.

links.label: AT&T — The transistor at Bell Labs

ticks.because: Von Neumann architecture (1945) had specified the stored-program computer's logical structure; Bush's Memex (1945) had imagined hypertext-like document interconnection. Gabor's holography (1947) demonstrated that wave physics could be engineered into useful devices. The transistor is the device that makes all the visions practical — small, cool, reliable solid-state switching, which scales from radio to mainframe to microprocessor over the next four decades.

ticks.name: FORTRAN / first high-level programming language
ticks.constraint: programming requiring direct instruction in machine code or assembly
ticks.detail: IBM's FORTRAN (1957) was the first compiled high-level language — programmers wrote mathematical formulas that a compiler translated into machine code. The productivity gain was 10-20x. COBOL (1959) followed for business. Every programming language since — C, Python, Java, JavaScript — descends from the concept FORTRAN established.
ticks.because: UNIVAC I (1951), the Cowan-Reines neutrino detection (1956), and the Dartmouth conference (1956) demonstrated that mid-1950s computing was rapidly maturing. IBM's FORTRAN — the first compiled high-level language with mathematical syntax — extends the same maturation to programming itself. Programs become readable and writable by scientists and engineers; software becomes a discipline.

ticks.name: Time-sharing / interactive computing (McCarthy)
ticks.constraint: computers as batch-processing machines serving one job at a time
ticks.detail: John McCarthy's time-sharing proposal (1959) and its implementation at MIT showed that a single computer could serve multiple users simultaneously by rapidly switching between them. Interactive computing — the ability to type a command and immediately get a response — transformed how computers were used. The terminal, the command line, and eventually the GUI all require time-sharing.

links.label: Stanford: McCarthy 1959 Time-Sharing memo to Morse

ticks.because: Magnetic tape recording (1948), the von Neumann stored-program architecture (1945), and Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958) bracket the early computer era when machines were single-user batch processors. McCarthy's time-sharing concept — multiple users at terminals sharing CPU cycles — converted the computer from a one-job-at-a-time machine into an interactive utility, and made conversational computing a daily practice for researchers two decades before it reached consumers.

ticks.name: Moore's Law observed
ticks.constraint: computing cost as a fixed rather than exponentially declining parameter
ticks.detail: Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling approximately every two years (later standardized to 18 months). His prediction became a self-fulfilling prophecy that organized the entire semiconductor industry's roadmap for 50 years. Moore's Law is why a 2024 smartphone has more computing power than 1990's entire world combined.
ticks.because: The Feminine Mystique (1963) had demonstrated that systematic observation could reframe an entire cultural domain. The quark model (Gell-Mann/Zweig, 1964) and the Higgs mechanism's theoretical proposal (1964) showed that mid-1960s science was making confident predictions. Gordon Moore's empirical observation in Electronics magazine — transistor counts doubling roughly every two years — turns out to be the most consequential industry-shaping prediction of the next sixty years.

ticks.name: Doug Engelbart's Mother of All Demos
ticks.constraint: computing as batch processing of text — not interactive visual manipulation
ticks.detail: Engelbart's December 9, 1968 demonstration showed the mouse, hypertext, videoconferencing, collaborative editing, and windowed interfaces — essentially previewing the modern PC. All of it was working software. The demo defined the trajectory of personal computing. Steve Jobs cited it as inspiration for the Macintosh. Every GUI computer interface today is Engelbart's vision.

links.label: Engelbart & English — Research Center for Augmenting Human Intellect (1968 paper)

ticks.because: Plate tectonics (1965), the cosmic microwave background (1965), and electroweak unification (1967) demonstrated that synthesis-level scientific advances were happening regularly. Engelbart's December 9, 1968 demo shows the same level of synthesis for computing — mouse, hypertext, videoconferencing, real-time collaborative editing — all working in a single demonstration. Most modern personal-computing affordances trace to this hour-long presentation.

ticks.name: C programming language (Ritchie)
ticks.constraint: systems programming as requiring assembly language
ticks.detail: Dennis Ritchie's C language allowed operating systems and low-level software to be written in a portable, human-readable language rather than machine-specific assembly code. Unix was rewritten in C (1973). Every major operating system — Linux, macOS, Windows — is still primarily written in C or languages derived from it. Python, Java, and JavaScript all run on C-based runtimes.

links.label: Bell Labs: Ritchie, C Reference Manual (PDF)
ACM HOPL-II: Ritchie, The Development of the C Language

ticks.because: ARPANET's first message (1969) showed that heterogeneous computers could be wired into one network — a fact that made portable software an economic priority. The Intel 4004 microprocessor (1971) put a computer on a single chip, multiplying machine variety. C is the response: a language portable enough to compile across any machine yet close enough to the metal to write an operating system. Unix, the runtime, and every operating system since stand on Ritchie's compromise.

ticks.name: Ethernet / local area networking (Metcalfe)
ticks.constraint: computers as isolated islands unable to share resources
ticks.detail: Robert Metcalfe's Ethernet (1973, standardized 1980) connected computers within a building into a local area network. Files, printers, and eventually the internet could be shared. Metcalfe's Law: the value of a network is proportional to the square of its connected users. Every office network, home router, and cloud data center uses Ethernet.
ticks.because: The C language (1972) gave software portability. Pong (1972) demonstrated that screens could be the medium. The PLATO IV touch panel (1972) showed that direct interaction with computing could be everyday. Metcalfe's Ethernet is the missing networking layer — a coaxial cable that lets every machine in a building talk to every other, with collision detection as the elegant arbitration protocol. Local area networking begins.

ticks.name: VisiCalc and the business computer revolution
ticks.constraint: business computing as requiring mainframe infrastructure and IT departments
