ticks.detail: VisiCalc on the Apple II (1979) and then Lotus 1-2-3 on the IBM PC (1983) made personal computers indispensable business tools. CFOs and executives adopted personal computers for financial modeling — the 'killer app' that justified the hardware purchase. The spreadsheet is still the most widely used business software, 45 years later.

links.label: Aresluna — Birthing the Visible Calculator (Ten Years of Rows and Columns)
Computer History Museum — Origins and Impact of VisiCalc

ticks.because: The Apple I (1976) had made the personal computer a real product. Usenet (1979) created online communities for distributed knowledge. RSA encryption (1977) demonstrated that consumer-grade computers could run serious math. VisiCalc on the Apple II is the first application that demands a computer rather than treating it as a curiosity — accountants buy machines just to run it. The personal-computer business case is made.

ticks.name: Macintosh / graphical user interface for everyone
ticks.constraint: personal computing as requiring command-line expertise
ticks.detail: The 1984 Macintosh brought the graphical user interface — windows, icons, mouse, pointer — to a mass market at an affordable price. It made computing visual, spatial, and manipulable rather than textual and memorized. The Mac didn't invent the GUI (Xerox PARC did, Engelbart before that) but it commercialized it. Windows followed. The command line receded.

links.label: MacRumors: The Mac Turns 40 — Apple's 1984 announcement

ticks.because: The Apple I (1976) had proven there was a personal-computer market. The TCP/IP transition (1983) and DNS (1984) made networking universal. The Macintosh applies the Xerox PARC GUI inheritance to a mass-market machine — windows, icons, mouse, fonts on the screen. Personal computing becomes operable by anyone, not just hobbyists with manuals.

ticks.name: World Wide Web (Berners-Lee) protocols
ticks.constraint: internet as requiring technical knowledge to navigate
ticks.detail: Berners-Lee's HTTP, HTML, and URL proposals (1989-1991) created the Web as a system of linked documents that any program (browser) could navigate. The Web was built on the internet but made it accessible. By 1993 (Mosaic), anyone could browse it. By 1995 (Netscape), it was transforming commerce, media, and communication.

links.label: CERN — A short history of the Web

ticks.because: Berners-Lee's WWW proposal (1989) had specified the concept. The 1990 protocols — HTTP, HTML, URLs — give the concept its operational form. The first website goes live in 1991. The Web's distinguishing technical insight: any document can link to any other, by global address, with no central registry. The information substrate of the next thirty years is set.

ticks.name: JavaScript / browser programming
ticks.constraint: web pages as static documents that only servers could change
ticks.detail: Brendan Eich created JavaScript in 10 days at Netscape in 1995. It allowed web pages to respond to user interactions without reloading. The dynamic, interactive web — Gmail, Google Maps, Facebook, every modern web application — runs on JavaScript. It's the most widely deployed programming language in history, despite Eich's own ambivalence about it.

links.label: Wirfs-Brock & Eich — JavaScript: the first 20 years (ACM)
Exploring JS — History and evolution of JavaScript

ticks.because: The Mosaic browser (1993) had made the Web accessible. Apple's Newton MessagePad (1993) and Linux 1.0 (1994) had each pushed computing in new directions. JavaScript, written by Brendan Eich in ten days at Netscape, is the missing scripting layer — making every web page programmable, interactive, and stateful. Two decades later it runs on servers, mobile phones, and embedded devices, the most-deployed runtime in computing history.

ticks.name: Facebook's News Feed / algorithmic social curation
ticks.constraint: social media feeds as chronological and user-curated
ticks.detail: Facebook's News Feed (2006) introduced algorithmic curation — a proprietary algorithm deciding what each user sees based on engagement predictions. Twitter, Instagram, TikTok all followed with increasingly sophisticated algorithmic feeds. The tick: attention became a product, algorithmically optimized. The downstream effects on democracy, mental health, and public discourse are still being assessed.

links.label: TechCrunch: New Facebook Redesign — News Feed launch (Sep 2006)
Web Archive: Zuckerberg open letter on News Feed (Sep 2006)

ticks.because: MySpace (2003) and early Facebook had presented friends' updates chronologically. Facebook's News Feed (September 2006) replaced the chronology with an algorithm predicting per-user engagement. Outcry was loud, opt-out demand strong, but the engagement metrics jumped and the feature stayed. Twitter (2016), Instagram (2016), and TikTok (2018) all moved to algorithmic feeds. The default information environment for billions of people became predictively curated rather than user-controlled.

ticks.name: GitHub / distributed version control
ticks.constraint: collaborative software development requiring a central authoritative server
ticks.detail: GitHub (2008) built a social layer on top of Git (Linus Torvalds' distributed version control system, 2005). Open-source collaboration became frictionless — fork a project, make changes, propose a merge. Every major open-source project (Linux, Python, TensorFlow) is now developed on GitHub. Microsoft acquired it for $7.5B in 2018.

links.label: ACM Queue — Linus Torvalds on Git

ticks.because: The App Store model (2008) and Kindle's launch (2007) demonstrated that platform-mediated distribution could create entirely new economies. GitHub took the same approach to source code: Git's distributed version control wrapped in a social layer of pull requests, issues, and visible profiles — and within a decade became the default substrate of open-source software collaboration.

ticks.name: Kubernetes / container orchestration
ticks.constraint: cloud application deployment as requiring custom infrastructure configuration
ticks.detail: Google's Kubernetes (2014) automated the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Docker containers + Kubernetes orchestration became the standard way to run cloud-native applications. Every major cloud provider, every large-scale web application, and the AI inference infrastructure running LLMs today uses Kubernetes.

links.label: Google Cloud Blog — Kubernetes Origin Story
Kubernetes Blog — Borg: The Predecessor to Kubernetes

ticks.because: AlexNet (2012) had triggered an industry-wide push toward GPU compute at scale, and GANs (2014) plus the rise of microservices made deployment topologies far more complex than a single VM cluster. Kubernetes — open-sourced from Google's Borg — gave every team a declarative system for scheduling containers across heterogeneous hardware, and became the substrate every cloud-native application now assumes.

ticks.name: Gregorian calendar reform
ticks.constraint: calendar drift from solar year accumulating to 10+ days
ticks.detail: Pope Gregory XIII's reform corrected the Julian calendar's 11-minute annual error — which had accumulated to 10 days by 1582. The solution: skip leap year in century years not divisible by 400. The Gregorian calendar coordinates global timekeeping, agriculture, religious observance, and international business. Adopted progressively: Britain 1752, Russia 1918, China 1912.
ticks.because: The Battle of Lepanto (1571, in both broadside warfare and Ottoman naval dominance facets) and the Columbian Exchange's demographic catastrophe (1492) demonstrated that the late sixteenth century was reordering European awareness of time and geography. Pope Gregory XIII's reform corrects the Julian calendar's eleven-minute-per-year accumulated drift. Modern global timekeeping eventually adopts Gregorian; even non-Christian states use it as the international standard.

ticks.name: Reflecting telescope (Newton)
ticks.constraint: refracting telescopes' chromatic aberration limiting magnification
ticks.detail: Newton's reflecting telescope used a curved mirror instead of a lens, eliminating chromatic aberration that blurred images in refracting telescopes. Larger, more powerful telescopes became possible. The Hubble Space Telescope, the James Webb Space Telescope, and all major modern observatories use reflecting optics. Newton's design is essentially unchanged.
ticks.because: The Sceptical Chymist (Boyle, 1661) had argued that scientific instruments should be designed against first principles, not tradition. Newton's universal gravitation (1666) had proven that the same physical laws governed the heavens and Earth. The reflecting telescope is Newton applying both moves to optics — mirrors instead of lenses to defeat chromatic aberration. The design is essentially unchanged in every modern observatory, including Hubble and James Webb.

ticks.name: Rømer measures speed of light
ticks.constraint: light as instantaneously propagating
ticks.detail: Ole Rømer noticed that Jupiter's moon Io appeared to orbit slightly faster when Earth moved toward Jupiter and slower when moving away — explaining the discrepancy by the finite travel time of light. The first measurement of the speed of light (within 25% of the correct value). It proved light has a finite speed and opened the question of what light travels through.

links.label: World Scientific — Speed of Light: Timing Jupiter's Moons (Paris 1671-76)
Physics Today — Rømer and the Finite Speed of Light

ticks.because: Newton's universal gravitation (1666) gave astronomers a reliable mathematical model of the planets. The reflecting telescope (1668) gave them an instrument with the resolution to time celestial events precisely. Rømer applies both — observing Io's eclipse times against Earth-Jupiter distance — and detects the discrepancy that only a finite light speed can explain. Light becomes a quantitative phenomenon for the first time.

ticks.name: Oersted / electromagnetism connection
ticks.constraint: electricity and magnetism as separate phenomena
ticks.detail: Hans Christian Oersted accidentally noticed that a compass needle deflected when placed near a current-carrying wire. Electricity could create magnetism. Faraday showed magnetism could create electricity. Maxwell unified both in his equations. The entire technology of electric motors, generators, radio, and wireless communication follows from Oersted's lecture-table accident.
ticks.because: Volta's pile (1800) gave chemistry a steady-state electrical source. Dalton's atomic theory (1808) had insisted matter was particulate and reactive in determinate ratios. Young's double-slit experiment (1801) had argued for the wave nature of light. Fraunhofer's solar absorption lines (1814) showed that light carried information about matter. Oersted notices that an electric current deflects a compass needle — electricity and magnetism are connected, and the substrate for Faraday-Maxwell unification is born.

ticks.name: Maxwell's equations / unified electromagnetism
ticks.constraint: electricity, magnetism, and light as separate phenomena
ticks.detail: James Clerk Maxwell's four equations unified electricity and magnetism into a single theory and predicted electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light — implying that light IS an electromagnetic wave. Radio, radar, microwave, X-ray, UV, and all of the electromagnetic spectrum follow from Maxwell. Einstein said Maxwell's equations were 'the most profound and the most fruitful that physics has experienced since Newton.'

links.label: Maxwell 1865 — A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field (Royal Society)

ticks.because: Kelvin's absolute temperature (1848) had completed thermodynamics's foundation. Foucault's pendulum (1851) and Kirchhoff-Bunsen spectroscopy (1859) had made fundamental physical phenomena directly observable. Maxwell's four equations are the unification act — Faraday's induction, Gauss's flux, Ampère's circuital law, all in symmetric vector form, predicting electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light. Light becomes a manifestation of electricity and magnetism.

ticks.name: Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom
ticks.constraint: the atom as a uniformly distributed charge (Thomson's plum pudding)
ticks.detail: Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed that most of an atom's mass is concentrated in a tiny, dense, positively-charged nucleus. The atom is mostly empty space. This nuclear model — a dense nucleus orbited by electrons — is still the mental model most people use. It directly enabled nuclear physics, the neutron discovery, and nuclear fission.

links.label: Nobel Prize — Ernest Rutherford Nobel Lecture
Rutherford — Scattering of α Particles (Phil. Mag. 1911 PDF)

ticks.because: Einstein's annus mirabilis (1905) — Brownian motion confirming atoms, special relativity, photoelectric effect — established that matter and energy obeyed quantum and relativistic rules, and Millikan's electron-charge measurement (1909) gave the electron a precise quantitative identity. Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed that atoms had a tiny dense charged nucleus, killing Thomson's plum-pudding model and setting up Bohr's quantum atom.

ticks.name: General relativity (Einstein)
ticks.constraint: gravity as a force acting across empty space
ticks.detail: General relativity replaced Newton's gravitational force with the geometry of curved spacetime — mass tells spacetime how to curve, curved spacetime tells mass how to move. Confirmed by the 1919 solar eclipse (light bending around the sun). GPS satellites require general relativistic corrections. Black holes, gravitational waves, the expanding universe, and cosmology all require GR.

links.label: CERN: Einstein, Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation (25 Nov 1915)
Internet Archive: Einstein, Foundation of the General Theory of Relativity (1916) PDF

ticks.because: Von Laue's X-ray crystallography (1912), Hess's discovery of cosmic rays (1912), and Bohr's atomic model (1913) demonstrated that early-twentieth-century physics was entering radically new territory. Einstein's 1915 general relativity replaces Newton's gravitational force with the geometry of curved spacetime. The 1916 paper formalizes; black holes, gravitational waves, and the expanding universe all become predictions of this theory.

ticks.name: Hubble's law / expanding universe
ticks.constraint: the universe as static and eternal
ticks.detail: Edwin Hubble's observation that galaxies are receding at velocities proportional to their distance proved the universe is expanding. Running the film backward implies a beginning — the Big Bang. Cosmology as a quantitative science was born. The CMB (1965), dark energy (1998), and the entire narrative of cosmic history all follow from Hubble's observation.

links.label: PNAS — Hubble 1929: A relation between distance and radial velocity

ticks.because: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle (1927) and Dirac's antimatter prediction (1928) had each pushed twentieth-century physics into fundamentally new territory. Hubble's law — distant galaxies receding at velocities proportional to their distance — gives cosmology its central observational fact. The universe is expanding; the Big Bang and the cosmic age both follow from this measurement.

ticks.name: Cyclotron / particle accelerator (Lawrence)
ticks.constraint: particle physics limited to natural cosmic ray energies
ticks.detail: Ernest Lawrence's cyclotron (1932) used magnetic fields to spiral charged particles to high energies. Artificial particle acceleration allowed physicists to probe nuclear and subnuclear structure at will. The technology scaled from Lawrence's 27cm device to CERN's 27km LHC. Every fundamental particle discovery since the neutron used accelerator technology.

links.label: UC Berkeley — The cyclotron's history at Berkeley
Livingston — The History of the Cyclotron (JACoW PDF)
AIP History — The Rad Lab: Lawrence and the Cyclotron

ticks.because: Anderson's positron discovery (1932) demonstrated that high-energy physics had entered a new precision regime. Lawrence's cyclotron — magnetic fields spiraling charged particles to high energy — provides the laboratory accelerator that will dominate experimental physics for the next forty years. Every modern collider, including the LHC, descends from this design.

ticks.name: Nuclear fission (Hahn and Strassmann / Meitner)
ticks.constraint: atomic energy as inaccessibly small-scale
ticks.detail: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann showed that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium — the uranium nucleus had split. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch correctly identified this as fission and calculated the energy released (E=mc²). From discovery to atomic bomb was 7 years. From discovery to nuclear power was 20. From discovery to modern civilization's energy mix is still ongoing.

links.label: Springer: Hahn & Strassmann, Über den Nachweis (Naturwiss 1939)
Nature: Meitner & Frisch, Disintegration of Uranium by Neutrons (1939)

ticks.because: Lawrence's cyclotron (1932) gave physicists a controllable particle accelerator; Anderson's positron (1932) had confirmed antimatter; Rabi's NMR (1938) had made nuclear states measurable. Hahn and Strassmann's chemical analysis showed barium emerging from neutron-bombarded uranium — Meitner and Frisch named this fission and computed E=mc² for the released energy. Atomic-scale energy becomes engineerable.

ticks.name: Cosmic microwave background discovered (Penzias/Wilson)
ticks.constraint: the Big Bang as a theoretical framework without direct observational evidence
ticks.detail: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, while trying to eliminate interference from their antenna, discovered a faint, uniform microwave radiation coming from all directions — the afterglow of the Big Bang. The CMB confirmed the Big Bang theory definitively. Subsequent CMB measurements (COBE, WMAP, Planck) have mapped the early universe with extraordinary precision.

links.label: APS — Penzias and Wilson discover CMB

ticks.because: Bell's theorem (1964) proved that quantum mechanics required nonlocal correlations — physics was committing to genuinely unintuitive predictions. Penzias and Wilson's noise-temperature measurement is the cosmological analog: the static they couldn't eliminate from their antenna turns out to be the predicted Big Bang afterglow. Cosmology stops being speculation and becomes a precision empirical science.

ticks.name: Dark energy discovered (Type Ia supernovae)
ticks.constraint: the universe's expansion as decelerating due to gravity
ticks.detail: Two independent teams observed that distant Type Ia supernovae were dimmer than expected — the universe's expansion was accelerating, not decelerating. Something (dark energy) was pushing the universe apart against gravity. Dark energy constitutes 68% of the universe's energy content. Its nature is completely unknown. The Standard Model of cosmology required fundamental revision.

links.label: Riess et al. — Observational Evidence from Supernovae for Accelerating Universe (AJ 1998)
Perlmutter et al. — Cosmology from Type Ia Supernovae (arXiv 1998)
Riess et al. — Evidence for Accelerating Universe (full text)

ticks.because: The W and Z discoveries (1983) gave physicists the confidence that the Standard Model held at the smallest scales. Hubble's launch (1990) extended observation to the largest. Bose-Einstein condensates (1995) confirmed quantum mechanics held in macroscopic samples. Two independent supernova teams in 1998 plot all three trust frames against the same data — and find the universe is expanding faster, not slower. Sixty-eight percent of the cosmos turns out to be something nobody's theory predicts.

ticks.name: First image of a black hole (Event Horizon Telescope)
ticks.constraint: black holes as theoretically inevitable but photographically inaccessible
ticks.detail: The Event Horizon Telescope linked radio telescopes across Earth to create an Earth-sized interferometer. The resulting image of M87*'s shadow — the first direct visual evidence of a black hole's event horizon — matched general relativity's predictions exactly. A century after Einstein predicted black holes, humanity photographed one.

links.label: HAL Open Science: First M87 EHT Results I (Akiyama 2019) PDF
IOPscience: First M87 EHT Results I — The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole

ticks.because: LIGO's gravitational-wave detections (2015–2016) had just confirmed that compact massive objects existed and merged. The Event Horizon Telescope — a global radio interferometer with Earth-scale baseline — produced the first image of a black hole's event horizon (M87*) in April 2019, and turned black holes from mathematical inevitabilities into directly photographed astrophysical objects.

ticks.name: Twelve Tables / Rome's first written law
ticks.constraint: Roman law as oral, customary, and known only to patricians
ticks.detail: The Twelve Tables, displayed publicly in the Forum, made Roman law accessible to plebeians for the first time. Written law that citizens could consult and cite changed the balance of power between social classes. The principle that law must be written and public — not the private knowledge of a privileged class — underlies every subsequent legal system.

links.label: Britannica — Law of the Twelve Tables

ticks.because: Pāṇini's Sanskrit grammar (500 BC) had codified linguistic rules with full formal precision. Draco's Athenian written law (621 BC) demonstrated the political utility of public, written codes. Athenian democracy (500 BC) made citizen access to law procedurally important. Rome's Twelve Tables, displayed publicly in the Forum, apply the same principle in Latin — written law accessible to plebeians, the foundation of Roman jurisprudence and the template for every later civil-law tradition.

ticks.name: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis / Roman law codified
ticks.constraint: Roman legal tradition as fragmented across thousands of incompatible texts
ticks.detail: Emperor Justinian commissioned the systematic compilation and codification of Roman law — the Institutes, Digest, Code, and Novels. The Corpus became the foundation of civil law systems across continental Europe, Latin America, and parts of Asia. Every French, Spanish, Italian, German, and Brazilian legal system traces to Justinian's codification.

links.label: JURIST — Justinian I issues Corpus Juris Civilis (April 7 529)
Britannica — Roman law: The law of Justinian

ticks.because: Galen's medical synthesis (200 AD) and the Julian calendar's standardization (46 BC) demonstrated that classical and Roman institutions could codify systems of knowledge or time. The Phoenician alphabet (1050 BC) had earlier built the substrate for legal record-keeping. Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis — Digest, Code, Institutes, Novellae — compiles a thousand years of Roman law into a systematic framework. The basis for civil law in most of continental Europe and Latin America.

ticks.name: English Bill of Rights / constitutional monarchy
ticks.constraint: English monarchy as absolute following Stuart restoration
ticks.detail: The Bill of Rights formalized the Glorious Revolution's settlement: parliamentary supremacy, free elections, free speech in Parliament, no excessive bail, no standing army in peacetime without Parliamentary consent. England became a constitutional monarchy. The American Bill of Rights is modeled directly on it.

links.label: Avalon Project (Yale) — English Bill of Rights 1689

ticks.because: The Petition of Right (1628) and the Habeas Corpus Act (1679) had constrained the English monarchy in pieces. The Glorious Revolution (1688) put William and Mary on the throne by parliamentary invitation. The Bill of Rights (1689) formalized the settlement: parliamentary supremacy, free elections, free speech in Parliament, no excessive bail, no standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent. England became a constitutional monarchy. The American Bill of Rights is modeled directly on it.

ticks.name: US Bill of Rights / individual rights against state
ticks.constraint: constitutional government as silent on individual liberties
ticks.detail: The first ten amendments to the US Constitution enumerated specific protections: free speech, free press, freedom of religion, right to bear arms, protection from unreasonable search, right to a fair trial, prohibition of cruel punishment. The concept of enumerated individual rights against government became the model for constitutional rights globally.

links.label: Cornell LII — Constitutional Convention, Ratification, and the Bill of Rights
Constitution Annotated — Bill of Rights (First Through Tenth Amendments)

ticks.because: Sir William Jones's comparative linguistics (1786), Kant's Critique of Pure Reason (1781), and Kant's Groundwork (1785) demonstrated that systematic Enlightenment principles could organize complex domains. The first ten amendments to the US Constitution — the Bill of Rights ratified 1791 — codify specific protections against government action. The constitutional tradition that becomes the global liberal-rights template begins.

ticks.name: International humanitarian law (Lieber Code)
ticks.constraint: treatment of prisoners and civilians in war as entirely discretionary
ticks.detail: Francis Lieber's Instructions for the Government of Armies of the United States in the Field (1863) was the first codification of the laws of land warfare. It prohibited torture of prisoners, protection of civilians, and destruction of property beyond military necessity. It directly influenced the Hague Conventions (1899, 1907) and the Geneva Conventions.

links.label: Library of Congress: Lieber Code Instructions for Government of Armies (PDF)
Library of Congress: Instructions for the Government of Armies (Lieber Code)

ticks.because: The penny press (1833), Roget's Thesaurus (1852), and Kierkegaard's existential anxiety (1843) demonstrated that mid-nineteenth-century institutional and philosophical frames were developing rapidly. Lieber's Instructions for the Government of Armies of the United States in the Field — issued during the Civil War — codifies the laws of war. The precursor to the Hague Conventions, Geneva Conventions, and modern international humanitarian law.

ticks.name: League of Nations Covenant / collective security
ticks.constraint: international dispute resolution as purely bilateral negotiation or war
ticks.detail: The League Covenant created the first multilateral dispute resolution mechanism with collective security obligations. It failed — but the institutional form it invented (permanent secretariat, regular assembly, arbitration procedures) was refined by the UN. International organizations as permanent institutions with their own legal personality begin here.

links.label: Avalon Project (Yale) — Covenant of the League of Nations

ticks.because: The US 16th Amendment income tax (1913) gave modern states a fiscal capacity adequate to global ambitions. Women's suffrage (1918) and the Treaty of Versailles (1919) had reordered political legitimacy. The League of Nations is the institutional form — permanent secretariat, regular assembly, arbitration procedures, mutual security obligations. It fails operationally but defines the template the UN inherits.

ticks.name: UN Charter / sovereign equality principle
ticks.constraint: international order as based on power hierarchy rather than legal equality
ticks.detail: The UN Charter's assertion that all member states are sovereign equals — regardless of size, power, or wealth — created a legal fiction that nonetheless structured international relations. Every state has one vote in the General Assembly. The veto in the Security Council was the concession to power reality. The tension between sovereign equality and great-power politics continues.

links.label: UN Treaties — Charter of the UN ratification record

ticks.because: The League of Nations Covenant (1920) had invented the institutional form of permanent multilateral organizations with their own legal personality, then failed to enforce it. The GI Bill (1944) showed Congress could legislate on a scale equal to the war just won. The UN Charter applied both lessons — a permanent body with universal sovereign-equality membership, backed by the political will of postwar democracies.

ticks.name: Genocide Convention / defining a new crime
ticks.constraint: the systematic destruction of an ethnic or national group as legally unnamed
ticks.detail: Raphael Lemkin coined 'genocide' in 1944 and the Convention criminalizing it was adopted in 1948. For the first time, the systematic destruction of a group based on ethnicity, nationality, race, or religion was defined as a crime under international law. The enforcement gap (Rwanda, Srebrenica) showed the definition's power and its limits.

links.label: UN Treaty Series: Convention on Prevention and Punishment of Genocide (1948)
UN Audiovisual Library: Schabas on Genocide Convention (PDF)

ticks.because: Mass killings of national, ethnic, racial, and religious groups had been recurrent in human history without a name in international law. Lemkin's 1944 coinage 'genocide' (Greek genos + Latin -cide) gave it one. The 1948 Convention defined the crime, criminalized intent (acts committed with intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part), and committed signatories to prevent and punish it. The legal basis for every subsequent prosecution from the ICTY to the ICC.

ticks.name: European Convention on Human Rights
ticks.constraint: human rights as aspirational declarations without enforcement
ticks.detail: The ECHR created the European Court of Human Rights — the first international court with compulsory jurisdiction over human rights cases, where individuals could bring claims against their own governments. Human rights became enforceable law, not just rhetoric. The template for regional human rights systems worldwide.

links.label: Council of Europe — European Convention on Human Rights

ticks.because: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) was aspirational. The European Convention on Human Rights (1950) made enforcement procedural: a court (the European Court of Human Rights) with compulsory jurisdiction over human rights cases brought by individuals against their own governments. The first international court that ordinary people could petition. Every regional human rights system since copies the architecture.

ticks.name: Amnesty International founded / human rights NGOs
ticks.constraint: human rights monitoring as requiring state cooperation
ticks.detail: Peter Benenson's Observer article 'The Forgotten Prisoners' (1961) launched Amnesty International — an NGO that independently documented and publicized human rights abuses regardless of which government committed them. Non-governmental human rights monitoring created accountability pressure outside diplomatic channels. Human Rights Watch, ACLU, and every human rights NGO follows this model.
ticks.because: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) stated principles. Amnesty International (1961) made them operational: a non-governmental network of letter-writers documenting and pressuring governments to release political prisoners. Peter Benenson's Observer article 'The Forgotten Prisoners' launched it. Every modern human-rights NGO inherited the model — name a prisoner, name a country, mobilize a constituency.

ticks.name: International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda
ticks.constraint: genocide as politically prosecutable only domestically by perpetrators' own government
ticks.detail: The ICTR was the first international tribunal to convict for genocide since Nuremberg. It established that genocide can be prosecuted internationally even against sitting heads of state. The International Criminal Court (2002) built directly on the ICTR and the ICTY (Yugoslavia tribunal) experience.

links.label: UN Security Council Resolution 955 (1994) — ICTR establishment
UN ICTR Mechanism: Cases and judgements

ticks.because: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) had ended the Cold War's veto-driven UN paralysis, and Singer's applied ethics movement (1979) had built the moral vocabulary for cross-border accountability. The ICTR — the first international tribunal to convict a head of state for genocide — applied that vocabulary to the 1994 Rwandan genocide, and prefigured the Rome Statute three years later.

ticks.name: GDPR / right to digital privacy as law
ticks.constraint: personal data as freely usable by those who collected it
ticks.detail: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation came into force in May 2018 — the most comprehensive privacy law in history. It gave Europeans rights over their personal data: the right to access, correct, delete, and port it. It imposed fines up to 4% of global revenue. Every tech company's privacy policy globally changed because of GDPR. It established digital privacy as a legal right.
ticks.because: By 2014, data brokers and ad-tech had built profiles on every European with internet access. The 1995 Data Protection Directive was no longer enforceable at scale. GDPR (2018) gave residents enforceable rights — access, deletion, portability, the right not to be profiled — and gave regulators teeth: 4% of global revenue. The first data-privacy regime that companies in California, Tokyo, and Bangalore actually had to engineer for. CCPA, LGPD, and the rest are GDPR copies.

ticks.name: Proto-cuneiform accounting tokens
ticks.constraint: commercial record-keeping as dependent on human memory alone
ticks.detail: Before writing proper, Mesopotamian merchants used clay tokens of various shapes to represent different commodities — 3 cones for wheat, 2 discs for oil. These accounting tokens are the immediate precursor to cuneiform writing. The click: externalizing memory into physical objects that outlast the transaction. Writing was invented for commerce, not literature.

links.label: Schmandt-Besserat — The Invention of Tokens (UT Austin)
Schmandt-Besserat — Token System of Ancient Near East (PDF)

ticks.because: Recursive language let humans agree on abstract claims (who owes whom). Cuneiform proved that such claims could be inscribed durably. Tokens sit between the two — a physical externalization of an abstract agreement, the moment commerce stops needing memory.

ticks.name: Ugaritic alphabet / simplified writing
ticks.constraint: Phoenician consonantal script as limited to Semitic languages
ticks.detail: The Ugaritic alphabet (1400 BC) was the first alphabetic script adapted for writing on clay tablets in cuneiform-style wedges — combining the simplicity of an alphabet with the durability of cuneiform. It accelerated the development of alphabetic writing as the dominant script technology across the Near East, eventually displacing syllabic scripts everywhere.

links.label: BAS Library: A Cuneiform Alphabet at Ugarit

ticks.because: The Epic of Gilgamesh (2100 BC) had proven that complex narrative could fit on clay. Akkadian as lingua franca (2000 BC) had standardized cuneiform across the Near East. The Urra=hubullu glossary (1800 BC) showed that comparative reference works were possible. Linear B (1450 BC) and Minoan frescoes (1440 BC) demonstrated that literate cultures could coexist around the Mediterranean. Ugaritic combines the alphabet's simplicity with cuneiform's clay durability — the script that accelerates the alphabet's eventual displacement of every syllabary it meets.

ticks.name: Papyrus scrolls / lightweight portable writing surface
ticks.constraint: durable writing requiring stone or clay tablets
ticks.detail: Egyptian papyrus, processed from the Nile reed Cyperus papyrus around 3000 BC, became the first portable, lightweight writing medium of the ancient world. Cheaper than parchment, lighter than clay, it made administrative records, letters, and literary scrolls possible at scale — and exported writing-as-practice across the Mediterranean for over three millennia until paper displaced it.
ticks.because: Cuneiform proved writing worked, but only on clay. Sexagesimal numbers gave writing precision but kept it heavy. Papyrus took the practice off the tablet and onto something a courier could roll up and carry — and exported writing-as-practice across the Mediterranean.

ticks.name: Arabic as global language of science
ticks.constraint: scientific and philosophical knowledge as accessible only in Greek or Latin
ticks.detail: From 800-1200 AD, Arabic was the dominant language of natural philosophy, mathematics, medicine, and astronomy. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad translated Greek texts into Arabic and extended them significantly. When Europeans sought ancient knowledge, they learned Arabic to access it. Scientific vocabulary in European languages (algebra, algorithm, almanac, alcohol, zenith) is Arabic because Arabic was the language of science.

links.label: Library of Congress — Medieval Islamic Science: Resource Guide
Montgomery — Mobilities of Science: Translation into Arabic (UChicago)
1001 Inventions — When the World Spoke Arabic

ticks.because: Each parent shows the same century-long pattern of literate societies building their own writing infrastructure to handle their own knowledge: the Diamond Sutra's printed-book proof in China, Cyrillic's creation for Slavic learning, Nepali's first inscriptions in the Himalayas. Arabic's rise as the language of science is the same pattern at imperial scale — a translation movement that absorbed Greek work, extended it, and ran scholarship for four centuries.

ticks.name: Gutenberg / text becomes reproducible
ticks.constraint: text as unique — each copy individually produced
ticks.detail: The printing press made text reproducible and identical. Before Gutenberg, each manuscript copy introduced errors and variations. After: the identical edition. Scholars could cite specific pages. Scientific priority could be established. The edition — a specific text at a specific moment — became the basic unit of written culture. Error correction, bibliographic control, and academic citation systems all follow.

links.label: Princeton Digital PUL: The Gutenberg Bible

ticks.because: Movable type (1440) was the mechanical breakthrough — interchangeable letter pieces. Gutenberg's Bible (1455) was the proof of scale. The reproducibility of text — identical pages from any press — turns reading from individual scribal interpretation into shared comparison. Citation by page number, error correction across editions, and scientific priority all become possible only once two copies of the same text are guaranteed identical.

ticks.name: Académie Française / standardized language
ticks.constraint: national language as dialectally fragmented and without authoritative standard
ticks.detail: Richelieu's Académie Française was established to standardize and purify the French language. The idea that a language could be institutionally governed — its vocabulary regulated, its grammar codified, its 'correct' usage enforced — was new. National language standardization became a European project: the Dictionary of the English Language (Johnson, 1755), Grimm's Deutsches Wörterbuch. Language as a national institution.
ticks.because: Bonet's first sign-language alphabet (1620) and the Zihui dictionary's 214-radical system (1615) demonstrated that languages could be formally codified by a deliberate authority. The King James Bible (1611) had set a comparable standard for English. Richelieu's Académie Française is the institutional template — a permanent body charged with maintaining a national language's standards. The model for every later language academy.

ticks.name: Johnson's Dictionary / lexicography standardized
ticks.constraint: English vocabulary as undefined, inconsistently spelled, and authority-less
ticks.detail: Samuel Johnson's Dictionary (1755) standardized English spelling, defined words with precision and illustrative quotations, and established the dictionary as an authoritative reference. Johnson's self-deprecating definition of lexicographer ('a writer of dictionaries, a harmless drudge') didn't diminish its impact. Every English dictionary since builds on Johnson's methodology.

links.label: Britannica — A Dictionary of the English Language

ticks.because: The Daily Courant (1702) had created a market for standardized written English consumed by a daily mass audience. Johnson's earlier lexicographic effort (1755) had assembled the team and the methodology — illustrative quotations, etymological notes. The dictionary itself is the synthesis — nine years, five assistants, definitions grounded in literary citation. English usage becomes describable, and the dictionary as authority is established.

ticks.name: International Phonetic Alphabet
ticks.constraint: language transcription as varying incompatibly across different national traditions
ticks.detail: The International Phonetic Alphabet (1888) provided a standardized system for transcribing any human speech sound using a consistent set of symbols. Linguists could describe any language's sounds precisely. Language documentation, foreign language teaching, speech therapy, and computational linguistics all use the IPA. Every language's pronunciation can now be precisely recorded.

links.label: International Phonetic Association — History of the IPA

ticks.because: Bell's telephone (1876) had begun transmitting voice across distance, requiring that phoneticians describe what sounds were being carried. Braille (1837) had demonstrated that articulation systems could be deliberately engineered. Edison's phonograph (1877) made speech recordable. The IPA is the systematic answer — one symbol per distinct human speech sound, applicable across any language. Linguistic transcription becomes universal.

ticks.name: Saussure / synchronic linguistics
ticks.constraint: linguistics as exclusively historical (how languages changed over time)
ticks.detail: Saussure distinguished synchronic linguistics (studying a language at a single moment) from diachronic (historical). He argued the synchronic perspective — language as a system of relationships — was the more fundamental. Structural linguistics, which analyzed language as a system rather than as historical development, dominates 20th-century linguistics.

links.label: Columbia University Press — Course in General Linguistics
Wikisource — Cours de linguistique générale (full French text)

ticks.because: The Universal Postal Union (1874) had proven that institutions could be defined by their internal structural relationships rather than the flow of historical accident. Saussure transposes that move into language: the meaning of a word is not its history but its relation to every other word in the system at the same moment. Structural linguistics dominates the twentieth century from this distinction.

ticks.name: Machine translation first attempts (Weaver memo)
ticks.constraint: translation as requiring human linguistic knowledge
ticks.detail: Warren Weaver's 1949 memo proposed using computers for translation, analogizing it to cryptography — finding the 'code' underlying natural language. The first MT systems emerged in the 1950s, overpromising and underdelivering. But the research program established NLP as a field. Statistical MT (1990s), neural MT (2016), and LLM-based translation (2020s) all trace to Weaver's memo.
ticks.because: The OED (1928) had completed the comprehensive lexical reference for English. Nuremberg's simultaneous interpretation (1945) demonstrated industrial-scale cross-language work was operationally possible. Abstract Expressionism's New York emergence (1947) showed cultural production was globalizing. Weaver's memo proposes the obvious next step — apply wartime cryptanalysis methods to translation. Computational linguistics becomes a research field.

ticks.name: Chomsky / universal grammar hypothesis
ticks.constraint: human language as infinitely diverse and mutually incomparable
ticks.detail: Chomsky proposed that all human languages share deep structural properties — a universal grammar — which is biologically innate. Language acquisition is not imitation learning but the triggering of an innate capacity. This positioned linguistics within cognitive science and biology. The debate about what is universal and what is culturally specific in language continues.
ticks.because: Weaver's machine-translation memo (1949) had reframed translation as a computational decoding problem. The Georgetown-IBM demo (1954) showed cross-linguistic mapping was technically tractable. Chomsky's Universal Grammar hypothesis is the linguistic answer — if all human languages can be mapped to a common abstract structure, that structure must be innate. Modern linguistics, computational linguistics, and the cognitive science of language begin from this argument.

ticks.name: Twitter / microblogging and public real-time discourse
ticks.constraint: public written discourse as requiring editorial infrastructure
ticks.detail: Twitter's 140-character limit (later 280) created a new form: the public microblog. Real-time commentary on events, direct access to public figures, and a global shared timeline emerged. The Arab Spring, #MeToo, and the 2016 election were all Twitter-shaped phenomena. The character limit was a design constraint that became an aesthetic and a genre.

links.label: LA Times: Twitter creator Jack Dorsey on the founding document

ticks.because: Unicode (1991) had made digital text language-agnostic; statistical machine translation (1993) extended cross-language reach; YouTube (2005) democratized video. Twitter applies the same democratization to short text — 140 characters, public by default, real-time global feed. Politics, news, and casual public discourse reorder around the timeline.

ticks.name: Hippocratic corpus / natural disease causation
ticks.constraint: disease as caused by divine punishment or demonic possession
ticks.detail: The Hippocratic school (5th century BC) rejected supernatural explanations for disease systematically for the first time. 'Sacred disease' (epilepsy) was caused by the brain, not the gods. Natural causes, clinical observation, prognosis, and diet became medicine's tools. The Hippocratic Oath established medical ethics. Western medicine's naturalistic tradition begins here.

links.label: Hippocrates — On the Sacred Disease (MIT Internet Classics Archive)

ticks.because: Trepanation (3100 BC) had proven physical intervention into the body could heal. Sushruta's surgical manual (400 BC) and Bian Que's moxibustion (500 BC) showed parallel naturalistic medical traditions in India and China. The Hippocratic synthesis is the Greek version — disease attributed systematically to natural causes, observation and prognosis become tools, and the Oath establishes professional ethics.

ticks.name: Galen's medical synthesis
ticks.constraint: Greek and Roman medical knowledge as fragmented across competing schools
ticks.detail: Claudius Galen systematized Greek medical knowledge into a comprehensive framework that dominated Western medicine for 1,400 years. His errors (blood is made in the liver; arteries carry air) were as consequential as his insights. Medicine couldn't advance until Vesalius (1543) and Harvey (1628) dismantled Galen — showing how a wrong authoritative synthesis can block progress.

links.label: West — Galen and the beginnings of Western physiology (AJP Lung)

ticks.because: Trepanation (3100 BC) proved surgery could heal. The Hippocratic corpus (400 BC) put disease into a naturalistic frame. Galen's earlier work (130 AD) had begun a comprehensive theory of pulse and circulation, mapped via vivisection of pigs (175 AD) and the doctrine of laudable pus (180 AD). The 200 AD synthesis is the binding move — one comprehensive medical theory readable across the empire, which dominates Western medicine for fourteen hundred years and proves the cost of an authoritative wrong synthesis.

ticks.name: Al-Zahrawi / surgical instruments and techniques
ticks.constraint: surgery as undocumented craft knowledge passed informally
ticks.detail: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi's Kitab al-Tasrif included the first illustrated surgical encyclopedia — describing over 200 surgical instruments, many of which he invented. Ligature of blood vessels, catgut sutures, and surgical treatment of cancer were documented. European surgery through the Renaissance drew heavily on Al-Zahrawi's translations.

links.label: Internet Archive: Albucasis on Surgery and Instruments (UC Press 1973)
UC Press: Albucasis On Surgery and Instruments

ticks.because: Galen's medical synthesis (200) had set the comprehensive medieval frame; Qusta ibn Luqa's On Numbness (900) and Ibn Tulun's hospital (872) had built institutional infrastructure for systematic practice. Al-Zahrawi's Kitab al-Tasrif catalogues two hundred surgical instruments, with operation-specific descriptions — the surgical reference text that runs European medicine for the next five centuries.

ticks.name: Black Death / quarantine invented
ticks.constraint: epidemic disease spread as unstoppable once it reached a port city
ticks.detail: Venice's 1377 law requiring ships from infected ports to anchor for 30 days (later 40 — quarantine from 'quarantina giorni') was the first systematic epidemic containment measure. Quarantine proved partially effective against the plague and was adopted across Mediterranean ports. Every subsequent epidemic response — COVID-19 lockdowns included — descends from Venice's 1377 law.
ticks.because: Eyeglasses (1286) and the first recorded autopsy (1286) demonstrated that medical practice was institutionalizing in late-medieval Italy. The Black Death's arrival forces the operational answer — Ragusa and Venice impose forty-day isolation periods on arriving ships in 1377. The institutional concept of quarantine, durable enough that we still use it word for word.

ticks.name: Crawford Long / first use of ether in surgery
ticks.constraint: surgical pain as an unavoidable feature of any operation
ticks.detail: Crawford Long removed a neck tumor from James Venable under ether anesthesia in Jefferson, Georgia in 1842 — four years before Morton's public Boston demonstration. Long didn't publish. The tick of surgical anesthesia was independently achieved and publicly demonstrated by multiple people within years of each other. The concept was ready; the first systematic demonstration mattered.

links.label: Harvard Countway — Long's Use of Sulphuric Ether
Georgia History — Marker Monday: Crawford W. Long and Anesthesia

ticks.because: Jenner's vaccination (1796) had introduced systematic preventive medicine. The 1842 cluster — Crawford Long's first ether anesthesia and the broader emergence of anesthesia practice — combines with Schleiden-Schwann's cell theory (1839) to mark the era's medical upheaval. Long's removal of a neck tumor under ether is the first painless surgery; the modern operating room becomes possible.

ticks.name: John Snow / cholera and epidemiology
ticks.constraint: cholera as transmitted by miasma (bad air)
ticks.detail: John Snow's mapping of cholera cases around the Broad Street pump during London's 1854 epidemic — and his removal of the pump handle — was the founding act of modern epidemiology. He proved cholera was waterborne before germ theory explained how. The detective work of tracing disease to a source — the epidemiological method — begins here.

links.label: John Snow Archive: On the Mode of Communication of Cholera
John Snow Archive: The Broad Street Pump 1854 episode

ticks.because: Semmelweis's handwashing intervention (1847), Phineas Gage's frontal-lobe case (1848), and the plaster-of-Paris fracture cast (Mathijsen, 1851) demonstrated that mid-nineteenth-century medicine was acquiring systematic empirical methods. Snow's mapping of cholera cases around the Broad Street pump — proving water-borne transmission — invents modern epidemiology. Public health interventions become evidence-based; sanitation infrastructure follows.

ticks.name: X-ray diagnosis (first clinical use)
ticks.constraint: internal structures as visible only after death or major surgery
ticks.detail: Within weeks of Röntgen's November 1895 discovery, X-rays were being used clinically — imaging broken bones, foreign objects, and lung disease. The first radiograph of a living hand (Röntgen's wife, Anna Bertha Ludwig) showed the skeleton and a wedding ring. Diagnostic medicine was fundamentally changed — the body became transparent to investigation without surgery.
ticks.because: Pasteur's rabies vaccine (1885) and the diphtheria antitoxin (1890s) demonstrated that nineteenth-century medicine could intervene at molecular precision. Röntgen's X-ray discovery in November 1895 is repurposed for clinical use within weeks — surgeons see broken bones without cutting, foreign objects locatable in tissue. Modern radiology begins almost instantly.

ticks.name: Insulin treatment of diabetes
ticks.constraint: type 1 diabetes as invariably fatal within months of diagnosis
ticks.detail: Before insulin, patients with type 1 diabetes were placed on starvation diets that extended life by months. Banting and Best's 1921 extraction of insulin from dog pancreas, first used in Leonard Thompson in January 1922, reversed the death sentence. Within a year, insulin was being manufactured industrially. The most immediate life-saving pharmaceutical discovery in history.

links.label: Zinman — Discovery of insulin in Toronto: 100-year journey (Diabetologia)
Canadian Encyclopedia — The Discovery of Insulin
Parks Canada — Discovery of Insulin National Historic Event

ticks.because: The Spanish flu (1918) had taught medicine the scale at which public health crises could move. The Banting-Best discovery of insulin (1921) provided the molecule. Insulin's use in clinical treatment — first administered to Leonard Thompson, January 1922 — is the moment Type 1 diabetes stops being a near-immediate death sentence. The first endocrine therapy; modern hormone medicine begins.

ticks.name: Sulfonamide drugs / first antibacterials
ticks.constraint: bacterial infection as untreatable by any pharmacological agent
ticks.detail: Gerhard Domagk discovered Prontosil's antibacterial effect in 1932 — the first sulfonamide drug. It was the first antibacterial effective enough to use clinically, saving lives from puerperal fever, pneumonia, and meningitis before penicillin. FDR's son's life was saved by sulfonamides in 1936, accelerating US adoption. They transformed infectious disease medicine before penicillin arrived.
ticks.because: Fleming's penicillin (1928), the EEG (1928), and the isolation of vitamin C (1928) had marked the late 1920s as a peak biomedical period. Domagk's Prontosil — synthesized as a textile dye, found to kill streptococcus in mice — is the first synthetic antibacterial, demonstrating that designer molecules can fight infection without the production complications of penicillin. Modern pharmaceutical chemistry begins on this success.

ticks.name: Coronary artery bypass surgery (Favaloro)
ticks.constraint: coronary artery disease as treatable only medically
ticks.detail: René Favaloro's development of the coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) in 1967 created a surgical treatment for blocked coronary arteries. A vein harvested from the leg bypasses the obstruction. CABG became the most common open-heart surgery — over 400,000 performed annually in the US. It demonstrably extended millions of lives with coronary disease.

links.label: Favaloro — Landmarks in Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery (Circulation 1998)
Favaloro — Critical Analysis of CABG: 30-Year Journey (JACC)
Encyclopedia of Cleveland History — René Favaloro

ticks.because: Starzl's liver transplant (1963) had proven that complex organ surgery was viable. The hepatitis B virus discovery (1965) demonstrated the era's biomedical investigative range. Favaloro's coronary bypass technique extends both — using a saphenous vein graft to route blood around a blocked coronary artery. Heart disease surgery becomes a reliable intervention.

ticks.name: CT scan (clinical widespread use)
ticks.constraint: imaging limited to flat X-ray shadows of three-dimensional structures
ticks.detail: Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack's CT scanner (first clinical use 1972, widespread by late 1970s) reconstructed three-dimensional cross-sections from multiple X-ray angles. Tumors, strokes, and internal bleeding that X-ray couldn't show became visible. CT scanning revolutionized emergency medicine, oncology, and surgical planning. The 2D X-ray became a 3D diagnostic tool.

links.label: PubMed: Ambrose & Hounsfield, Computerized transverse axial tomography (1973)
Royal Society: Hounsfield, The E.M.I. Scanner (1977)

ticks.because: The first clinical CT scanner (1971) was the platform. The first successful bone marrow transplant (1968) had demonstrated that complex medical-engineering interventions were succeeding. CT's widespread clinical use after 1972 — Hounsfield and Cormack's reconstruction algorithm operating on x-ray slice projections — gives medicine its first three-dimensional non-invasive imaging. Diagnosis becomes radically more precise across neurology, oncology, and emergency medicine.

ticks.name: HIV identified / AIDS crisis response
ticks.constraint: retroviruses as medically unimportant human pathogens
ticks.detail: The identification of HIV (Gallo/Montagnier, 1983-1984) and the subsequent development of HIV tests, AZT treatment (1987), combination therapy (1996), and eventually pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP, 2012) tracked medical science's response to a pandemic in real time. AIDS also transformed drug approval processes, patient advocacy in medicine, and the science of antiviral pharmacology.

links.label: Science 1983 — Barré-Sinoussi et al. discovery of HIV

ticks.because: Smallpox declared eradicated (1980), HIV identified with the ELISA test (1983), and PCR (1983) demonstrated that early-1980s biomedical infrastructure was advancing rapidly. The HIV identification and the AIDS-crisis response — activism reordering FDA processes, antiretroviral development, public health communication — become a template for every later epidemic response. Direct medical, social, and political consequences continue thirty-five years later.

ticks.name: Viagra / erectile dysfunction treatment
ticks.constraint: male sexual dysfunction as untreatable by pharmacology
ticks.detail: Sildenafil (Viagra) was discovered as a side effect of cardiovascular research. Its 1998 approval demonstrated that sexual function was pharmacologically modifiable — and that a medication could address conditions previously treated as purely psychological. It also launched the era of direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical advertising and changed how openly sexual health is discussed medically.

links.label: CNN — Viagra: The little blue pill that could (timeline)
Ghofrani et al. — Sildenafil: from angina to ED (Nature Reviews Drug Discovery)

ticks.because: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy's standardization (1990), deep brain stimulation's FDA approval (1997), and the metagenomic discovery of the microbiome (1998) demonstrated late-1990s medicine's rapid maturation. Sildenafil — Viagra — is discovered as a side effect of cardiovascular research. Pharmaceutical companies thereafter actively investigate side effects of trial compounds; modern lifestyle pharmacology takes off.

ticks.name: Human papillomavirus vaccine (Gardasil)
ticks.constraint: cervical cancer as unpreventable
ticks.detail: The HPV vaccine prevented the leading viral cause of cervical cancer — a cancer killing 300,000 women annually. It was the first vaccine explicitly designed to prevent cancer (rather than preventing infection as a side effect). Cancer prevention through vaccination became a demonstrated reality. The principle is being extended to other cancer-causing viruses.
ticks.because: The da Vinci robotic surgery system (2000), the Human Genome Project's completion (2003), and the CRISPR discovery (2003) had each marked early-2000s medicine as a high-technology era. Gardasil — Merck's HPV vaccine — prevents the leading viral cause of cervical cancer. Cancer prevention via vaccination becomes a clinical reality, with public-health implications still unfolding.

ticks.name: Liquid biopsy / cancer detection from blood
ticks.constraint: cancer monitoring requiring tumor tissue biopsies
ticks.detail: Circulating tumor DNA in blood can now detect cancer recurrence, monitor treatment response, and screen for early-stage cancer without surgical biopsy. Liquid biopsy companies (GRAIL, Foundation Medicine) promise multi-cancer early detection from a single blood draw. If validated at scale, catching cancers at stage 1 rather than stage 4 would transform oncology outcomes.

links.label: NCBI PMC — Liquid biopsy clinical applications
Wikipedia: Liquid biopsy / cancer detection from blood

ticks.because: Gardasil's HPV vaccine (2006), CRISPR-Cas9 as genome editing tool (2012), and the first successful partial face transplant on Isabelle Dinoire (2005) demonstrated that early-twenty-first-century medicine was rapidly innovating. Liquid biopsy — detecting circulating tumor DNA in blood — gives cancer detection a non-invasive monitoring tool. Recurrence detection, treatment response, and early diagnosis all become possible from a blood draw.

ticks.name: Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius / telescope astronomy
ticks.constraint: astronomical knowledge as limited to naked-eye observations of the same sky for 2000 years
ticks.detail: Galileo's Starry Messenger (1610) reported mountains on the Moon, four moons of Jupiter, and thousands of stars invisible to the naked eye. The telescope extended human perception beyond its biological limits for the first time in astronomy. The Milky Way resolved into individual stars. The universe was suddenly, demonstrably, vastly larger than anyone had known.
ticks.because: Galileo's earlier telescope work (1609) gave him the instrument; Eratosthenes (250 BC) had established that careful measurement could derive astronomical truths. Galileo's Two New Sciences (1589) had proven motion was mathematically describable. Kepler's first two laws (1609) gave a mathematical model of planetary motion that needed observational tests. Sidereus Nuncius is the field report — Jupiter's moons, lunar craters, the phases of Venus — that settles the Copernican question observationally.

ticks.name: Newton's calculus / mathematics of change
ticks.constraint: continuous change as undescribable by existing mathematics
ticks.detail: Newton (and independently Leibniz) invented calculus — the mathematics of continuous change. It allowed the calculation of instantaneous velocity, areas under curves, and the behavior of functions at any point. Every physics equation involving rates of change uses calculus. Engineering, economics, statistics, and machine learning all depend on calculus as their mathematical language.

links.label: Newton Project Oxford: Front Matter to Principia (1687)
Project Gutenberg: Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica

ticks.because: Rømer's speed-of-light measurement (1676) had introduced rates-of-change into astronomy. Hooke's elasticity law (1678) showed that physical response was proportional to displacement — a derivative relation in everything but name. Papin's steam digester (1679) demonstrated that pressure responded continuously to temperature. Newton's calculus is the formal machinery for all those rate-and-accumulation relations — invented in parallel with Leibniz, and now the mathematics of change underlying every physics equation since.

ticks.name: Lavoisier / conservation of mass
ticks.constraint: chemical reactions as transforming the fundamental nature of matter
ticks.detail: Antoine Lavoisier demonstrated that mass is conserved in chemical reactions — matter is neither created nor destroyed, only transformed. This demolished phlogiston theory and established stoichiometry. Modern chemistry's ability to predict and control reactions, design drugs, and engineer materials all depend on conservation of mass as a foundational principle.
ticks.because: The Celsius scale (1742) had made temperature standardized. Black's latent heat (1762) had introduced thermochemistry as quantitative. Franklin's kite (1752) and Camper's facial-angle work (1768) showed natural philosophy applying measurement to electricity and to anatomy. Lavoisier's combustion experiments close the loop on chemistry — mass in equals mass out, every reaction balances. The bookkeeping principle of all subsequent chemistry.

ticks.name: Electromagnetism unified (Faraday/Oersted)
ticks.constraint: electricity and magnetism as independent phenomena
ticks.detail: Faraday's discovery that changing magnetic fields generate electrical currents (1831) completed the electromagnetic unity that Oersted's 1820 discovery had begun. The electric generator, the electric motor, and all electrical power technology depend on electromagnetic induction. Maxwell's later mathematical unification (1865) made the connection theoretical.

links.label: Niels Bohr Institute — Ørsted's electromagnetism discovery
Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Physics — Electromagnetism in the 19th Century

ticks.because: Dalton's atomic theory (1808) had insisted that matter was particulate and rule-governed. Fraunhofer's solar absorption lines (1814) proved that light carried information about the matter it touched. Oersted noticed that an electric current deflected a compass needle (1820), and Faraday closed the loop with electromagnetic induction (1831). Electricity and magnetism stop being two phenomena and become one — the precondition for every motor, generator, and Maxwell equation that follows.

ticks.name: Second law of thermodynamics (Clausius/Kelvin)
ticks.constraint: perpetual motion machines as conceivable
ticks.detail: Clausius and Kelvin independently formulated the second law: heat flows from hot to cold, entropy never decreases in a closed system, and perpetual motion is impossible. The universe tends toward disorder. Time has a direction. Every engine efficiency limit, every refrigerator design, every understanding of why aging happens traces to the second law.

links.label: SMU: Howard, S is for Entropy — What Was Clausius Thinking? (PDF)
NASA ADS: Clausius, Annalen der Physik 1854

ticks.because: Oersted (1820) and Faraday's electrolysis (1833) had unified electricity and chemistry. Joule's mechanical equivalent of heat (1845) showed energy could be quantified across forms. Kelvin's absolute scale (1848) anchored temperature. Clausius and Kelvin's second law completes the framework — entropy increases, heat flows downhill, perpetual motion is impossible. Thermodynamics becomes a complete theory.

ticks.name: Michelson-Morley experiment / no ether
ticks.constraint: light as requiring a medium (ether) through which to travel
ticks.detail: Michelson and Morley's interferometer found no difference in the speed of light regardless of Earth's direction of travel through the supposed ether. Light didn't need a medium. The ether didn't exist. The result was called 'the most important negative result in physics.' It set the stage for Einstein's special relativity 18 years later.

links.label: Michelson & Morley 1887 — On the Relative Motion of Earth (American Journal of Science)

ticks.because: Mendeleev's periodic table (1869), Maxwell's demon (1867 / 1873), Boltzmann's H-theorem (1872), and Edison's light bulb (1879) had each pushed nineteenth-century physics into precise quantitative territory. Michelson and Morley's interferometer measures the speed of light in two perpendicular directions, expecting to see Earth's motion through the luminiferous ether. They find nothing — the null result that destroys ether and forces relativity.

ticks.name: Einstein's annus mirabilis (four papers)
ticks.constraint: Newtonian mechanics, electromagnetism, and thermodynamics as complete and compatible
ticks.detail: In 1905, Einstein published four papers that each transformed physics: the photoelectric effect (quantum theory), Brownian motion (atomic theory), special relativity (space-time), and mass-energy equivalence (E=mc²). Any one would have secured his reputation. Together they define the modern physical worldview. No single year in science's history has been as productive.

links.label: Smithsonian — The Year of Albert Einstein

ticks.because: Einstein's photoelectric effect paper (1905) and special relativity paper (1905) are facets of the same cluster. The four 1905 papers — photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity, and mass-energy equivalence — collectively transform physics. Atomic theory becomes confirmed; relativistic mechanics replaces Newtonian; the photon enters physics; E = mc² is established. Modern physics's foundational year.

ticks.name: Superconductivity discovered (Kamerlingh Onnes)
ticks.constraint: electrical resistance as an unavoidable property of conductors at any temperature
ticks.detail: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered that mercury's electrical resistance dropped to exactly zero at 4.2 Kelvin. Superconductors have no resistance — current flows forever without energy loss. Applications include MRI magnets, particle accelerator magnets, and potentially lossless power transmission. High-temperature superconductors (1986+) brought the phenomenon closer to practical use.

links.label: KNAW: Kamerlingh Onnes 1911 Disappearance of resistance of mercury (PDF)
Lorentz: Van Delft & Kes, The discovery of superconductivity (PDF)

ticks.because: Einstein's Brownian motion (1905) had clinched atomic theory experimentally, and Millikan's measurement of the electron charge (1909) plus Rutherford's nuclear atom (1911) settled the constituents of matter. Kamerlingh Onnes — having just liquefied helium — cooled mercury below 4.2 K and observed resistance vanish, an effect classical physics could not explain. The phenomenon waited 46 years for the BCS theory to explain it.

ticks.name: Nuclear magnetic resonance discovered
ticks.constraint: atomic nuclei as unobservable without disturbing them
ticks.detail: Isidor Rabi's discovery of nuclear magnetic resonance (1938) showed that atomic nuclei, placed in a magnetic field and exposed to radio waves, absorb energy at characteristic frequencies. NMR spectroscopy became chemistry's most powerful analytical tool for determining molecular structure. Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell extended it (1946). Paul Lauterbur's spatial encoding (1973) created MRI.
ticks.because: Chadwick's neutron (1932) gave physicists a probe that could enter the nucleus without electrical interference. Rabi's beam-resonance technique uses that probe — placing nuclei in a strong magnetic field and reading their characteristic radio-frequency response. NMR turns the inside of an atom into a measurable signal, enabling molecular structure determination, then MRI, then most of modern chemistry's analytical toolkit.

ticks.name: Solar cell (Bell Labs / practical photovoltaics)
ticks.constraint: solar energy as thermally convertible but not electrically
ticks.detail: Chapin, Fuller, and Pearson's silicon solar cell (1954) converted sunlight to electricity at 6% efficiency — enough to run a radio. Bell Labs' goal was powering remote telephone equipment. The cell was too expensive for general use for 50 years. Solar panel costs have dropped 99.7% since 1977. Solar is now the cheapest source of electricity in history.

links.label: Chapin, Fuller, Pearson — A New Silicon p-n Junction Photocell (J. Appl. Phys. 1954)
APS — Bell Labs Demonstrates First Practical Silicon Solar Cell (April 25 1954)

ticks.because: Fermi's controlled chain reaction (1942) had proven nuclear physics could engineer energy. Holography (1947) and radiocarbon dating (1949) had each turned exotic physical effects into practical instruments. The maser (1953) showed quantum physics yielding usable devices. Bell Labs's silicon photovoltaic cell is the same trick applied to sunlight — 6% efficient initially, 99.7% cheaper now, and currently the cheapest source of electricity in history.

ticks.name: Feynman's 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom'
ticks.constraint: manufacturing as limited to top-down machining and chemistry
ticks.detail: Richard Feynman's 1959 lecture proposed building machines atom by atom — bottom-up nanotechnology. He suggested writing the Encyclopedia Britannica on a pinhead and building machines of molecular scale. The lecture launched nanotechnology as a conceptual field 25 years before it became experimentally feasible. Every molecular machine, nanoscale drug delivery system, and quantum dot display traces to Feynman's vision.

links.label: Zyvex: Feynman, There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom (1959 transcript)
Caltech Magazine: Original publication (Engineering and Science 1960)

ticks.because: The Bell Labs solar cell (1954), the neutrino detection (1956), and the integrated circuit (1958) demonstrated that physics-engineering precision was rapidly compounding. Feynman's 1959 lecture is the call to arms — proposing atom-by-atom assembly, with implications for storage density, surgery, and computation. Nanotechnology as a research aspiration begins from this talk.

ticks.name: Altair 8800 / personal computing as hobbyist
ticks.constraint: computers as institutional property requiring professional operation
ticks.detail: The Altair 8800 kit computer (Popular Electronics cover, January 1975) made computing available to individual hobbyists for the first time. Bill Gates and Paul Allen saw the cover and wrote BASIC for it — founding Microsoft. Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs saw the Homebrew Computer Club built around it — founding Apple. The personal computer revolution began in a hobbyist kit.
ticks.because: Xerox PARC's Alto and the modern computing interface (1973) had specified what personal computing should look like. SQL's emergence (1974) showed that database access was becoming standardized. The Altair 8800 kit on Popular Electronics' January 1975 cover is the affordable kit form — sold for $397, programmable in switches and lights. The hobbyist personal computer market and the Homebrew Computer Club (where Jobs and Wozniak meet) start here.

ticks.name: Recombinant insulin / biotech industry born
ticks.constraint: pharmaceutical production as limited to extraction from biological sources
ticks.detail: Genentech's recombinant human insulin (approved 1982, licensed to Eli Lilly) was the first recombinant DNA pharmaceutical product. Previously, insulin came from pig and cow pancreases — a limited, allergenic supply. Recombinant technology produced unlimited, human-identical insulin. It also created the biotechnology industry and the business model of pharma-biotech partnership.

links.label: NSF Impacts: Biotech Pioneers — rDNA and Insulin
Genentech: First Successful Laboratory Production of Human Insulin (Sep 1978)

ticks.because: The 401(k) defined contribution retirement plan (1978), Woodward's total synthesis (1970), and the Wyoming LLC introduction (1977) demonstrated that late-1970s American institutional and scientific innovation was rapidly maturing. Genentech's recombinant human insulin — produced by inserting the human insulin gene into bacteria — is the first commercial product of the new molecular biology. The biotech industry as a category is born.

ticks.name: Hubble Space Telescope launch
ticks.constraint: astronomical observation as limited by atmospheric distortion
ticks.detail: The Hubble Space Telescope — once its flawed mirror was corrected by the 1993 servicing mission — provided images of unprecedented clarity from above Earth's atmosphere. Its ultra-deep field images revealed galaxies 13 billion light-years away. Hubble's images changed humanity's sense of the universe's scale and age, and enabled precision cosmology.

links.label: NASA Science — April 25 1990 Deployment of Hubble

ticks.because: Inflation theory (1981) gave cosmology a coherent framework; the W and Z boson discoveries (1983) had validated the Standard Model at the smallest scales. Hubble launches into space to give cosmology its instrument — a telescope above the atmosphere with the resolution to see galaxies thirteen billion light-years out. After the 1993 mirror correction, precision cosmology becomes possible.

ticks.name: Bitcoin whitepaper implemented / blockchain live
ticks.constraint: digital scarcity as impossible without a trusted central authority
ticks.detail: Satoshi Nakamoto's blockchain made digital assets scarce for the first time — each bitcoin can only be spent once, enforced by a distributed ledger. Solving the double-spend problem without a central authority was the tick. Ethereum (2015) extended this to programmable smart contracts. DeFi, NFTs, DAOs, and programmable money follow from the blockchain's ability to create digital scarcity.

links.label: bitcoin.org: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (PDF)
Wikipedia: Bitcoin whitepaper implemented / blockchain live

ticks.because: Kindle (2007), GitHub (2008), Stack Overflow (2008), and Django (2008) bracket a moment when both consumer and developer infrastructure was being rebuilt around networked, asynchronous platforms. Satoshi's Bitcoin — a peer-to-peer electronic cash system using proof-of-work to achieve consensus without a central authority — solved the digital double-spend problem and started the entire blockchain ecosystem.

ticks.name: Watson wins Jeopardy / NLP crosses human performance
ticks.constraint: natural language question-answering as requiring human-level understanding
ticks.detail: IBM's Watson defeated Jeopardy! champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter in February 2011. Watson used statistical machine learning on massive text corpora to answer questions requiring inference, wordplay, and broad knowledge. The demonstration was symbolic but real: machine question-answering had crossed a human-level threshold on a well-defined task. AI's public credibility changed.

links.label: Wikipedia: Watson wins Jeopardy / NLP crosses human performance

ticks.because: The iPad (2010) had just normalized always-connected mobile computing, and Node.js (2009) plus MongoDB (2009) showed that web infrastructure was scaling to handle real-time queries at consumer scale. Watson combined statistical language processing with massive parallel evidence retrieval — beating Jennings and Rutter — and signaled that natural-language QA was no longer a research toy.

ticks.name: AlphaGo Zero / self-taught superhuman play
ticks.constraint: superhuman game performance requiring human expert knowledge for training
ticks.detail: AlphaGo Zero learned Go entirely through self-play against itself, with no human games as training data — and surpassed all previous AlphaGo versions within days. It discovered moves and strategies that human players had never conceived. The tick: reinforcement learning from self-play could achieve superhuman performance in complex domains without human knowledge as a starting point.

links.label: Singh, Okun, Jackson — Learning to play Go from scratch (Nature)
Silver et al. — Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge (Nature 2017)
Gibney — Self-taught AI is best yet at Go (Nature)

ticks.because: ResNet (2015), AlphaGo's defeat of Lee Sedol (2016), and federated learning (2016) demonstrated that deep learning's capabilities and infrastructure were rapidly compounding.
