AlphaGo Zero — trained entirely through self-play, no human game data — defeats the previous AlphaGo a hundred to zero. Self-supervised learning becomes credible at superhuman performance levels.

ticks.name: GPT-2 / language generation crosses coherence threshold
ticks.constraint: machine-generated text as obviously non-human in quality
ticks.detail: OpenAI's GPT-2 generated text coherent enough that OpenAI initially refused to release the full model citing misuse concerns. The debate itself was the tick — it was the first time a language model's output was taken seriously enough to consider withholding. GPT-2 established that scale and training data could produce qualitatively new language capability.

links.label: OpenAI: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2 paper PDF)
OpenAI: Release Strategies and Social Impacts of Language Models (GPT-2 staged release)

ticks.because: Google's Neural Machine Translation (2016) had shown that end-to-end neural systems could match decades of statistical MT, and BERT (2018) demonstrated that transformer-pretrained representations transferred across NLP tasks. GPT-2 took the same transformer pretraining and turned it into open-ended generation — the first system whose multi-paragraph output was indistinguishable from human writing on quick read.

ticks.name: Codex / GitHub Copilot (code generation)
ticks.constraint: software development requiring a programmer to write every line of code
ticks.detail: OpenAI's Codex model, trained on billions of lines of code, could generate functional code from natural language descriptions. GitHub Copilot (2021) made it available to developers as an AI pair programmer. Productivity gains of 20-55% were documented. The click: programming became less about remembering syntax and more about specifying intent. Non-programmers could produce working code.

links.label: Chen et al. 2021 — Evaluating LLMs Trained on Code (arXiv)

ticks.because: GPT-2 (2019) had crossed the coherence threshold for open-ended natural-language generation. Codex extended the same approach to programming languages — fine-tuned on GitHub's public code — and made AI-assisted line-by-line code completion a daily developer practice via Copilot.

ticks.name: Bronze weapons / military metallurgy
ticks.constraint: weapons as limited to stone, bone, and wood
ticks.detail: Bronze—copper and tin alloyed—produced weapons far harder and sharper than stone while retaining workability. The Bronze Age military balance depended on access to both metals. Armies with bronze weapons dominated those without. The metallurgical arms race that began with bronze runs through iron, steel, aluminum, titanium, and carbon fiber.

links.label: Chen — Sumerian Arsenic Copper and Tin Bronze Metallurgy 5300-1500 BC (PDF)
Maddin — Mesopotamian bronze metallurgy in 3rd millennium BC (ScienceDirect)
Dong — The King's Spear: Bronze Weapons in Ur III Period (Academia)

ticks.because: Organized warfare (3000 BC) had created standing armies; fortification walls (3000 BC) had made cities defensible. Bronze weapons are the offensive answer — alloyed copper-and-tin tools and blades vastly superior to stone, distributed through the same long-distance trade networks that fed the cities. Military metallurgy and the Bronze Age power structure begin together.

ticks.name: Battle of Marathon / citizen-soldier victory
ticks.constraint: professional or mercenary armies as necessarily superior to citizen soldiers
ticks.detail: Ten thousand Athenian citizen hoplites defeated a Persian army twice their size at Marathon. The victory established that motivated citizens, fighting for their own city, could defeat professional imperial armies. The civic-military connection — the idea that political freedom produces military effectiveness — shaped Western military thought for 2,500 years.

links.label: History Guide: Herodotus on the Victory at Marathon

ticks.because: Assyrian siege warfare (700 BC) and the Persian Immortals corps (500 BC) demonstrated professional military elite power. The Greek phalanx (500 BC) gave hoplites an answer in formation. Marathon — ten thousand Athenian citizen hoplites defeating a Persian force twice their size — is the proof that disciplined citizen-soldiers can decide a war. Athenian confidence in citizen virtue underwrites democratic politics for the next two centuries.

ticks.name: Alexander's siege of Tyre / naval and siege warfare
ticks.constraint: island cities as impregnable to land-based armies
ticks.detail: Alexander the Great besieged Tyre — an island fortress — for seven months by building a causeway from the mainland. He combined naval blockade, siege towers, and engineering to take what everyone assumed was safe. The siege established that no position is truly impregnable given sufficient engineering resources and political will.

links.label: World History Encyclopedia — Siege of Tyre
Wikipedia: Alexander's siege of Tyre / naval and siege warfare

ticks.because: Sun Tzu's Art of War (400 BC) had codified strategic principles. The Chinese repeating crossbow (400 BC) showed sustained projectile warfare. Combined arms warfare under Philip and Alexander (350 BC) integrated multiple formation types. Alexander's seven-month siege of island Tyre — building a causeway from the mainland — is the operational breakthrough that combines naval assault with siege engineering at unprecedented scale.

ticks.name: Hannibal crosses the Alps / strategic surprise
ticks.constraint: Alpine mountain ranges as an impassable barrier to military movement
ticks.detail: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps with 37 elephants and 50,000 troops achieved total strategic surprise. Three subsequent victories (Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae) nearly destroyed Rome. Cannae (216 BC) — where Hannibal encircled a larger Roman army — remains the paradigmatic example of operational encirclement studied at military academies worldwide.

links.label: Smithsonian — How (and Where) Did Hannibal Cross the Alps?

ticks.because: Roman roads (312 BC) and the manipular legion (264 BC) gave Rome the era's dominant logistics-and-tactics combination. The Roman Navy's Corvus boarding bridge (260 BC) demonstrated naval engineering precedent. Hannibal's Alps crossing — thirty-seven elephants and fifty thousand troops over snowed passes — is the strategic surprise that defeats Roman expectation. Strategy as deception and unexpected approach becomes a permanent military category.

ticks.name: Caesar's Gallic Wars / total conquest doctrine
ticks.constraint: conquest as requiring the submission of ruling elites only
ticks.detail: Caesar's conquest of Gaul (58-50 BC) killed approximately 1 million Gauls and enslaved another million — roughly a third of the total population. The deliberate destruction of the population's capacity to resist, not just its military forces, was systematic. Caesar's Commentarii documented the doctrine that would be called 'total war' in its modern form.

links.label: Internet Archive: Gallic War complete edition

ticks.because: Roman military logistics (100 BC) and cataphract heavy cavalry (53 BC) had just given the late Republic the operational reach to conduct campaigns across northern Europe. Caesar's eight-year Gallic campaign — 800 cities taken, a million enemies killed in his own count — applied the same doctrine to entire peoples rather than ruling elites: total subjugation as a strategic goal.

ticks.name: Battle of Teutoburg Forest / limits of Roman expansion
ticks.constraint: Roman military superiority as unlimited in any terrain
ticks.detail: Germanic tribes under Arminius ambushed three Roman legions (17,000 men) in the Teutoburg Forest and annihilated them. Rome never again seriously attempted to conquer Germania. The Teutoburg Forest established that military superiority is terrain-dependent — the Roman legion optimized for open terrain was vulnerable to ambush in forests. Asymmetric warfare against a superior conventional force begins here.

links.label: Britannica — Battle of the Teutoburg Forest

ticks.because: Iron smelting (1200 BC) and chariot warfare (1300 BC) had defined the dominant military technologies. Roman testudo formation (36 BC) had demonstrated tactical discipline. Arminius's ambush of Varus's three legions in the Teutoburg Forest is the strategic counter — Germanic tribes using terrain to defeat Roman discipline. Rome's expansion into Germania halts permanently; the Rhine becomes the structural border for four hundred years.

ticks.name: Mongol invasions / mobile warfare doctrine
ticks.constraint: cavalry armies as limited to raiding and harassment
ticks.detail: The Mongol Empire's military system — extreme mobility, feigned retreats, coordinated multi-column attacks, psychological warfare, and siege engineer experts — defeated every army it faced for 50 years. The Mongol system showed that mobile cavalry could conduct sustained campaigns over thousands of miles and defeat much larger sedentary armies. At their peak, they controlled more territory than any empire in history.

links.label: Ramirez — Genghis Khan and Maneuver Warfare (DTIC PDF)
WarHistory — Mongol: Doctrine, Strategy, and Tactics
WarHistory — Storm from the East: The Mongol Art of War

ticks.because: The Crusades' military religious orders (1095) and Genghis Khan's Yam communications system (1200) demonstrated that medieval military organization was capable of continental projection. The Mongol horse-archer tactics (1206) provide the operational core. The 1241 invasions reach the gates of Vienna and Bohemia; mobility, feigned retreat, and intelligence-driven combined arms create a doctrine European armies don't match for centuries.

ticks.name: Agincourt / longbow defeats armored cavalry
ticks.constraint: the armored knight as the decisive military instrument of medieval Europe
ticks.detail: At Agincourt, 6,000 English (mostly longbowmen) defeated 20,000 French including the flower of French nobility. English longbow arrows penetrating plate armor at short range, combined with the mud that slowed the French advance, produced a slaughter. The medieval military aristocracy's military dominance ended here. The feudal social order it supported began its long decline.

links.label: Medieval History: The Battle of Agincourt (with Gesta Henrici Quinti)
Wikipedia: Agincourt / longbow defeats armored cavalry

ticks.because: The longbow at Crécy (1346) had demonstrated that infantry missile fire could defeat armored cavalry. Agincourt in 1415 makes the lesson decisive — six thousand English defeating twenty thousand French in a muddy field. Plate-armor knight dominance ends; gunpowder is poised to complete the transition over the next century.

ticks.name: Battle of Lepanto / end of Ottoman naval dominance
ticks.constraint: Ottoman naval power as unchallengeable in the Mediterranean
ticks.detail: The Holy League's fleet defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto — the largest naval battle since Actium. Over 200 Ottoman galleys were destroyed. The battle checked Ottoman western expansion and ended the perception of Ottoman invincibility. It also demonstrated that the galley's era was ending — galleons with broadside artillery were the future.

links.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Lepanto / end of Ottoman naval dominance
Google Scholar: Battle of Lepanto / end of Ottoman naval dominance

ticks.because: Pike and shot formation (1534) had shown that gunpowder weapons could be combined into stable infantry doctrine. Ortelius's Theatrum Orbis Terrarum atlas (1570) demonstrated that the era's geographic and tactical knowledge was systematizing. Lepanto's broadside warfare and the Holy League's victory ends Ottoman naval dominance in the Mediterranean — a strategic shift that reorders Mediterranean trade and Christian-Muslim balance for two centuries.

ticks.name: Thirty Years' War / religious vs. political warfare
ticks.constraint: European warfare as primarily dynastic or religious in motivation
ticks.detail: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) began as a religious war and ended as a political one — by 1635, France (Catholic) was supporting Protestant states against the Catholic Habsburgs because the strategic balance mattered more than religion. The Peace of Westphalia that ended it established state sovereignty and religious tolerance as the organizing principles of European order.

links.label: Britannica — Thirty Years War and Peace of Westphalia

ticks.because: Musket warfare and drill (1599), the plug bayonet (1606), and Marin le Bourgeoys's flintlock (1610) had each remade early-modern infantry firepower. The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) deploys all of it at continental scale — and ends with the Peace of Westphalia, which establishes sovereign-state secularism as the basic principle of European international relations. The transition from religious to political warfare is set.

ticks.name: Frederick the Great's oblique order / tactical geometry
ticks.constraint: linear battlefield tactics as static and symmetrical
ticks.detail: Frederick the Great's oblique order — advancing one wing of the army at an angle while holding the other back — allowed smaller Prussian armies to defeat larger opponents by concentrating force on one flank before the enemy could respond. Prussian drill and discipline made this executable in battle. The idea that tactics could be analyzed geometrically influenced military theory through WWI.

links.label: Perseus: Schalk, Art of War — Oblique Order at Leuthen 1757

ticks.because: Gustavus Adolphus's military reforms (1631) and the Thirty Years' War (1618) demonstrated that early-modern military organization could systematize tactical innovation. Boyle's Law (1662) is among the era's broader markers of quantitative confidence. Frederick the Great's oblique order — concentrating force on one wing — defeats numerically superior armies at Leuthen and Rossbach. Tactical geometry as formal doctrine; the model studied by Napoleon and Moltke.

ticks.name: Napoleon's defeat / logistics and overextension
ticks.constraint: military genius as capable of overcoming strategic overextension
ticks.detail: The Russian campaign (1812) and subsequent campaigns showed that even Napoleon's operational genius couldn't overcome the strategic reality that an army operating 1,000 miles from its supply base, in Russian winter, against an opponent willing to trade territory for time, was doomed. The limits of operational genius against strategic geography is Napoleon's lesson.
ticks.because: Napoleon's corps system (1798) and his Egyptian campaign (1798) demonstrated the reach and limits of his strategic innovations. Volta's pile (1800) is among the era's broader markers of accelerating physical understanding. The Russian campaign (1812) and Leipzig (1813) prove the limits — the same logistical chains that enabled French dominance break under continental-scale extension. Coalition warfare, total mobilization, and the modern industrial battle all emerge from this defeat.

ticks.name: Schlieffen Plan failure / war becomes attritional
ticks.constraint: the assumption that a modern industrial war could be short
ticks.detail: Germany's Schlieffen Plan assumed France could be knocked out in six weeks before Russia mobilized. It failed at the Marne. Both sides dug trenches. For four years, industrial nations threw resources into a deadlocked front. The lesson that industrial war between roughly equal powers tends toward attrition — and that attrition favors the side with more resources — shaped all subsequent strategic planning.

links.label: Imperial War Museums — The Schlieffen Plan explained
War History Online — How the Schlieffen Plan Failed

ticks.because: The Wright brothers's powered flight (1903) and HMS Dreadnought (1906) showed that single technologies could obsolete entire categories of military hardware. The Schlieffen Plan's failure — Germany's invasion of France stalled at the Marne — exposed that 1914-era industrial mobilization, defensive firepower, and rail-supplied armies were too capable for the rapid decisive war the plan assumed, and turned WWI into four years of attritional trench combat.

ticks.name: Stormtrooper tactics / infiltration assault
ticks.constraint: trench warfare deadlock as militarily insoluble
ticks.detail: German Stormtrooper (Sturmtruppen) infiltration tactics in 1918 — small groups bypassing strong points, penetrating deep into rear areas, disrupting command and supply — broke the Western Front's tactical deadlock. The German Spring Offensive (1918) advanced further in days than years of previous combat had managed. The method influenced blitzkrieg, modern special operations, and counterinsurgency.

links.label: FirstWorldWar.com: Ludendorff on the Spring Offensive (21 Mar 1918)

ticks.because: The Battle of the Somme (1916) and air-power doctrine (1917) showed that WWI's industrial slaughter required new tactical answers. German Stormtrooper infiltration tactics — small groups bypassing strongpoints to attack rear positions — break the trench-warfare deadlock briefly in 1918. Modern combined-arms infantry doctrine, with maneuver replacing line assault, traces to Sturmtruppen practice.

ticks.name: V-2 rocket / ballistic missile warfare
ticks.constraint: aerial attack as requiring manned aircraft
ticks.detail: The V-2 was the world's first ballistic missile — it flew to the edge of space and fell unpredictably on London from 300 miles away. No defense was possible. Wernher von Braun's team that built it was captured by the Americans and became the core of NASA. The V-2 directly begat the ICBM, the space race, and the satellite — the most consequential weapons program's civilian legacy.

links.label: Smithsonian National Air & Space — V-2 Rocket

ticks.because: Goddard's liquid-fuel rocket (1926) and the German Army's funding of Peenemünde (1932) produced the first ballistic missile. The V-2 (1944) flew to the edge of space and fell unpredictably on London from 300 miles away — defenseless. Wernher von Braun's team was captured by the Americans and became the foundation of NASA. The Soviet program, the ICBM, the moon program, and the modern space industry are all von Braun's V-2 with successively cleaner provenance.

ticks.name: Hiroshima and Nagasaki / nuclear warfare reality
ticks.constraint: the absolute destruction of a city as requiring months of conventional bombing
ticks.detail: A single aircraft, a single bomb, a city gone. Hiroshima (August 6) and Nagasaki (August 9) demonstrated that nuclear weapons were not just more powerful bombs but qualitatively different instruments. Japan's surrender within days ended the Pacific War. The shadow of August 1945 has governed every great-power calculation about war ever since.

links.label: National Archives — Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Britannica — Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
DOE Manhattan Project — Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima

ticks.because: The atomic bomb's development (1945) had been a strategic asset; its actual use in August 1945 establishes the operational reality. A single aircraft, a single bomb, a city gone — the demonstration that nuclear weapons would not be used again for another seventy-five years partly because their first use was so unambiguously total. Nuclear deterrence, MAD, and the bipolar Cold War order all begin from these two days.

ticks.name: U-2 incident / aerial reconnaissance satellites
ticks.constraint: strategic intelligence as requiring risky human infiltration
ticks.detail: The U-2 spy plane shot down over the USSR (1960) exposed American aerial reconnaissance, creating a diplomatic crisis. The solution: reconnaissance satellites, which orbit above airspace rights, provided intelligence without violating sovereignty. The Corona satellite program (1960) photographed the USSR with impunity. Every military satellite — GPS, signals intelligence, imagery — traces to this transition.

links.label: CIA: The U-2 Program — A Russian Officer Remembers (PDF)
CIA: Powers Tells of His U-2 Mission

ticks.because: Sputnik (1957) had demonstrated that strategic surveillance could be done from orbit, and counterinsurgency doctrine (1960) was forcing the US to think about intelligence as a continuous capability rather than a war-time scramble. The U-2 incident — Powers shot down over Sverdlovsk — accelerated the move from manned reconnaissance to satellite reconnaissance, and made the Corona program the model for every later strategic intelligence asset.

ticks.name: Tet Offensive / information warfare and public opinion
ticks.constraint: military success as determinative of war's outcome regardless of political will
ticks.detail: The Tet Offensive (1968) was a military failure for North Vietnam — most objectives were quickly retaken. But Walter Cronkite's assessment that the war was a stalemate, broadcast to 27 million Americans, destroyed public confidence in the Johnson administration's optimism. Tet demonstrated that in a democracy, the information war can be more decisive than the military war.

links.label: Wikipedia: Tet Offensive / information warfare and public opinion

ticks.because: Gagarin's first human spaceflight (1961) had demonstrated that strategic perception could be reordered by single events. The Six-Day War's preemptive strike doctrine (1967) and electroweak unification (1967) demonstrated late-1960s ambition. The Tet Offensive in 1968 is the same logic applied via media — North Vietnam loses militarily but wins the narrative as American public opinion turns. Information warfare as a strategic category enters mainstream military thinking.

ticks.name: Falklands War / precision strike lessons
ticks.constraint: surface ships as protected against missile attack by point-defense systems
ticks.detail: Argentine Exocet missiles sinking British ships demonstrated that ship-launched and air-launched anti-ship missiles had outpaced naval defensive systems. The lesson: surface ships are vulnerable to precision strike and must operate with layered air defense. Every naval doctrine revision since 1982 addresses the Falklands lesson about precision anti-ship weapons.

links.label: CSMonitor — What the Falklands fighting teaches for modern warfare
Lui — The Falklands War: Technological Deployments (DTIC PDF)
Marine Corps GlobalSecurity — Falklands Conflict: Air Defense Of The Fleet

ticks.because: Apollo 11 (1969) had demonstrated that complex coordinated technology could project power at extreme range. Precision-guided munitions in the Yom Kippur War (1973) showed the era's improving terminal accuracy. QCD (1973) marked physics' confidence in describing fundamental forces. The Falklands War's Exocet missile sinkings of British ships demonstrate that ship-launched anti-ship missiles can outrange traditional naval gunnery — a tactical lesson that reorders naval doctrine globally.

ticks.name: Iraq War / shock and awe doctrine
ticks.constraint: rapid military victory as insufficient without post-conflict planning
ticks.detail: Operation Iraqi Freedom achieved military objectives in 21 days. The subsequent insurgency lasted years. The lesson — that rapid military victory without political consolidation produces strategic failure — has been called 'the Iraq syndrome.' Military operations must integrate governance, reconstruction, and political legitimacy from day one. Every subsequent COIN doctrine reflects this.

links.label: Project Gutenberg: Ullman & Wade, Shock and Awe — Achieving Rapid Dominance
Internet Archive: Shock and Awe (Ullman & Wade 1996)

ticks.because: The Gulf War's precision-guided munitions era (1991), drone warfare (2001), and the Stryker brigade combat team (2000) demonstrated the operational shape of post-Cold-War American military doctrine. Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2003 deploys all of it as 'shock and awe' — overwhelming precision strike intended to collapse decision loops. The conventional phase ends in twenty-one days; the subsequent insurgency teaches the limits of the doctrine.

ticks.name: VOC / first multinational corporation
ticks.constraint: commercial ventures as bounded by the capital of individual merchants
ticks.detail: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was the first company to issue tradeable shares to the public, pay dividends, maintain a permanent standing organization, and operate across continents. It had its own army and navy, could declare war, and governed territories. The multinational corporation — the dominant organizational form of global capitalism — begins here.

links.label: World History Encyclopedia: Dutch East India Company
New World Encyclopedia: Dutch East India Company

ticks.because: Medici banking (1400), the Dutch East India Company's joint-stock founding (1602), and double-entry bookkeeping (Pacioli, 1494) established financial-institutional infrastructure. The VOC adds the multinational corporate form — operations across continents under a single charter, with shares traded on a public exchange. The corporation as a legal-economic structure enables capitalism's scaling.

ticks.name: South Sea Bubble / speculation and crash
ticks.constraint: share price as tethered to underlying business value even loosely
ticks.detail: The South Sea Company's stock rose 10x in months based on anticipated monopoly profits from trading with South America — profits that never materialized. The crash wiped out thousands of investors, including Isaac Newton, who reportedly said 'I can calculate the movement of stars, but not the madness of men.' The bubble established that financial mania and crash are recurring features of market economies.

links.label: UK National Archives: South Sea Bubble of 1720
Royal Museums Greenwich: South Sea Bubble

ticks.because: The Bank of England (1694) and the British perpetual national debt model (1694) established that financial innovation could underwrite imperial ambition. The decline of the guild system (1700) opened markets to less-restricted speculation. The South Sea Company's tenfold rise and crash in 1720 demonstrates that financial markets can detach from underlying value at scale. Boom-and-bust as a recurring economic phenomenon enters Western consciousness.

ticks.name: Corn Laws debate / free trade vs. protection
ticks.constraint: trade policy as obviously favorable to domestic producers
ticks.detail: The Corn Laws (1815) protected British landowners by taxing grain imports. Ricardo's comparative advantage argument and the Anti-Corn Law League's campaign produced their repeal in 1846. The Corn Law debate established free trade as an economic doctrine, Cobden and Bright as its political champions, and the tension between producer and consumer interests as the permanent fault line of trade policy.

links.label: UK National Archives: The Corn Laws

ticks.because: Watt's steam engine (1783), the Buttonwood Agreement (1792), and the expiration of the Boulton-Watt patent (1800) demonstrated that late-eighteenth-and-early-nineteenth-century industrial economy was rapidly compounding. The Corn Laws debate — Britain's 1815 protectionist grain tariffs vs. free-trade arguments from Ricardo and others — initiates the modern free-trade-vs-protection political fault line. The 1846 repeal is a key political-economy victory; globalization's political economy traces here.

ticks.name: Telegraph and financial markets
ticks.constraint: price information as limited to the speed of physical transport
ticks.detail: The telegraph (1844) allowed price information to travel faster than goods. For the first time, commodity prices in New York and Chicago could converge — arbitrage opportunities disappeared in seconds rather than days. Financial markets became integrated across geography. Reuters (1851) built its news agency on telegraph arbitrage information. Real-time global financial markets begin with the telegraph.

links.label: Library of Congress: Invention of the Telegraph (Morse Papers)
Cambridge Journal of Economic History: Atlantic Telegraph Cable and Capital Market Information Flows

ticks.because: The Corn Laws debate (1815) and Ricardo's comparative advantage (1817) demonstrated that early-nineteenth-century economic theory was systematizing into political principle. Babbage's Difference Engine (1822) showed that mechanical reasoning could industrialize calculation. The 1844 telegraph is the same systematizing applied to information — price information now travels faster than goods. Arbitrage, financial integration, and the modern global market begin.

ticks.name: Das Kapital (Marx) / critique of capitalism
ticks.constraint: capitalism as a natural or eternal economic arrangement
ticks.detail: Marx's analysis of capitalism as a historically specific mode of production — with its own internal contradictions (falling rate of profit, capital concentration, class conflict) that would produce its own supersession — provided the most systematic critique of capitalist economics ever written. Whether or not one accepts his conclusions, every subsequent economics engages with his framework.

links.label: Deutsches Textarchiv: Marx, Das Kapital Buch I (Hamburg 1867)
Online Library of Liberty: Das Kapital, Buch 1 (1867)

ticks.because: Otis's elevator brake (1852) had just made dense industrial cities physically possible, and the Bessemer process plus Perkin's mauveine (1856) had remade manufacturing into chemical-and-metallurgical industries that absorbed massive proletarian labor pools. The Homestead Act (1862) and National Bank Act (1863) marked the same period in the US. Marx synthesized: capitalism is a historically specific arrangement, not a natural one — and therefore can change.

ticks.name: Sherman Antitrust Act / competition law
ticks.constraint: monopoly power as a market outcome requiring no legal remedy
ticks.detail: The Sherman Act (1890) established that combinations in restraint of trade were illegal — that market dominance achieved through predatory means violated the public interest. Standard Oil, AT&T, and Microsoft were all eventually broken up or constrained under antitrust. Competition policy as an ongoing regulatory function begins here.

links.label: US National Archives: Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890)

ticks.because: The telephone (1876) and Edison's electric grid (1879) showed that network industries naturally consolidated into dominant firms, and compulsory primary education (1880) demonstrated that the state was willing to use law to shape market and social outcomes. The Sherman Antitrust Act made restraint of trade and monopolization federal crimes, and gave the executive a tool that — used by Theodore Roosevelt's administration — broke up Standard Oil and the Northern Securities Company.

ticks.name: Federal Reserve Act / US central banking
ticks.constraint: US financial panics as manageable only through J.P. Morgan's personal intervention
ticks.detail: After the Panic of 1907 required JP Morgan to personally organize the banking system's rescue, Congress created the Federal Reserve. The Fed's ability to provide emergency liquidity — the lender of last resort function — prevented panics from cascading into depressions. The 2008 crisis demonstrated both the Fed's power and its limits.

links.label: Federal Reserve: Centennial — About the Fed

ticks.because: The San Francisco earthquake (1906) had exposed the fragility of New York-centric financial response to crisis, and the assembly line (1913) was simultaneously demonstrating that systematic infrastructure could absorb mass-scale demand. The Federal Reserve Act (1913) gave the United States its central bank — twelve regional banks under a federal board — and ended J.P. Morgan's role as the lender of last resort during financial panics.

ticks.name: Glass-Steagall Act / banking separation
ticks.constraint: commercial banks' ability to gamble depositors' money in securities markets
ticks.detail: The Glass-Steagall Act (1933) separated commercial banking (deposits, loans) from investment banking (securities underwriting). It created the FDIC (deposit insurance). For 60 years, it prevented bank runs by guaranteeing deposits. Its repeal (1999) is credited by some with contributing to the 2008 financial crisis. The tension between financial integration and stability continues.

links.label: Federal Reserve History: Banking Act of 1933 (Glass-Steagall)
US House of Representatives: Engrossed Copy of Glass-Steagall Act

ticks.because: The Smoot-Hawley tariffs (1930) had deepened the Great Depression by collapsing world trade, and MFS's first open-end mutual fund (1924) gave retail investors new exposure to securities markets that the 1929 crash then destroyed. Glass-Steagall separated commercial deposit-taking banks from investment banks — a structural firewall that lasted 66 years until repeal in 1999, with consequences that the 2008 crisis re-litigated.

ticks.name: Bretton Woods / dollar as world reserve currency
ticks.constraint: international trade as requiring bilateral currency negotiations
ticks.detail: The 1944 conference established the US dollar (pegged to gold at $35/oz) as the world reserve currency. All other currencies were pegged to the dollar. The IMF and World Bank were created to manage the system. When Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971, the dollar remained the reserve currency despite no longer being gold-backed — pure US geopolitical and economic dominance.

links.label: Federal Reserve History: Launch of the Bretton Woods System
NBER: Bordo — The Operation and Demise of the Bretton Woods System (PDF)
Federal Reserve History: Creation of Bretton Woods (PDF)

ticks.because: Hayek's Road to Serfdom (1944) had set out the price-mechanism case for postwar order. The Bretton Woods Agreement of the same year is the institutional implementation — fixed exchange rates anchored to a gold-convertible US dollar at $35 per ounce, with the IMF and World Bank as supervisory institutions. The dollar becomes the world reserve currency, and US monetary policy structures global finance.

ticks.name: Floating exchange rates / end of Bretton Woods
ticks.constraint: currency exchange rates as fixed by international agreement
ticks.detail: Nixon's closing of the gold window ended fixed exchange rates. Currencies now float against each other, set by market supply and demand. Currency markets became the world's largest financial markets ($7 trillion daily turnover). Exchange rate volatility became a new source of business risk and speculation. The IMF's purpose was partially made obsolete overnight.

links.label: US State Dept Office of the Historian: Nixon and the End of Bretton Woods
IMF: End of the Par Value System (1972-1973)

ticks.because: Akerlof's market for lemons (1970) had recently formalized that information asymmetries break markets in characteristic ways. Nixon's closing of the gold window (1971) is the macroeconomic counterpart — fixed exchange rates collapse under accumulating dollar overhang, currencies float. Foreign-exchange trading and currency derivatives become central to global finance.

ticks.name: Index funds (Vanguard) / passive investing
ticks.constraint: investment success as requiring active stock-picking skill
ticks.detail: John Bogle founded Vanguard and launched the first index mutual fund (1976). The idea: if most active managers underperform the market after fees, why not own the whole market at minimal cost? Index funds have grown from a curiosity to managing $15+ trillion — more than half of all US equity fund assets. The active management industry's economics have been permanently disrupted.

links.label: Bogle: The Professor, the Student, and the Index Fund (PDF)
Bogle: The First Index Mutual Fund (PDF)

ticks.because: Black-Scholes (1973) had just made derivatives quantitatively tractable, and Ethernet plus Xerox PARC (1973) signaled that computation was becoming abundant enough to support real-time portfolio operations. Bogle's index fund applied the same quantitative discipline to retail investment — match the market by holding all of it — and demonstrated that most active managers could not justify their fees.

ticks.name: Big Bang / financial deregulation (London)
ticks.constraint: London's Stock Exchange as a gentlemen's club with fixed commissions
ticks.detail: Margaret Thatcher's 'Big Bang' (October 27, 1986) deregulated London's financial markets — abolishing fixed commissions, allowing foreign ownership of brokers, and introducing electronic trading. London competed with New York for global financial dominance. Financial services grew to dominate the UK economy. The template for financial deregulation that preceded the 2008 crisis.

links.label: Cambridge Financial History Review: Big Bang in the City of London
Washington Post: London Stock Market Readies for Complete Deregulation (1986)

ticks.because: Floating exchange rates (1971) had made currency markets a constant trading opportunity. Recombinant insulin (1978) showed that scientific innovation could create entirely new commercial categories. The IBM/World Bank currency swap (1981) demonstrated that financial engineering could bridge previously disconnected markets. Thatcher's Big Bang deregulation in 1986 takes London the next step — fixed commissions abolished, traditional separations between brokers and dealers ended, foreign banks admitted. The City becomes a global derivatives hub.

ticks.name: NAFTA / regional free trade
ticks.constraint: hemispheric trade as managed through bilateral tariff negotiations
ticks.detail: NAFTA created a trilateral free trade zone encompassing 450 million people and $19 trillion in GDP. Manufacturing supply chains integrated across North America. Mexico became a major US manufacturing partner. NAFTA's distributional effects — job losses in US manufacturing, agricultural disruption in Mexico — fueled the populist backlash that produced Trump's 2016 victory and USMCA renegotiation.

links.label: Britannica: North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)
Government of Canada: NAFTA Fast Facts

ticks.because: Linux (1991) had demonstrated that open systems could outcompete proprietary alternatives at scale. Amazon.com (1994) was the same lesson in commerce — global reach via low friction. NAFTA applies the same logic to continental trade — North American manufacturing, services, and investment integrated across three economies. Regional trade blocs become a major form of postwar economic governance.

ticks.name: Microfinance / Grameen Bank model global spread
ticks.constraint: small-scale entrepreneurship in developing countries as requiring conventional bank credit
ticks.detail: Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank (founded 1983, Nobel Peace Prize 2006) demonstrated that small loans to poor women — with peer group accountability replacing collateral — could generate repayment rates exceeding conventional banking. Microfinance spread globally. Its impact is contested — later research showed mixed effects on poverty reduction — but it fundamentally changed development economics.
ticks.because: NAFTA (1994) had codified continental-scale free trade. The dot-com bubble (2000) had demonstrated both the power and the fragility of distributed financial speculation. Facebook (2004) showed that mass coordination could scale on personal networks. Yunus's Grameen Bank model spreads globally — small unsecured loans to poor borrowers, often women, underwriting micro-enterprise. A counter-model to Wall Street capitalism, with 2006's Nobel Peace Prize as recognition.

ticks.name: Global financial crisis / shadow banking collapse
ticks.constraint: mortgage risk as diversified away through securitization
ticks.detail: The creation of mortgage-backed securities, CDOs, and CDO-squareds distributed subprime mortgage risk throughout the global financial system — and then concentrated it in institutions that hadn't disclosed their exposure. When housing prices fell, the entire chain collapsed. Lehman Brothers' failure triggered a global credit freeze. The $700B TARP bailout and Fed intervention prevented another Great Depression.

links.label: FDIC: Crisis and Response — The Financial Crisis (Chap 1, PDF)
Dallas Fed: Shadow Banking and the Financial Crisis (PDF)
NY Fed: Adrian & Shin — The Shadow Banking System (PDF)

ticks.because: Securitization (since the 1980s) had let mortgage originators pass loan risk to the broader market. Mortgage-backed securities, CDOs, and CDO-squareds (2002-2007) layered the risk into instruments rated AAA by the same agencies the issuers paid. The collapse of Lehman Brothers (September 2008) revealed the connections: the shadow banking system — money-market funds, repo markets, hedge-fund borrowing — held more risk than the regulated system. The Treasury and Fed extended unlimited liquidity. The financial regulatory system that emerged (Dodd-Frank 2010, Basel III 2010-13) is the answer to that revealed connection map.

ticks.name: Sharing economy / Uber and Airbnb
ticks.constraint: asset utilization requiring ownership by the service provider
ticks.detail: Airbnb (2008) and Uber (2009) demonstrated that underutilized private assets — spare bedrooms, personal cars — could be economically deployed through a platform matching supply with demand. The sharing economy created a new economic sector worth hundreds of billions and disrupted hotels and taxis globally. It also created new regulatory challenges around labor classification and safety.
ticks.because: AWS commoditization (2006) and the iPhone App Store (2008) had just made consumer-grade platforms with global reach a routine business model. Uber and Airbnb extended the same logic to physical assets: cars and rooms underutilized by their owners became services available on-demand to strangers — and produced the first wave of the platform-mediated 'sharing economy' that has since restructured taxis, hotels, and labor markets.

ticks.name: ICO boom / cryptocurrency fundraising
ticks.constraint: startup fundraising as requiring accredited investors or IPO infrastructure
ticks.detail: Initial Coin Offerings raised $5.6B in 2017 by selling cryptocurrency tokens directly to the public without SEC registration. It democratized startup funding — and also enabled massive fraud. The SEC's subsequent enforcement actions established that most ICOs were unregistered securities. The episode revealed how existing financial regulation struggled to address cryptographic assets.

links.label: Cointelegraph: History of Crypto — The ICO Boom and Ethereum's Evolution
Gemini Cryptopedia: Initial Coin Offerings — The Ethereum ICO Boom
Zerocap: Crypto ICOs — A Brief History

ticks.because: Bitcoin's blockchain (2009) proved a public ledger could exist without a central authority. AWS (2006) had shown that startup infrastructure was rentable by the hour. The 2017 ICO boom combined them: companies raised $5.6B by selling cryptocurrency tokens directly to the public, bypassing accredited-investor rules and IPO infrastructure. Most ICOs were fraud or unregistered securities. The SEC's enforcement responses defined how regulation would treat cryptographic assets.

ticks.name: COVID pandemic / remote work as default
ticks.constraint: knowledge work as requiring physical co-location in offices
ticks.detail: The COVID-19 pandemic forced the largest work-from-home experiment in history — 45% of US workers shifted to remote work in spring 2020. Zoom, Slack, and remote collaboration tools became essential infrastructure. The experiment proved that much knowledge work could be done remotely without productivity collapse. The geography of work and commercial real estate were permanently changed.

links.label: NCBI/PMC: Working from Home Before and After the Pandemic (Silver, 2024)
NBER: COVID-19 and Remote Work — An Early Look at US Data (Brynjolfsson et al.)
BFI Chicago: WFH after the COVID Pandemic (Davis, PDF)

ticks.because: Slack (2013), Zoom (2011), and broadband everywhere made remote work technically possible for a decade — and culturally rare. The COVID-19 pandemic in spring 2020 sent 45% of US workers home overnight. The largest involuntary work-from-home experiment in history proved that much knowledge work could be done remotely without productivity collapse. The geography of work and commercial real estate were permanently changed.

ticks.name: Avicenna's floating man / pure self-awareness
ticks.constraint: self-knowledge as requiring sensory or bodily experience
ticks.detail: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) proposed a thought experiment: imagine a person floating in air, senses blocked, unable to feel their own body. They would still be aware that they exist. This anticipates Descartes' cogito by 600 years — and locates self-awareness in pure mental existence, independent of body. Islamic philosophy's contribution to epistemology is systematically underappreciated.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna)

ticks.because: Diophantus's symbolic algebra (250 AD) and al-Khwarizmi's algebra (820 AD) had treated abstract reasoning as systematically expressible. Al-Farabi's Islamic political philosophy (950 AD) had legitimized rational argument as a tool for social and metaphysical questions. Avicenna's floating-man thought experiment is the same systematic move applied to consciousness — strip away every sensation, every body part, every memory, and the self that remains is undeniable. The cogito predates Descartes by six centuries.

ticks.name: Aquinas' synthesis / faith and reason
ticks.constraint: Christian theology and Aristotelian philosophy as incompatible
ticks.detail: Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica synthesized Aristotle's philosophical system with Christian theology — showing that reason and faith are complementary, not opposed. Natural theology (proving God's existence through reason) and systematic theology (elaborating revealed doctrine) were both legitimate intellectual enterprises. Thomism became Catholic philosophy's official framework and remains so.

links.label: CCEL — Summa Theologica: Of the Act of Faith

ticks.because: Al-Khwarizmi's algebra (820) and Avicenna's floating man (1040) had brought Islamic philosophy to a level Western scholasticism had to engage. Robert Grosseteste's On Light (1225) had applied geometric reasoning to theology. Aquinas's Summa is the comprehensive Latin synthesis — Aristotelian philosophy reconciled with Christian doctrine, and the route by which Western universities inherit a coherent intellectual tradition.

ticks.name: Francis Bacon / inductive method
ticks.constraint: natural knowledge as derivable from first principles through deduction
ticks.detail: Bacon's Novum Organum proposed induction — systematic collection of observations and generalization — as the method of natural philosophy. Knowledge should rise from particulars to generals, not descend from assumed generals. Bacon founded the empiricist tradition in philosophy and the Royal Society's experimental program. The tension between induction (Bacon) and deduction (Descartes) structures modern epistemology.

links.label: Wikisource: Novum Organum Book II (Spedding translation)

ticks.because: Galileo's telescope (1609) had proven that instruments could overrule received doctrine. Napier's logarithms (1614) showed that systematic computation could industrialize a procedure. Bacon's Novum Organum extends the move to method itself — induction from systematically gathered observation, replacing Aristotle's a priori syllogism. The blueprint for modern experimental science.

ticks.name: Locke's Essay on Human Understanding / tabula rasa
ticks.constraint: innate ideas as the source of human knowledge
ticks.detail: Locke argued the mind at birth is a blank slate (tabula rasa) — all knowledge comes from experience, either sensation or reflection. Against Descartes' innate ideas and rationalism. Locke's empiricism, continued by Berkeley and Hume, became the dominant philosophical tradition in English-speaking philosophy. The nature-nurture debate originates here.

links.label: Locke — Essay Concerning Human Understanding (Project Gutenberg)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — John Locke

ticks.because: Descartes's cogito (1637) had grounded knowledge in the certainty of the thinking self. Pascal's wager (1654) had introduced decision-theoretic reasoning into theology. Newton's Principia (1687) had made physics mathematically certain. Locke's Essay rejects innatism — the mind is a blank slate, knowledge is built from experience. The empiricist epistemology that runs through Berkeley, Hume, and modern cognitive science begins here.

ticks.name: Berkeley / idealism (esse est percipi)
ticks.constraint: the material world as existing independently of minds
ticks.detail: George Berkeley's 'to be is to be perceived' — objects exist only as ideas in minds. There is no mind-independent material world. This idealist position was designed to defeat skepticism (you can't doubt that you have experiences) while preserving common sense. Kant partially responded to Berkeley. The debate between idealism, realism, and pragmatism about the nature of reality continues.

links.label: Project Gutenberg — Berkeley Treatise Concerning Principles of Human Knowledge
PhilPapers — Berkeley Principles of Human Knowledge

ticks.because: Newton's Principia (1687) had made the physical universe mathematical. Locke's Essay (1689) and the Two Treatises (1689) had built knowledge and politics on empirical foundations. Halley's comet (1705) demonstrated that the Newtonian universe was predictively accurate. Berkeley pushes the empiricism to its radical conclusion — to be is to be perceived, and matter outside perception is incoherent. The strongest form of idealism in modern philosophy.

ticks.name: Hume's problem of induction
ticks.constraint: inductive reasoning as philosophically justified
ticks.detail: Hume pointed out that induction — inferring a general principle from particular observations — cannot be logically justified. No amount of past experience logically guarantees future regularity. The sun has always risen, but there's no logical proof it must rise tomorrow. This 'problem of induction' has never been solved. Popper's falsificationism and Bayesian probability are the best responses.

links.label: Hume Texts Online: Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748)
Early Modern Texts: Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (PDF)

ticks.because: Berkeley's idealism (1710) had pushed empiricism to a radical extreme. Euler's graph theory (1736) demonstrated that mathematics could model relational structures abstractly. Hume's own Treatise of Human Nature (1739) had laid out the problem at length. The Enquiry's compressed presentation of the induction problem is the form that troubles philosophy ever after — past patterns give no logical warrant for future expectations.

ticks.name: Kant's Groundwork / categorical imperative
ticks.constraint: moral philosophy as based on consequences or divine command
ticks.detail: Kant's categorical imperative — act only according to rules you could will to become universal laws — provided a reason-based alternative to both consequentialism and divine command ethics. You could derive moral obligations from pure reason, regardless of desire or consequences. Kantian deontology remains one of ethics' two main frameworks (alongside consequentialism).

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Kant's Moral Philosophy

ticks.because: Rousseau's social contract (1762) had argued that legitimate authority derived from consent. Kant's Critique of Pure Reason (1781) had specified the limits of theoretical knowledge. The Groundwork applies the same critical method to ethics — moral law as derivable from rational agency alone, with the categorical imperative as the formal test. Modern moral philosophy's deontological tradition begins here.

ticks.name: Kierkegaard / existential anxiety and choice
ticks.constraint: philosophy as addressing universal reason rather than individual existence
ticks.detail: Søren Kierkegaard wrote under pseudonyms to enact the subjective perspective he was philosophizing about. The 'stages' of existence (aesthetic, ethical, religious) required genuine personal choice, not rational demonstration. The anxiety of freedom — that we must choose without guarantee — is the fundamental human condition. Kierkegaard founded existentialism and influenced Heidegger, Sartre, and Camus.

links.label: Cambridge — Kierkegaard: Fear and Trembling (Walsh trans)

ticks.because: Kant's Critique of Pure Reason (1781) and the Groundwork (1785) had bound rationalism to procedural duty. Galvani's bioelectricity (1791) demonstrated that the human animal had measurable physical specifics. Kierkegaard pushes against the systematizing — the individual's anxious choice in front of God cannot be reduced to a Kantian universal. Existentialism's foundational author.

ticks.name: Mill's On the Subjection of Women
ticks.constraint: women's legal and social inequality as natural or inevitable
ticks.detail: John Stuart Mill's argument that women's inequality was the product of custom and law, not nature, and that equality would benefit both women and society, was the most rigorous philosophical defense of women's rights before the suffrage movement. Mill connected liberal political philosophy's premises to feminist conclusions — you cannot consistently believe in liberty while denying it to half the population.

links.label: Project Gutenberg: Mill, The Subjection of Women (1869)
Bodleian OTA: Mill, The Subjection of Women

ticks.because: The Communist Manifesto (1848) had proven that systematic critique of social structures could move politics. Boole's algebra (1854) showed that received categories could be reduced to logical operations. Spencer's social Darwinism (1864) had attempted to naturalize hierarchy. Mill's Subjection answers all three — gender hierarchy is a contingent social arrangement, not natural law, and analytical argument can dismantle it. Liberal feminism's foundation.

ticks.name: Logical positivism / Vienna Circle
ticks.constraint: metaphysics as a legitimate philosophical enterprise
ticks.detail: The Vienna Circle's logical positivism (Schlick, Carnap, Neurath) held that only empirically verifiable statements or logical tautologies were meaningful — all other philosophical statements were literally nonsensical. Most of traditional metaphysics was dismissed. The verification principle collapsed under its own weight (itself unverifiable), but logical positivism permanently shaped analytic philosophy's scientific orientation.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Vienna Circle
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Logical Empiricism

ticks.because: Heidegger's Being and Time (1927) had pushed continental philosophy toward existential phenomenology. Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) had set hard limits on what formal systems could prove. The Vienna Circle responds with the opposite move — only empirically testable claims have meaning, metaphysics is nonsense. Twentieth-century analytic philosophy's foundational program.

ticks.name: Popper's falsificationism / philosophy of science
ticks.constraint: scientific theories as verified by confirming evidence
ticks.detail: Karl Popper proposed that science advances not by confirming theories but by trying to falsify them — a genuinely scientific theory must make predictions that could be proven wrong. Freudian psychoanalysis and Marxism, he argued, were unfalsifiable and therefore not science. Falsificationism defined the 'demarcation problem' and shaped how scientists talk about what science is and isn't.

links.label: IEP — Karl Popper: Philosophy of Science
Google Books — Popper Logic of Scientific Discovery
Popper — The Open Society and Its Enemies (PDF)

ticks.because: Tarski's undefinability theorem (1933) had shown that formal systems contained hard limits on what they could represent. Popper applies the same constraint-finding to science — theories advance not by accumulating confirmations but by surviving falsification attempts. Logical positivism's verification criterion is replaced; modern philosophy of science inherits the falsificationist frame.

ticks.name: Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions
ticks.constraint: science as cumulative progress toward truth
ticks.detail: Thomas Kuhn's paradigm shift — normal science works within an established framework until anomalies accumulate and a revolution replaces the paradigm — challenged the linear, cumulative view of scientific progress. Science is sociological as well as logical. 'Paradigm shift' entered common language. Kuhn's analysis of how revolutionary science actually works changed philosophy of science, science studies, and how scientists understand their own activity.

links.label: Internet Archive: Kuhn, Structure of Scientific Revolutions
Wikipedia: Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions

ticks.because: Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations (1953) had reframed meaning as use and language as embedded in practice. Anscombe's Modern Moral Philosophy (1958) had argued that ethical concepts depend on the framework they sit in. Kuhn's Structure applies the same situational logic to science — paradigms govern normal practice, anomalies accumulate, revolutions replace one paradigm with another. Science itself becomes historically and sociologically conditioned.

ticks.name: Derrida's deconstruction / Of Grammatology
ticks.constraint: texts as having determinate, author-intended meanings
ticks.detail: Jacques Derrida's deconstruction showed that texts contain internal contradictions and undecidabilities that undermine their apparent meanings. There is no 'transcendental signified' — meaning is endlessly deferred in a play of differences. Poststructuralism, literary theory, cultural studies, and the 'linguistic turn' in humanities all follow from Derrida's destabilization of the text-meaning relationship.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Jacques Derrida

ticks.because: Kuhn's paradigm shifts (1962) had loosened the assumption that scientific frameworks were fixed. Friedan's Feminine Mystique (1963) showed received categories could be challenged at the social level. Foucault's Order of Things (1966) had treated knowledge itself as historically contingent. Derrida's Of Grammatology extends the move to language — texts contain internal contradictions and undecidabilities that destabilize any claim to a final meaning. The linguistic turn dominates humanities for decades.

ticks.name: Foucault's Discipline and Punish / power-knowledge
ticks.constraint: power as primarily coercive and authority as primarily legitimate
ticks.detail: Foucault's genealogy of the prison showed that modern power operates not through force but through surveillance, normalization, and the production of docile subjects. Power and knowledge are inseparable — disciplines produce truth. Foucault's analytics of power influenced sociology, political science, gender studies, critical race theory, and every field that examines how institutions shape subjects.

links.label: Google Books — Foucault Discipline and Punish (1991 ed)
Penguin Random House — Discipline and Punish summary

ticks.because: Rawls's Theory of Justice (1971) had treated political philosophy in deontological terms. Singer's Animal Liberation (1975) and Nagel's What Is It Like to Be a Bat? (1974) had each pushed the moral and metaphysical scope outward. Foucault's Discipline and Punish goes the other direction — power produces knowledge, the prison is a model for modern social institutions, and the panopticon is the visualization of the new social contract. Cultural studies, critical theory, and post-1970 humanities trace to this book.

ticks.name: Singer's practical ethics / applied ethics movement
ticks.constraint: ethics as a purely theoretical enterprise with no implications for action
ticks.detail: Peter Singer's Practical Ethics (1979) and subsequent work argued that philosophical ethics should guide action — about what we eat, how we donate, and what we owe future generations. Effective altruism, animal rights law, global poverty campaigns, and environmental ethics all draw from applied ethics. The movement made philosophy practically consequential rather than academically self-contained.

links.label: Open Library: Practical Ethics by Peter Singer (1979 first ed.)

ticks.because: Singer's earlier Animal Liberation (1975) and Foucault's Discipline and Punish (1975) had each pushed ethical thinking outside traditional academic philosophy boundaries. Practical Ethics extends the same project — applying utilitarian reasoning to abortion, euthanasia, global poverty, and animal welfare. Applied ethics as a recognized philosophical specialty becomes established; modern bioethics, business ethics, and environmental ethics all owe Singer's framing.

ticks.name: Rawls / public reason and political liberalism
ticks.constraint: liberal political philosophy as requiring agreement on comprehensive moral doctrines
ticks.detail: John Rawls's Political Liberalism (1993) argued that in pluralist societies, political justification must appeal to 'public reason' — reasons all citizens can in principle accept — not to any particular comprehensive moral or religious doctrine. Courts and legislation should be justifiable without invoking Christianity, utilitarianism, or any other contested worldview. Constitutional democracies' secular justification requirements reflect this.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — John Rawls
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Public Reason

ticks.because: Rawls's Theory of Justice (1971) had relied on a thick conception of fairness derived behind the veil of ignorance. By the 1990s, communitarian critiques (Sandel, MacIntyre) had pressed: how could one liberal moral theory justify a society of moral disagreement? Political Liberalism (1993) answered: in pluralist societies, political justification must appeal to 'public reason' — reasons all citizens can in principle accept — not to any particular comprehensive moral or religious doctrine. Constitutional law in pluralist democracies took this turn.

ticks.name: Hebrew prophetic tradition / social justice theology
ticks.constraint: religion as primarily concerned with ritual correctness rather than social ethics
ticks.detail: Amos, Isaiah, Micah, and Jeremiah's prophetic tradition argued that God cared more about justice, treatment of the poor, and honesty than about ritual observance. 'What does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God' (Micah 6:8). This fusion of religious and social justice motivates everything from abolitionism to liberation theology.

links.label: My Jewish Learning — Isaiah ben Amoz: Political Prophet
My Jewish Learning — Hosea & Amos: Prophets to the North
COJS — Isaiah the Prophet, 8th century BCE

ticks.because: The Gilgamesh Epic's literary theology (2100 BC) and Zoroaster's Gathas establishing ethical dualism (1000 BC) demonstrated that ancient theology could be carried by literature. The Hebrew prophets — Amos, Isaiah, Micah, Jeremiah — extend the move to social criticism: God demands justice for the poor and oppressed, not just ritual observance. Liberation theology, Christian and Islamic ethics, and Western social-justice traditions all stand on this prophetic substrate.

ticks.name: Muhammad's Hijra / the first Islamic community
ticks.constraint: religious authority as requiring control of a specific sacred geography
ticks.detail: Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina (622 AD) established the first Islamic community governed by the Constitution of Medina — the first pluralist constitutional document in history, governing Muslims, Jews, and pagans. The Hijra demonstrated that Islam was not a place-religion but a community-religion — it could be established anywhere the faithful gathered under divine law.

links.label: Constitution.org: Constitution of Medina (Dustur al-Madinah, 622 CE)
JSTOR: Constitution of Medina — Muhammad's First Legal Document

ticks.because: Muhammad's first Quranic revelation (610) gave the early community its scripture, but the persecution in Mecca prevented institutionalization. The Hijra to Medina (622) made the same revelation governable: the umma became a polity with treaties, a constitution (Sahifat al-Madina), and its own legal jurisdiction — and the Islamic calendar was anchored to this moment, not to the Prophet's birth or first revelation.

ticks.name: Anselm's ontological argument
ticks.constraint: God's existence as an article of faith rather than a logical necessity
ticks.detail: Anselm of Canterbury's ontological argument: God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived; if God exists only in the mind, something greater (God existing in reality) can be conceived; therefore God must exist in reality. Invalid according to Kant and most philosophers, but still argued about. The attempt to prove God's existence through pure logic defined 'natural theology' as a philosophical enterprise.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Ontological Arguments
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Saint Anselm

ticks.because: Muhammad's revelation (610) and the Hijra (622) established a theology demanding rational engagement with God's nature, and the Diamond Sutra (868) plus Arabic-as-scientific-language (1000) had spread philosophical reasoning across Eurasia. Anselm's Proslogion proposed that God's existence followed from the very concept of God — that than which nothing greater can be conceived — opening the medieval ontological tradition that Aquinas, Descartes, and Kant would all engage with.

ticks.name: Aquinas' five ways / proving God's existence
ticks.constraint: God's existence as demonstrable only by faith or revelation
ticks.detail: Thomas Aquinas' Summa Theologica contained five cosmological arguments for God's existence (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, contingency, gradation, design). Each starts from observable facts and argues God must exist as the ultimate explanation. These arguments — and their refutations by Hume and Kant — defined natural theology and the philosophical debate about God's existence.

links.label: New Advent — Summa Theologiae: The existence of God (Q. 2)
Lumen — Aquinas on the Five Ways

ticks.because: Avicenna's floating man (1040) had treated philosophy of self with rational rigor. Anselm's ontological argument (1078) had offered an a priori proof of God. Maimonides's Guide for the Perplexed (1190) integrated Aristotelian philosophy with Jewish theology. Robert Grosseteste's On Light (1225) demonstrated reasoned argument applied to metaphysics. Aquinas's five ways formalize the project for Christian theology — a posteriori arguments from motion, causation, contingency, gradation, and design.

ticks.name: Council of Trent / Catholic Counter-Reformation
ticks.constraint: the Catholic Church's ability to ignore Protestant critique
ticks.detail: The Council of Trent (1545-1563) was the Catholic Church's systematic response to Protestantism — reforming genuine abuses (indulgence sale, clerical corruption) while clarifying doctrine against Protestant challenges. It defined Catholic theology for 400 years. The Council's reforms made Catholicism more coherent and disciplined, producing the Jesuit order, Catholic missions, and the Baroque artistic program.

links.label: Hanover Historical Texts: Canons and Decrees of the Council of Trent
Documenta Catholica Omnia: Council of Trent Documents (PDF)

ticks.because: Luther's 95 Theses (1517) and the Church of England's establishment (1534) demonstrated that the Catholic Church's monopoly on Christian authority could be broken. Copernican heliocentrism (1543) added a cosmological challenge. The Council of Trent (1545-1563) is the systematic Catholic response — doctrinal codification, the Index of Forbidden Books, the Roman Inquisition's expansion, the Society of Jesus established. Catholicism reorganizes for the next four centuries.

ticks.name: King James Bible / English language theology
ticks.constraint: Bible translation as requiring learned clerical specialists to access
ticks.detail: The King James Bible (1611) was translated by 47 scholars to be read aloud in English churches. Its prose shaped the English language as profoundly as Shakespeare. It standardized English vocabulary and syntax for Protestant theology, political rhetoric, and literary tradition. Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, Martin Luther King's speeches, and virtually all American public rhetoric are KJV-shaped.

links.label: Wikipedia: King James Bible / English language theology

ticks.because: Gutenberg's reproducible text (1455) had made the case for standardized scripture; Italian as Renaissance lingua franca (1600) showed that vernacular literature could carry sophisticated content. The first illustrated printed book (1461) demonstrated that mass production and craft could combine. The King James Bible is the anglophone equivalent — forty-seven scholars producing English designed to be read aloud, with cadence that shapes the language for four centuries.

ticks.name: John Wesley / Methodist revival
ticks.constraint: religious practice as bounded by established church institutions
ticks.detail: Wesley's open-air preaching to miners and workers outside established churches created Methodism — a pietist revival movement that reached populations the Church of England didn't serve. Methodism's emphasis on personal conversion, small group accountability, and social action (temperance, prison reform, abolitionism) was the model for evangelical Christianity's social reform movements.

links.label: Christianity Today — Aldersgate: An Epoch in British History

ticks.because: Spinoza's Tractatus (1670), Newton's natural theology (1687), Bayle's Critical Dictionary (1697), and the first daily newspaper (1702) bracket the late-17th and early-18th centuries when religious authority was being unsettled by both biblical criticism and Enlightenment rationalism. John Wesley's Methodist revival (from 1738) gave English-speaking Protestantism a populist alternative — open-air preaching, lay preachers, small-group accountability — and started the evangelical revival traditions of the next two centuries.

ticks.name: Millerite movement / apocalyptic expectation and failure
ticks.constraint: prophetic failure as necessarily ending a religious movement
ticks.detail: William Miller predicted Christ's return in 1843-1844. When it didn't happen ('The Great Disappointment'), most followers left — but some reinterpreted the prophecy. The Seventh-day Adventist Church emerged from the ruins of Millerism. The tick: religious movements can survive the failure of their core predictions by reinterpreting rather than abandoning them. Cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger) was built on studying such groups.

links.label: EGW Writings: William Miller's Apology and Defence (Aug 1845)
Internet Archive: Miller, Apology and Defence (1845) full text

ticks.because: The French Revolution's dechristianization (1793), the Oxford Movement (1833), and the Baha'i faith's emergence (1844) bracket a long century of European and American religious upheaval. William Miller's Adventist movement — predicting Christ's return on October 22, 1844 — gave American religion its most public apocalyptic disappointment, and started the Seventh-day Adventist Church and the broader pattern of millennial movements that survive prophetic failure through doctrinal reframing.

ticks.name: First Vatican Council / papal infallibility
ticks.constraint: the pope's authority as primary but not absolute in Catholic doctrine
ticks.detail: Vatican I's declaration of papal infallibility (in specific formal teaching on faith and morals) centralized Catholic authority dramatically. It was the culmination of the ultramontane movement. The declaration — controversial even among Catholics — shaped Catholicism's relationship to modern scholarship, biblical criticism, and scientific findings throughout the 20th century.
ticks.because: Darwin's Origin of Species (1859) had just challenged Genesis as a literal account, and the Salvation Army (1865) plus the Baháʼí Faith (1863) signaled that Christian authority was fragmenting into new movements. Vatican I responded by tightening — declaring papal infallibility on faith and morals — drawing a hard line that Catholic doctrine has worked within ever since.

ticks.name: The Fundamentals / evangelical-modernist split
ticks.constraint: Protestant Christianity as a theological unity
ticks.detail: The 1910-1915 publication of 'The Fundamentals' — 90 essays defending biblical inerrancy, the virgin birth, bodily resurrection, and other doctrines against liberal theology — formalized the conservative-liberal split in Protestantism that had been building since Darwin. The word 'fundamentalism' emerged from this context. The American culture wars have their theological origin in the fundamentalist-modernist controversy.

links.label: Keas — The Fundamentals and R.A. Torrey (PSCF PDF)
Christianity Today — Who Were the Fundamentalists?
Academia — The Spirit of The Fundamentals Project 1909-1915

ticks.because: The first telephone call (1876), the international postal union (1874), and the IPA (1888) bracket a late-19th-century moment when communication standards were being globalized. The Fundamentals — twelve volumes published 1910-1915 by conservative Protestants — drew a hard line against modernist accommodation of biblical criticism, evolution, and higher criticism, and split American Protestantism into evangelical-fundamentalist and mainline-modernist branches that have not reunified.

ticks.name: Nostra Aetate / Catholic-Jewish reconciliation
ticks.constraint: Catholic theology's traditional teaching of Jewish collective guilt for crucifixion
ticks.detail: Vatican II's Nostra Aetate declaration repudiated the charge of Jewish collective guilt for the crucifixion, condemned antisemitism, and acknowledged the validity of other religions' spiritual paths. It transformed Catholic-Jewish relations after 2,000 years of persecution and the Holocaust. The declaration's influence on Christian-Jewish dialogue, Jewish-Christian relations, and Catholic approaches to other faiths continues.
ticks.because: Catholic teaching had carried 'deicide' — Jewish collective guilt for the Crucifixion — for nineteen centuries. The Holocaust forced a reckoning. Vatican II's Nostra Aetate declaration (1965) explicitly repudiated the charge, condemned antisemitism, and acknowledged spiritual truth in non-Christian religions. Centuries of Catholic-Jewish relations turned in five paragraphs. Subsequent papal apologies and the Catholic-Jewish theological dialogue all build on this declaration.

ticks.name: Iranian Revolution / political Islam
ticks.constraint: secularization as an inevitable feature of modernization
ticks.detail: Ayatollah Khomeini's Islamic Revolution overthrew the Shah — and Western modernization theory. The assumption that development necessarily produces secular politics was refuted. Political Islam — the organization of government around Islamic law — became a global force. The revolution's influence spread to Sunni movements (Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas, eventually ISIS) in ways Khomeini didn't intend.

links.label: Library of Congress — Iran country study

ticks.because: Modernization theory had assumed development would produce secular politics. The Shah's White Revolution (1963) imposed top-down modernization on Iran. Khomeini's Islamic Revolution (1979) overthrew the Shah, the theory, and the assumption that secularism was the inevitable destination of every modernizing society. Political Islam became a global force — from the Muslim Brotherhood to Hamas to ISIS — in forms Khomeini didn't intend.

ticks.name: Azusa Street Revival / Pentecostalism founded
ticks.constraint: Christian worship as decorum, hierarchy, and inherited liturgy
ticks.detail: The Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles (1906–1915), led by African-American preacher William J. Seymour, ignited modern Pentecostalism: ecstatic worship, speaking in tongues, divine healing, and racially-mixed congregations in segregated America. Within a century, Pentecostal/charismatic Christianity grew from a single LA mission to ~600 million adherents — the fastest-growing religious movement of the modern era, central to the global South's twentieth-century Christianization.

links.label: Anderson — Origins of Pentecostalism and Global Spread (Sage)
Robbins — The Globalization of Pentecostal-Charismatic Christianity (Annual Reviews)
Christianity Today — Rise of Pentecostalism Timeline (Synan)

ticks.because: The Mormon church renouncing polygamy (1890) and the World's Parliament of Religions (1893) demonstrated that late-nineteenth-century religious institutions were being reordered. The Azusa Street Revival in 1906 — led by African American preacher William Seymour, multi-racial, emphasizing speaking in tongues — launches Pentecostalism. Now nearly half a billion Christians globally; the fastest-growing major religious tradition.

ticks.name: Galen's medical theory / 1400 years of authority
ticks.constraint: contradicting ancient medical authority as a legitimate intellectual move
ticks.detail: Galen's synthesis of Greek medical knowledge — however wrong in many particulars — was so comprehensive and authoritative that it set medicine back by making the questioning of Galen feel impious rather than scientific. His authority lasted 1,400 years. The most consequential instance of a wrong but authoritative synthesis blocking progress.

links.label: Project Gutenberg: Galen, On the Natural Faculties (Brock trans.)
Perseus: Galen, On the Natural Faculties Book I

ticks.because: The Hippocratic corpus (400 BC) had separated medicine from religion. Trepanation (3100 BC) proved that intervention into the body had ancient precedent. Galen's earlier work on pulse and circulation (129 AD) and Soranus's pediatric synthesis (120 AD) had codified procedural medicine. Galen's 130 AD theory locks them into a comprehensive system — and the very comprehensiveness makes it impious to question, freezing Western medicine for fourteen hundred years.

ticks.name: Guy de Chauliac / medieval surgical synthesis
ticks.constraint: surgery as beneath the dignity of physicians
ticks.detail: Guy de Chauliac's Chirurgia Magna was the most comprehensive surgical text of the medieval period. He distinguished surgery from medicine as a discipline with its own principles, techniques, and instruments. He also survived the Black Death and described it clinically. The professionalization of surgery as a learned discipline — not just a manual craft — begins with Chauliac.

links.label: NCBI PMC — Guy de Chauliac and the Chirurgia Magna

ticks.because: The Black Death (1347), as social disruptor and as occasion for quarantine, had massively expanded medical practice while exposing its limits. Guy de Chauliac's Chirurgia Magna integrates the Greek, Arab, and contemporary surgical traditions into one comprehensive medieval text — the surgical manual of record for the next two centuries.

ticks.name: Harvey / quantitative physiology
ticks.constraint: bodily functions as unmeasurable and mathematical analysis as inapplicable to medicine
ticks.detail: Harvey's proof of blood circulation was primarily quantitative — he calculated that the heart pumps about 3.5 liters per minute, which is far more than the body could produce and consume. The body as a quantifiable system — one amenable to mathematical analysis — was established.
