Cantillon's Essay on the Nature of Commerce articulates the price mechanism — supply, demand, and entrepreneur arbitrage as the coordinating system. Classical economics begins.

ticks.name: Rochdale Principles / cooperative movement
ticks.constraint: economic organization as limited to proprietary firms or public institutions
ticks.detail: The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers (1844) established the cooperative principles — democratic member control, open membership, surplus distributed by patronage — that governed the cooperative movement globally. The Mondragon Corporation, the cooperative agricultural sector, and the credit union movement all trace to Rochdale. A third economic form between private firm and state enterprise.

links.label: International Co-operative Alliance: The Rochdale Pioneers
Rochdale Pioneers Museum: The Rochdale Principles

ticks.because: Ricardo's comparative advantage (1817) gave economic theory its case for specialization. The Cooke-Wheatstone telegraph (1837) made distant coordination feasible. The Rochdale Principles — open membership, democratic control, distribution of surplus, education promotion — establish cooperative business as a third structural form alongside capitalist firm and state enterprise. Credit unions, agricultural co-ops, and modern cooperatives all trace to Rochdale.

ticks.name: Fordism / mass production and mass consumption
ticks.constraint: manufacturing productivity gains as limited by worker skill variation
ticks.detail: Henry Ford's moving assembly line (1913) didn't just produce cars faster — it changed economic logic. High wages paid to assembly line workers (Ford's $5 day, 1914) created mass consumers for mass-produced goods. The Fordist economy — high wages, high productivity, mass consumption — was the 20th-century prosperity engine until it hit its limits in the 1970s.

links.label: The Henry Ford: Ford's Five-Dollar Day
Ford Corporate: The Moving Assembly Line and the Five-Dollar Workday
Northwestern Kellogg: Henry Ford's Five-Dollar Day case

ticks.because: Ford's assembly line (1913) had cut the time to build a Model T from 12 hours to 90 minutes, and the Federal Reserve Act (1913) had just created the institutional capacity to absorb the credit demand that mass-market consumer durables would generate. Fordism named the doctrine: pay workers enough to buy what they make, sell standardized products at low margin and high volume — and the 20th-century mass consumer economy followed.

ticks.name: Smoot-Hawley tariffs / trade war
ticks.constraint: protectionist tariffs as a rational response to economic depression
ticks.detail: The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act (1930) raised US tariffs to historic highs. Retaliatory tariffs followed globally. World trade fell 65% between 1929 and 1934. The act deepened the Great Depression and damaged international relations. The lesson — that competitive protectionism destroys more than it protects — produced the GATT/WTO system and trade economist's near-unanimous opposition to tariffs.

links.label: NBER: The Smoot-Hawley Trade War (Mitchener, O'Rourke, Wandschneider)

ticks.because: Fordism (1913), Fedwire (1918), and MFS's first open-end mutual fund (1924) bracket the early-20th-century moment when American industrial and financial institutions were being industrialized at scale. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act (1930) — raising US tariffs on 20,000 imported goods — triggered retaliatory tariffs from 25 trading partners, collapsed world trade by 65% over four years, deepened the Depression, and stands as the canonical warning against protectionism in modern economics teaching.

ticks.name: European Economic Community / customs union
ticks.constraint: European national economies as separate markets with independent trade policies
ticks.detail: The Treaty of Rome (1957) created the EEC — a customs union with a common external tariff and free movement of goods, services, capital, and people among members. It was the first successful large-scale economic integration project. The EU (and its €17 trillion economy) grew from this six-country customs union. The principle that economic integration reduces conflict while increasing prosperity became the post-war consensus.

links.label: EUR-Lex: Treaty establishing the European Economic Community (Summary)
European Commission archives: Treaty of Rome (PDF)

ticks.because: The Arrow-Debreu model (1954) gave economics its rigorous mathematical foundation for competitive markets. The Treaty of Rome's EEC (1957-1958) is the institutional implementation — France, Germany, Italy, the Benelux states pooling tariffs, agricultural policy, and labor mobility. The EU's institutional substrate begins; sixty years later it integrates twenty-seven economies.

ticks.name: Nixon shock / floating currencies
ticks.constraint: international monetary stability as requiring a gold anchor
ticks.detail: Nixon's closing of the gold window on August 15, 1971 ended Bretton Woods and created the floating exchange rate system that still governs international finance. Currencies are now worth whatever markets decide. Currency speculation became a multi-trillion dollar industry. The IMF's stabilization role changed. Developing country exchange rate crises became more frequent and severe.

links.label: US State Dept Office of the Historian: Nixon and the End of Bretton Woods
Federal Reserve History: Nixon Ends Convertibility of US Dollars to Gold
TIME: Gold and the Value of the US Dollar (Nixon Shock at 45)

ticks.because: Floating exchange rates and the end of Bretton Woods are the two facets of this single tick — Nixon closing the gold window on August 15, 1971 ends the postwar fixed-rate system. Currencies float against each other from this moment; foreign-exchange trading becomes a constant global activity, and currency derivatives become central to international finance.

ticks.name: Washington Consensus / development economics
ticks.constraint: development economics as accepting state-led industrialization
ticks.detail: John Williamson's 1989 'Washington Consensus' codified the IMF/World Bank's policy prescriptions: fiscal discipline, market liberalization, privatization, and free trade. Applied across Latin America, Africa, and post-Soviet states with mixed results — some successes, some catastrophic failures. The backlash produced 'heterodox' development economics and the emphasis on institutional capacity that succeeded it.

links.label: PIIE: Williamson — A Short History of the Washington Consensus
IMF Finance & Development: Williamson — From Reform Agenda to Damaged Brand Name (PDF)
ScienceDirect: What happened to the Washington Consensus? (Gore)

ticks.because: The first IBM/World Bank currency swap (1981) and Big Bang deregulation (1986) had institutionalized financial liberalization. The capability approach (1980s, Sen, Nussbaum) provided a moral language for development outcomes. Williamson's 1989 Washington Consensus codifies the IMF/World Bank development policy package — fiscal discipline, trade liberalization, privatization, deregulation — and shapes development economics globally for the next quarter century.

ticks.name: Dot-com bubble and crash / irrational exuberance
ticks.constraint: internet companies as valued on future potential rather than current earnings
ticks.detail: The NASDAQ peaked in March 2000 at 5,048 — then fell 78% over two years. $5 trillion in market value evaporated. Companies with no revenue and no path to profitability had traded at billions. The crash validated the principle that asset prices must eventually connect to cash flows — but also that investor enthusiasm can sustain disconnection for years. Amazon, Google, and eBay survived and thrived.
ticks.because: Black-Scholes (1973) had made derivatives a commodity-priced market. NAFTA (1994) extended free-trade thinking globally. Tversky-Kahneman's heuristics-and-biases work (1972) had documented how systematically markets misprice. The dot-com bubble's NASDAQ peak in March 2000 and 78% fall is all three colliding — derivative use, easy global capital, and herd behavior. The crash teaches a generation about the gap between technology promise and earnings reality.

ticks.name: Sundial / first time measurement instrument
ticks.constraint: time of day as knowable only approximately by sun position
ticks.detail: Egyptian and Babylonian sundials (c.1500 BC) divided daylight into measured hours. The concept of a day divided into measurable, comparable units was the first step toward the standardized time that coordinates civilization. The clock's invention makes this abstract — the sundial makes it concrete.
ticks.because: Hammurabi's Code (1750 BC) required an administrative apparatus that could record events in time. The ramp (4000 BC) and pulley (1991 BC) had introduced mechanical use as design principle. The sundial is the first quantitative time instrument — sun angle as a measurable function of hour, deployable anywhere with a flat surface. Time joins length and mass as a measurable quantity.

ticks.name: Eratosthenes / Earth's circumference calculated
ticks.constraint: the Earth's size as unmeasurable without circumnavigation
ticks.detail: Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference by measuring shadow angles at Alexandria and Syene simultaneously. His answer — about 40,000 km — was within 2% of the correct value. The method: geometry applied to Earth-scale measurement without leaving Egypt. Scientific measurement at planetary scale, without planetary-scale travel, begins here.

links.label: Loeb Classics: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, Mathematical Works

ticks.because: The sundial (1600 BC) gave humans the angle of solar elevation as a measurable quantity. Archimedes (250 BC) had proven mathematics could describe physical reality. Ctesibius's force pump (270 BC) showed engineering precision. Eratosthenes uses sun angles at two cities and a measured distance between them to calculate Earth's circumference within a few percent — the planet itself becomes a measurable object.

ticks.name: Galileo's Two New Sciences / kinematics
ticks.constraint: qualitative Aristotelian physics
ticks.detail: Galileo's quantitative laws of falling bodies and projectile motion were published in Two New Sciences (1638).

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Galileo Galilei

ticks.because: Archimedes's mathematical statics (250 BC) and Eratosthenes's circumference calculation (250 BC) had demonstrated that nature could be measured precisely. Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics (1021) had insisted on experiment and observation. Ockham's razor (1320) provided the simplicity criterion. Galileo's Two New Sciences brings them all together — falling bodies obey simple mathematical laws, gathered through controlled experiments. Modern physics's experimental method begins here.

ticks.name: Boyle's Law / gas pressure and volume
ticks.constraint: gas behavior as qualitative and unpredictable
ticks.detail: Robert Boyle showed that at constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional (PV = constant). The first quantitative relationship between physical variables in chemistry. Boyle's Law is the foundation of pneumatics, scuba diving physiology, altitude medicine, and every engine that compresses gas.

links.label: Purdue Chem — Robert Boyle and Boyle's Law

ticks.because: Galileo's kinematics (1589) and Sidereus Nuncius (1610) had established that physical motion follows mathematical relations. Pascal's Puy-de-Dome experiment (1648) had measured atmospheric pressure as a function of altitude. Boyle's Law is the next quantitative step — pressure × volume = constant, the first inverse-proportionality relation in chemistry, the foundation of pneumatics, scuba physiology, and every gas-law problem since.

ticks.name: Celsius temperature scale
ticks.constraint: temperature measurement as using arbitrarily defined local reference points
ticks.detail: Anders Celsius's 100-point scale between water's freezing and boiling points gave temperature a reproducible, universal reference. Combined with Fahrenheit's earlier scale and later Kelvin's absolute temperature, standardized temperature measurement enabled thermodynamics, meteorology, materials science, and chemistry. Measurement standardization is often more important than theoretical insight.

links.label: AbeBooks/Huxley: Celsius, Observationer om tvänne beständiga Grader (1742) original print
Wikipedia: Celsius (with citation to original 1742 paper)

ticks.because: Newton's Principia (1687) and calculus (1687) had established that nature obeyed mathematical laws expressible in equations. Huygens's wave theory of light (1690) and Bernoulli's hydrodynamics (1738) had extended the mathematical frame to optics and fluids. Celsius's choice of water's freeze and boil as zero and one hundred is the convenience: a temperature scale anchored to a substance everyone could verify, with linear behavior across the everyday range.

ticks.name: Dalton's atomic theory / atoms as real
ticks.constraint: atoms as philosophical speculation rather than scientific hypothesis
ticks.detail: John Dalton proposed that elements consist of indivisible atoms with characteristic weights, and that compounds are formed by atoms combining in simple whole-number ratios. His atomic theory made chemistry predictive. The relative atomic weights he calculated were wrong in detail but right in principle. Every stoichiometric calculation in chemistry descends from Dalton's atomic hypothesis.
ticks.because: Galvani's bioelectricity and the voltaic pile demonstrated that matter could be sorted by electrical affinity — different substances reacted with electricity differently. Lavoisier's chemical revolution insisted nothing was created or destroyed, only rearranged. Young's wave optics added that physical reality had measurable structure even at the smallest scales. Dalton synthesizes them into atomic stoichiometry: definite weights, definite ratios, definite particles.

ticks.name: Kelvin absolute temperature / thermodynamics
ticks.constraint: temperature scales as having arbitrary zero points
ticks.detail: William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) defined absolute zero — the temperature at which molecular motion ceases — as the natural zero for temperature measurement. The Kelvin scale made thermodynamic equations clean and universal. Absolute zero (-273.15°C) is the foundation of cryogenics, quantum phenomena at low temperature, and the behavior of superconductors.

links.label: Kelvin — On an Absolute Thermometric Scale (1848 PDF)
NIST — How Low Can Temperature Go? Lord Kelvin

ticks.because: Faraday's laws of electrolysis (1833) had proven that chemical change was governed by quantitative electrical relationships. Joule's mechanical equivalent of heat (1845) showed that heat and work were the same physical quantity in different forms. Helmholtz's conservation of energy (1847) made the unification general. Kelvin's absolute temperature is the natural completion — defining the zero point at which molecular motion ceases, anchoring thermodynamics to a fundamental constant rather than a melting-ice convention.

ticks.name: Maxwell's demon / information and thermodynamics
ticks.constraint: thermodynamics as independent of information theory
ticks.detail: Maxwell proposed a thought experiment: a demon controlling a valve between two gas chambers could create temperature differences without work, violating the second law. The resolution (Szilard 1929, Landauer 1961): the demon must erase information to reset, and information erasure requires energy. This linked information theory to thermodynamics — computation has physical thermodynamic costs.

links.label: Notre Dame: Maxwell, Theory of Heat (1872) PDF
La web de fisica: Maxwell on the Limitation of the Second Law

ticks.because: Maxwell's equations (1865) had just unified electromagnetism. Mendeleev's periodic table (1869) had imposed structure on chemistry. Boltzmann's H-theorem (1872) had reframed entropy as statistical. Maxwell's demon thought experiment is the philosophical puzzle that follows — a hypothetical agent that could violate the second law by sorting molecules. Information and thermodynamics get linked here, and the question is still alive in modern computing.

ticks.name: Bose-Einstein statistics / quantum identical particles
ticks.constraint: all particles as distinguishable in principle
ticks.detail: Satyendra Nath Bose and Einstein showed that particles with integer spin (bosons) are fundamentally indistinguishable — swapping two identical bosons changes nothing. Bose-Einstein statistics explains lasers (photon bunching), superconductivity, and superfluidity. Einstein predicted Bose-Einstein condensates in 1924; they were first made in 1995. The tick was recognizing quantum indistinguishability as physically fundamental.

links.label: Bose 1924 — Plancks Gesetz und Lichtquantenhypothese (Zeitschrift für Physik archive)

ticks.because: Eddington's eclipse confirmation of general relativity (1919) had demonstrated that twentieth-century physics could decisively settle theoretical predictions. The Stern-Gerlach experiment (1922) showed spatial quantization directly. Bose's calculation for photon statistics, extended by Einstein to massive particles, derives the distribution that integer-spin particles obey at low temperatures. Bose-Einstein condensates, lasers, and superfluidity all rely on this statistics.

ticks.name: Holography (Gabor)
ticks.constraint: photography as recording only light intensity, not phase
ticks.detail: Dennis Gabor invented holography — recording the phase of light waves as well as their intensity, producing three-dimensional images. Practical holography required the laser (1960) to produce coherent light. Security holograms, holographic data storage, and potential holographic displays all trace to Gabor's 1947 insight that phase information is physically recordable.

links.label: Gabor — Microscopy by reconstructed wave-fronts (Royal Society 1949)
Johnston — On 1940s-50s developments on in-line holography (Glasgow PDF)

ticks.because: NMR (1938) had taught physicists to record nuclear states by capturing their phase response to electromagnetic stimulus. Fermi's controlled chain reaction (1942) demonstrated that wave-mechanics predictions held precisely at engineering scale. Gabor's holography is the same lesson applied to optics — record not just intensity but phase, and a two-dimensional plate can reconstruct three dimensions. Practical holography has to wait for the laser thirteen years later.

ticks.name: Bell's theorem / quantum entanglement proved
ticks.constraint: quantum mechanics' 'spooky action at a distance' as a philosophical problem rather than testable claim
ticks.detail: John Bell's 1964 theorem proved that if quantum mechanics' predictions were correct, no local hidden variable theory could explain them. Aspect's 1982 experiments confirmed quantum mechanics — entangled particles really are correlated faster than light can travel between them (without transmitting information). Quantum entanglement is real. Quantum cryptography and quantum computing exploit it.

links.label: CERN: Bell, On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen Paradox (1964) PDF
APS: Bell 1964 paper Physics Physique Fizika

ticks.because: The Feminine Mystique (1963) and the Dartmouth AI workshop (1956) demonstrated that fundamental conceptual frames in different fields could be challenged systematically. Bell's theorem applies the same questioning to quantum mechanics — proving that hidden-variables theories cannot reproduce QM's predictions, and that Einstein's spooky action at a distance is real. Quantum entanglement becomes a fact, not an interpretation.

ticks.name: QCD / strong force theory
ticks.constraint: the force binding atomic nuclei as theoretically unexplained
ticks.detail: Quantum chromodynamics — the theory of quarks bound by gluons exchanging the strong force — was formulated in 1973 (Gross, Politzer, Wilczek). QCD explains why protons and neutrons hold together, why quarks can't be isolated, and the spectrum of hadrons. It completes the Standard Model's description of three of four fundamental forces.
ticks.because: Electroweak unification (Weinberg/Salam/Glashow, 1967) had completed half of the Standard Model's gauge structure. Woodward's total synthesis (1970) demonstrated that engineering precision was achievable in chemistry. Quantum chromodynamics is the strong-force counterpart — quarks bound by gluons, asymptotic freedom at high energy, confinement at low energy. The Standard Model's final theoretical pillar.

ticks.name: Inflation theory / Big Bang solved
ticks.constraint: the Big Bang's flatness problem and horizon problem as unexplained
ticks.detail: Alan Guth's cosmic inflation theory (1981) proposed that the universe underwent exponential expansion in the first 10^-36 seconds. This explained why the universe looks so uniform (it was once causally connected), why it's spatially flat, and the absence of magnetic monopoles. CMB observations since have confirmed inflationary predictions with extraordinary precision.

links.label: Guth — Inflationary Universe (Phys. Rev. D 1981 PDF)
APS Physics — Landmarks: The Inflationary Universe

ticks.because: QCD (1973) and the GPS satellite constellation (1973) demonstrated that high-precision physical theories could be applied to engineering. Guth's inflation theory is the same level of formal precision applied to the very early universe — exponential expansion in the first 10^-36 seconds explains why the cosmos looks uniform, why it's spatially flat, and why magnetic monopoles aren't observed. Cosmology's mysteries are solved with one mechanism.

ticks.name: Draco's code / Athenian written law
ticks.constraint: Athenian law as oral, known only to aristocratic judges
ticks.detail: Draco's written law code (621 BC) made Athenian law public for the first time — carved on wooden tablets displayed in the Agora. 'Draconian' entered the language because most offenses were punishable by death. But the principle — that law must be written and publicly accessible, not privately held by aristocrats — was revolutionary. Solon's reforms kept the principle while humanizing the penalties.

links.label: Attic Inscriptions Online: Decree to republish Draco's law on homicide
Attic Inscriptions: OR 183A Decree to republish Draco's homicide law

ticks.because: The Greek alphabet with vowels (800 BC) made law inscribable in a script any literate citizen could read, and the Covenant Code's earlier limits on retaliation (1200 BC) had already established the idea that law could constrain power rather than just expressing it. Draco moved law out of the heads of aristocratic judges and onto wooden tablets in the Agora — an irreversible change visible to anyone who could walk past them.

ticks.name: Justinian Code / Roman law systematized
ticks.constraint: Roman law as thousands of inconsistent imperial edicts and juristic writings
ticks.detail: The Corpus Juris Civilis codified centuries of Roman law into a coherent system. Its Digest compiled the most authoritative legal opinions; its Institutes became the teaching text; its Code collected imperial legislation. Justinian's compilation became the foundation of civil law systems used by 4 billion people today in continental Europe, Latin America, and parts of Asia and Africa.

links.label: Wikipedia: Justinian Code / Roman law systematized
Google Scholar: Justinian Code / Roman law systematized

ticks.because: Roman law by 500 AD was a sprawl of imperial edicts, juristic writings, and senatorial decrees accumulated over a millennium. Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis (529-534) compiled them into a coherent system: the Digest (most-authoritative juristic opinions), the Code (imperial legislation), the Institutes (teaching text), the Novels (Justinian's own laws). Lost in the West for five hundred years. Rediscovered at Bologna in the eleventh century, it became the foundation of every civil-law legal system.

ticks.name: Magna Carta confirmed / rule of law established
ticks.constraint: royal authority as above law
ticks.detail: Edward I's 1297 confirmation of Magna Carta into statute law made it permanent — no longer just a royal concession but an enforceable law. The principle that even the sovereign is subject to law was constitutionalized. Every subsequent constitutional document — the English Bill of Rights, the US Constitution, the UN Charter — builds on this foundation.

links.label: National Archives UK — Magna Carta 1297 transcript
National Archives UK — Magna Carta 1215 and beyond

ticks.because: Aquinas's synthesis (1265–1270) and the Sachsenspiegel (1220) bracket a high-medieval moment when systematic legal and theological frameworks were being codified. The 1297 confirmation of Magna Carta — entered into English statute by Edward I — re-established the principle that royal authority was bounded by written law, and created the legal precedent every later constitutional argument in the English-speaking world has drawn on.

ticks.name: Petition of Right / habeas corpus strengthened
ticks.constraint: imprisonment without stated cause as royal prerogative
ticks.detail: The Petition of Right (1628) prohibited imprisonment without cause shown, forced loans, billeting of soldiers in private homes, and martial law in peacetime. Charles I assented under pressure. Habeas corpus — the right to challenge unlawful detention — was strengthened. Every subsequent due process protection in English and American law builds on the Petition's protections.
ticks.because: Magna Carta (1215) constrained the king once. Coke's reading of common law in the early 1600s made it a living tradition. The Petition of Right (1628) made imprisonment without stated cause illegal — Charles I assented under fiscal pressure he couldn't escape. Habeas corpus moved from custom to enforceable law. Every due-process protection in English and American law is downstream.

ticks.name: Habeas Corpus Act / detention rights formalized
ticks.constraint: imprisonment as requiring only a monarch's word
ticks.detail: The Habeas Corpus Act (1679) codified the right of prisoners to challenge the legality of their detention before a court. Judges could order the release of anyone imprisoned without sufficient legal cause. The writ of habeas corpus — 'produce the body' — remains a fundamental protection in every common law jurisdiction. Guantanamo detention debates are essentially about habeas corpus.

links.label: Wikipedia: Habeas Corpus Act / detention rights formalized

ticks.because: The Petition of Right (1628) had stated the principle of detention only for cause. The Habeas Corpus Act (1679) made it procedural: a writ that any judge could issue, returnable within three days, requiring the government to produce the body of the detained person and state the cause. Indefinite detention without trial was foreclosed. Eleven years later, the Glorious Revolution made constitutional government permanent in England. The act's language survives in the US Constitution's suspension clause.

ticks.name: Plessy v. Ferguson / separate but equal
ticks.constraint: the 14th Amendment as prohibiting racial segregation
ticks.detail: The Supreme Court's 7-1 decision upholding Louisiana's Separate Car Act established 'separate but equal' as constitutional doctrine. It provided legal cover for Jim Crow segregation for 58 years until Brown v. Board (1954). Plessy is studied as the paradigm case of law ratifying and enabling social injustice — and of how legal doctrine can be simultaneously coherent and morally catastrophic.

links.label: Cornell Law — Plessy v. Ferguson (163 U.S. 537)
Library of Congress — Plessy v. Ferguson Primary Documents

ticks.because: The first telephone call (1876), the IPA (1888), the international postal union (1874), and the Braille standard (1837) bracket a 19th-century moment when communication was becoming systematically codified for accessibility. The Supreme Court's Plessy v. Ferguson decision moved the opposite direction: it constitutionalized 'separate but equal' as a defensible reading of the 14th Amendment, and entrenched legal segregation in the US for the 58 years until Brown v. Board.

ticks.name: Nuremberg Charter / crimes against humanity
ticks.constraint: 'crimes against humanity' as a legal category
ticks.detail: The Nuremberg Charter created the category of 'crimes against humanity' — atrocities so severe that they are crimes regardless of whether domestic law permits them. It also established individual criminal responsibility for following orders. Every subsequent international criminal tribunal (ICTY, ICTR, ICC) and the concept of universal jurisdiction trace to Nuremberg's legal innovations.

links.label: Wikisource: London Charter of the International Military Tribunal
Wikipedia: Nuremberg Charter / crimes against humanity

ticks.because: International law had treated war crimes as offenses against the laws and customs of war between states. The Holocaust required a category that didn't yet exist: crimes against humanity, atrocities so severe they were criminal regardless of whether domestic law permitted them. The Nuremberg Charter (August 1945) defined the category, established individual criminal responsibility, and rejected 'following orders' as a defense. The legal substrate for every war-crimes prosecution since.

ticks.name: Miranda rights / confession law
ticks.constraint: police interrogation as unconstrained by suspects' rights to silence or counsel
ticks.detail: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) required police to inform suspects of their rights before interrogation: the right to remain silent, the right to an attorney. Statements obtained without Miranda warnings are inadmissible. The decision changed criminal procedure in every US jurisdiction and influenced similar rules in Canada, Australia, and the UK. 'You have the right to remain silent' entered popular culture.

links.label: Library of Congress — Miranda v. Arizona

ticks.because: The Civil Rights Act (1964) had outlawed discrimination in public accommodations. Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) gave defendants the right to counsel. Miranda v. Arizona (1966) closed the interrogation gap: police must inform suspects of their right to remain silent and their right to an attorney before questioning. Statements obtained without warnings are inadmissible. Criminal procedure in every US jurisdiction (and in Canada and the UK) was rewritten.

ticks.name: Roe v. Wade / abortion rights
ticks.constraint: abortion regulation as entirely within state discretion
ticks.detail: The Supreme Court's 7-2 decision established a constitutional right to abortion based on privacy rights implied by the 14th Amendment. It nationalized a previously state-level debate. For 49 years, Roe structured American political conflict. Its 2022 overturning (Dobbs) reversed the constitutional holding but confirmed the tick: Roe had defined the legal and political landscape for half a century.

links.label: Cornell Law — Roe v. Wade (410 U.S. 113)
Cornell LII — Roe v. Wade (1973) overview
Library of Congress — U.S. Reports: Roe v. Wade

ticks.because: ARPANET email (1969) was reordering how women's-movement organizing could communicate. Rawls's Theory of Justice (1971) had established a procedural frame for thinking about rights behind a veil of ignorance. Loving v. Virginia (1967) had set the precedent for using constitutional argument to overturn restrictive marriage laws. Roe v. Wade applies the same constitutional argument to abortion access — locating it in privacy rights derived from the Fourteenth Amendment.

ticks.name: Rome Statute / International Criminal Court
ticks.constraint: international criminal prosecution as requiring ad hoc tribunals
ticks.detail: The Rome Statute (1998) created the permanent International Criminal Court — the first standing court with jurisdiction over genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity worldwide. 124 nations ratified it (the US, China, and Russia did not). The ICC's first conviction came in 2012 (Thomas Lubanga, DRC). Imperfect but real: the first permanent international criminal jurisdiction.

links.label: UN Treaties: Rome Statute of the ICC (PDF)

ticks.because: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) had freed UN Security Council action, and the Rwanda tribunal (1994) demonstrated that cross-border criminal prosecution could work when politically supported. The Rome Statute fused both into a permanent court with jurisdiction over genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity — international law's first standing criminal venue.

ticks.name: Chauvet Cave paintings / naturalistic art
ticks.constraint: animal representation as schematic and symbolic only
ticks.detail: The Chauvet Cave paintings (32,000 BC) depict lions, rhinoceroses, and horses with extraordinary naturalism — accurate anatomy, implied movement, and even perspective. They're twice as old as Lascaux. They demonstrate that fully modern artistic capacity — the ability to observe and represent the visual world accurately — was present from the beginning of behavioral modernity. 'Primitive art' is not primitive.

links.label: French Ministry of Culture — Chauvet Cave
UNESCO — Decorated Cave of Pont d'Arc, Chauvet

ticks.because: Cave painting (40,000 BC) had established symbolic representation. Venus figurines (35,000 BC) had carried symbolic forms across continents. Chauvet's Aurignacian paintings combine the threads with new naturalism — lions, rhinoceroses, and horses rendered with anatomical fidelity, multi-figure compositions that read as scenes. Art as narrative observation, not just symbol.

ticks.name: Egyptian canon / artistic proportion system
ticks.constraint: artistic proportion as intuitive and variable
ticks.detail: Egyptian art was governed by a rigid canon of proportion — figures divided into 18 units from soles to hairline — that remained nearly constant for 3,000 years. The canon encoded ideal human proportion as a repeatable system. Greek art adopted and modified Egyptian proportional systems. The idea that beauty can be codified mathematically runs from Egyptian canon to the golden ratio to modernist grid systems.

links.label: Digital Egypt UCL — Construction of formal compositions with grids
Robins — Proportion and Style in Ancient Egyptian Art (JSTOR)
Open University — Egyptian art: from plan to wall

ticks.because: Proto-cuneiform tokens (3200 BC) and Sumerian writing (3200 BC) had provided record-keeping for administered systems. Chauvet cave paintings (32,000 BC) had shown human figures rendered with anatomical fidelity. The Great Sphinx (2566 BC) had demonstrated monumental sculpture. The Egyptian canon is the systematic codification — figures divided into eighteen units from soles to hairline, every body part proportioned to a standard. Three thousand years of consistent visual culture.

ticks.name: Mona Lisa / psychological portraiture
ticks.constraint: portraiture as recording physical appearance rather than psychological state
ticks.detail: Leonardo's Mona Lisa (1503-1519) depicted not just a sitter's face but an interior psychological state — the ambiguous smile, the sfumato technique that softens edges as the eye sees them, the atmospheric perspective. Portraiture became a psychological art. The sitter's inner life, not just their social status, became the subject. Every subsequent psychological portraiture tradition begins with Leonardo.

links.label: Wikisource: Vasari, Lives — Leonardo da Vinci (Mona Lisa passage)
Fordham IHSP: Vasari, Life of Leonardo da Vinci 1550

ticks.because: The first illustrated book with printed woodcuts (1461) had merged image with text reproduction. Michelangelo's David (1501) had demonstrated Renaissance figural mastery. Leonardo's Mona Lisa (1503-1519) takes the same craft into psychological territory — sfumato, the smile, the gaze that seems to follow. Portrait as the depiction of an interior life rather than just a likeness; the model for five centuries of psychological painting.

ticks.name: Caravaggio / chiaroscuro drama
ticks.constraint: religious painting as idealized and timeless
ticks.detail: Caravaggio's revolutionary use of extreme light-dark contrast (chiaroscuro) placed holy figures in real, dirty, contemporary settings. His apostles had dirty feet; his saints were clearly Roman street people. Religious narrative became viscerally immediate rather than transcendently ideal. Caravaggio influenced Rembrandt, Velázquez, and every painter who has used dramatic lighting for psychological effect.
ticks.because: Baroque music's emotional expression in form (1600) is the contemporaneous artistic move — content carried by intense, formally controlled feeling. Caravaggio's chiaroscuro — saints painted as ordinary people in extreme light-dark contrast — applies the same logic to painting. The drama of religious subjects rendered as immediate human moments; the Baroque visual style runs for the next century.

ticks.name: Haydn's string quartet / chamber music form
ticks.constraint: serious music as requiring orchestral forces or operatic staging
ticks.detail: Joseph Haydn essentially invented the mature string quartet form — four instruments, roughly equal in importance, conversing in private domestic space. Chamber music as a distinct genre, requiring intimate listening rather than theatrical spectacle, enabled a new relationship between composer, performer, and audience. Beethoven's late quartets and Schubert's chamber music are the form's greatest achievements.

links.label: Cambridge — The Quartets (Cambridge Companion to Haydn)
Earsense — The String Quartet: First 250 Years

ticks.because: L'Épée's school for sign language (1755) and Johnson's Dictionary (1755) demonstrated that systematic frameworks could produce expressive elaboration in newly codified domains. Haydn applies the same systematizing impulse to chamber music — four roughly equal voices in conversation, the formal architecture of the string quartet established once and reused for two centuries.

ticks.name: Gothic novel / horror as literary genre
ticks.constraint: serious literature as concerned with rational, moral, or historical subjects
ticks.detail: Horace Walpole's Castle of Otranto (1764) and Ann Radcliffe's subsequent novels invented the Gothic novel — a literature of fear, supernatural threat, ancient guilt, and psychological terror. Horror as a serious literary genre begins here. Frankenstein, Dracula, Poe's tales, and the entire horror film tradition descend from Gothic conventions. The unconscious as subject matter for art predates Freud by a century.

links.label: Wikipedia: Gothic novel / horror as literary genre

ticks.because: Richardson and Fielding's novel (1750) had established prose fiction as the dominant literary form. Haydn's string quartet (1760) showed that emotional architecture could be designed formally. Walpole's Castle of Otranto (1764) is the next experiment — psychological terror, supernatural threat, ancient guilt as legitimate literary subjects. The horror genre, the unconscious-as-subject-matter for art, and the modern thriller all descend from this Gothic invention.

ticks.name: Melville's Moby-Dick / the American epic
ticks.constraint: the novel as a form requiring a unified, accessible plot
ticks.detail: Moby-Dick is simultaneously a whaling manual, a philosophical meditation on obsession and fate, a democratic epic, and one of the most formally ambitious novels ever written. Its commercial failure was complete; its subsequent canonization was total. Moby-Dick established that the novel could hold contradictory things — documentation and symbol, comedy and tragedy — without resolving them.
ticks.because: Daguerre's photography (1839) and the same photography liberating painting from representation (1839) showed that mass-produced imagery was reordering how culture was consumed. Melville's Moby-Dick is prose's parallel response — a whaling manual, philosophical meditation, and racial-political exploration in one text. American literature's first great novel; its reputation grows for the next century.

ticks.name: Monet's Impression, Sunrise / Impressionism named
ticks.constraint: painting as requiring finished, smooth surfaces and academic subjects
ticks.detail: The derisive term 'Impressionism' came from a critic mocking Monet's 1872 painting. The movement embraced it. Impressionism's broken brushwork, attention to light effects, and everyday subjects were initially scandalous. Within 20 years, they were celebrated. The Impressionist revolution is the model for how art movements work: avant-garde to mainstream to museum classic in a generation.

links.label: Normandy Tourism — Impression Sunrise: story of a legendary painting

ticks.because: Manet's Salon des Refusés (1863) had broken the academic monopoly on what could be exhibited. Photography's liberation of painting from documentation (1863) freed artists to pursue perception itself. Monet's Impression, Sunrise — mocked by a critic in 1872 as 'Impressionism' — gives the movement its name. The label sticks; broken brushwork and changing light become the dominant late-nineteenth-century painting mode.

ticks.name: The Great Train Robbery / narrative cinema
ticks.constraint: film as recording performances rather than constructing narratives
ticks.detail: Edwin Porter's The Great Train Robbery (1903) was the first film to use editing to create a story — cutting between locations, creating temporal continuity, and ending with a close-up revolver shot at the audience. It established that film could tell stories by assembling separate shots. Every film narrative technique — cross-cutting, montage, close-up — derives from Porter's demonstration.

links.label: Library of Congress: The Great Train Robbery (1903 film)
Internet Archive: The Great Train Robbery 1903

ticks.because: The Lumière brothers' first film screening (1895) had proven that motion pictures could be a public spectacle. Cinema (1895) had the technology. The Great Train Robbery (1903) is the formal innovation — narrative continuity, cuts between locations, stories told visually rather than as filmed plays. Hollywood's grammar is set here.

ticks.name: Stravinsky's Rite of Spring / rhythmic modernism
ticks.constraint: musical time as regular meter and harmonic consonance
ticks.detail: The Rite of Spring's premiere (May 29, 1913) provoked a riot — not because of Nijinsky's choreography alone, but because Stravinsky's music was so rhythmically violent and harmonically harsh. The irregular, relentless rhythms of the Sacrificial Dance had no precedent. Stravinsky established rhythm rather than melody as music's primary parameter, influencing jazz, rock, minimalism, and electronic music.

links.label: Library of Congress — Rite of Spring

ticks.because: Picasso's Chair Caning collage (1912) had already broken the rule that art represents a single coherent subject in a single coherent style; Marinetti's Futurism (1909) gave European art permission to celebrate dissonance and machine violence. Stravinsky carried the same fracture into musical time, putting rhythm rather than melody at music's center.

ticks.name: Nouvelle Vague / auteur theory
ticks.constraint: film directors as craftsmen executing studio-defined projects
ticks.detail: Godard, Truffaut, Resnais, and Varda's French New Wave — low budgets, location shooting, jump cuts, direct sound — established the director as a film's primary author. Truffaut's 'auteur theory' gave directors the cultural status of novelists or painters. The director's personal vision as the film's organizing principle changed how films were made, marketed, and discussed globally.

links.label: Routledge Encyclopedia of Modernism — French New Wave
FilmReference — French film culture in the 1950s

ticks.because: Elvis on Ed Sullivan (1956) and Allan Kaprow's coining of 'happening' (1959) demonstrated that 1950s mass culture was being reorganized around individual creative authority. Godard, Truffaut, Resnais, and Varda's French New Wave applies the same logic to film — low budgets, location shooting, jump cuts, the director as auteur. Modern art-cinema is born.

ticks.name: Earth Day / environmental art and activism
ticks.constraint: environmental concern as scientific and political but not aesthetic
ticks.detail: The first Earth Day (April 22, 1970) and the environmental movement produced a new kind of engaged art: Christo's wrapped islands, Andy Goldsworthy's natural sculptures, environmental photography (Ansel Adams, Sebastião Salgado). Art that took nature as both subject and material, and that aimed to change environmental consciousness, not just represent nature beautifully.

links.label: Esquire archive: Mondale, Environment — The Commitment for Survival (Apr 22 1970) PDF
Senate.gov: Gaylord Nelson Promotes the First Earth Day

ticks.because: ARPANET email (1969) had compressed global information distance to seconds. Minimalism (1963), conceptual art (1968), and Judd's specific objects (1964) had stripped art down to material and idea, making the medium itself a subject. Earth Day combines them — environmental crisis as a global information event, addressed through art that takes natural materials, ecological systems, and political action as both subject and medium.

ticks.name: Punk graphic design / DIY typography
ticks.constraint: graphic design as requiring professional training and production facilities
ticks.detail: Punk's cut-and-paste ransom-note aesthetic — Xeroxed zines, hand-lettered show flyers, deliberately 'ugly' typography — was a deliberate rejection of professional design's polish. Jamie Reid's Sex Pistols imagery and the fanzine culture established that design could be a democratic practice. Grunge typography, indie record design, and the entire DIY aesthetic in digital design trace to punk's graphic revolution.

links.label: Wikipedia: Punk graphic design / DIY typography

ticks.because: Hip-hop (1973) had legitimized the cut-and-paste aesthetic in music. Punk rock's DIY ethos (1976) extended the same logic to performance and recording. Punk graphic design completes the visual side — Xeroxed zines, hand-lettered flyers, deliberately ugly typography that rejects professional polish. Jamie Reid's Sex Pistols imagery, the fanzine culture, and grunge typography all begin here.

ticks.name: Creative Commons / open culture
ticks.constraint: all creative works as automatically fully copyrighted for author's life plus 70 years
ticks.detail: Creative Commons licenses (2001, widespread by 2005) allowed creators to specify exactly what rights they retained and what they gave to the public. A photographer could allow non-commercial reuse while retaining commercial rights. Wikipedia runs on Creative Commons. The open culture movement — open-source software's equivalent in creative content — depends on CC's legal infrastructure.

links.label: Creative Commons — A History of Creative Commons

ticks.because: The Web's digital art and net art (1993), the Sistine Chapel restoration (1994), and Banksy's stencilled street art (1997) demonstrated that art's reception was being globally reorganized. Creative Commons licenses — Lawrence Lessig's 2001 framework — applies the same logic to copyright. Authors retain rights but specify reuse permissions; Wikipedia, Flickr, and the entire open-culture movement run on Creative Commons.

ticks.name: Epic of Gilgamesh / first narrative literature
ticks.constraint: story as purely oral and ephemeral
ticks.detail: The Epic of Gilgamesh, preserved on clay tablets from ~2100 BC (though earlier versions existed), is the world's oldest surviving major literary narrative. A king's quest for immortality after his companion's death. It contains the first recorded flood narrative, the first meditation on friendship and mortality, and the first exploration of what it means to be human. Literature as a way of exploring the human condition begins here.

links.label: Wikisource: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic (Jastrow & Clay)
Cambridge JRAS: Notes on the Philadelphia and Yale Tablets of the Gilgamish Epic (Langdon)

ticks.because: Proto-cuneiform tokens (3200 BC) had externalized memory; Sumerian literature (3200 BC) had applied that externalization to story. Indus script (2600 BC), the Egyptian artistic canon (2500 BC), and Eblaite syllabic writing (2500 BC) showed that scripts and image systems were proliferating across the era. Gilgamesh is the moment one of those scripts inscribes a complete narrative — kingship, friendship, mortality — durable enough to outlast its author by four thousand years.

ticks.name: Diamond Sutra / first dated printed book
ticks.constraint: text reproduction as purely manual and therefore slow and error-prone
ticks.detail: The Diamond Sutra (868 AD), found in the Dunhuang caves, is the world's oldest dated printed book — produced by woodblock printing with a colophon stating it was printed 'for universal free distribution.' Printing technology existed in China 600 years before Gutenberg. The Chinese commitment to universal distribution rather than commercial printing is why the technology's cultural impact differed from Europe's.

links.label: International Dunhuang Programme — Buddhist Texts: The Diamond Sutra
Oxford Cabinet — World's earliest dated printed book (868)
UW Dunhuang Project — Printed Diamond Sutra

ticks.because: Papyrus (3000 BC) and paper (Cai Lun, 105 AD) gave printers something cheap to print on. The Nestorian Stele (781) and Sibawayh's Arabic grammar (796) showed that 9th-century Asia already systematized writing across scripts and languages. The Diamond Sutra applies woodblock printing to that infrastructure — the first dated, printed book, declaring itself for universal free distribution.

ticks.name: Gutenberg's Bible / mass text production
ticks.constraint: Bible production as requiring months of monastic scribal labor
ticks.detail: Gutenberg's 42-line Bible (1455) could be produced at a fraction of the cost and time of manuscript copying. The first 200 copies were sold before they were finished. Within 50 years, 15 million books had been printed in Europe. The democratization of literacy — and with it, the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and mass education — begins with Gutenberg's Bible.

links.label: Princeton Digital PUL: The Gutenberg Bible

ticks.because: Gutenberg's printing press (1440) was the mechanical breakthrough; movable type (1440) was the typographic one. The Bible was the proof — produced in fifty copies in the time monks would have copied one, identical to the page. By 1500 fifteen million books were in circulation across Europe. Reformation, scientific revolution, and mass literacy follow because text reproduction stops being the bottleneck.

ticks.name: Johnson's dictionary / lexicographic authority
ticks.constraint: English spelling and usage as unstandardized and contested
ticks.detail: Samuel Johnson's dictionary took nine years and five assistants. It standardized spelling, provided etymologies, and illustrated meaning with literary quotations — Shakespeare, Milton, Pope. Johnson's definitions are often miniature essays. The dictionary established that English usage could be described (not prescribed) and that literary authority could ground linguistic stability. Every dictionary since builds on his methodology.
ticks.because: L'Épée's school for French Sign Language (1755) had demonstrated that linguistic systems could be engineered for distinct communities. Johnson's earlier dictionary work (1755) had assembled the team and methodology. The 'lexicographic authority' tick is the consolidation — Johnson's dictionary as the authoritative reference, with literary citations grounding each definition. English usage becomes describable rather than prescribable, and the authority of literary reference is established.

ticks.name: Braille system invented
ticks.constraint: text access requiring sighted reading
ticks.detail: Louis Braille, blinded at age 3, developed his tactile reading system by age 15 (1824). Based on a 6-dot cell, Braille enabled blind people to read and write at speeds approaching sighted reading. Musical Braille, mathematical Braille, and computer Braille followed. The principle that information can be encoded in any sensory modality — not just visual — extends to Morse code, sign language, and haptic interfaces.
ticks.because: Sir William Jones's comparative linguistics (1786) had legitimized the study of writing systems as an analytic project. Champollion's hieroglyphic decipherment (1822) and Grimm's law (1822) had both demonstrated that scripts and sound systems followed discoverable rules. Braille's tactile six-dot cell, developed by a fifteen-year-old in 1824, is the deliberate engineering of those rules into a new modality — touch instead of sight, but the same combinatorial logic.

ticks.name: First telephone call / voice transmission
ticks.constraint: spoken communication requiring physical proximity of speaker and listener
ticks.detail: Bell's first telephone call ('Mr. Watson, come here') transmitted intelligible speech over wire. Unlike the telegraph, the telephone carried the full acoustic complexity of voice — tone, emotion, nuance. It restructured social and business communication, creating new intimacy at distance. The telephone network became the first ubiquitous real-time global communication infrastructure.

links.label: Library of Congress: Bell Papers — March 10 1876 notebook
Library of Congress: First release of Bell Papers online

ticks.because: The penny press (1833) had created mass real-time information markets. Roget's Thesaurus (1852) built a structural map of English vocabulary by concept. Manet's Salon des Refusés (1863), Impressionism (1872, 1874), and photography's liberation of painting (1863) all assumed perceptual experience could be captured and transmitted. The telephone is the literal version of that idea — Bell's wire carries voice with all its tone and emotion intact, restructuring distance.

ticks.name: Esperanto / engineered international auxiliary language
ticks.constraint: cross-language communication requiring native speakers as intermediaries
ticks.detail: L. L. Zamenhof published Unua Libro in 1887, introducing Esperanto: a constructed language with regular grammar and a Slavic-Romance-Germanic vocabulary, designed to be learnable in months by speakers of any background. It demonstrated that language could be engineered like a tool, not only inherited — a precursor to programming language design and the modern intuition that linguistic structures are designable artefacts.
ticks.because: Bell's telephone proved voice could cross any distance once an infrastructure existed. Braille proved a script could be designed deliberately for an audience without one. Esperanto applied both lessons to spoken language — engineered grammar, designed vocabulary, built to be learned in months by speakers of any background.

ticks.name: ARPANET / email precursor
ticks.constraint: written communication as either synchronous (in person) or requiring physical delivery
ticks.detail: The first ARPANET messages (1969-1971) demonstrated that text could be transmitted between computers almost instantaneously. Ray Tomlinson's email system (1971), with the @ symbol to specify destination, formalized asynchronous digital text communication. Email changed work, personal communication, and the pace of business. The average office worker now sends and receives 120 emails per day.
ticks.because: Esperanto established the principle that communication infrastructure could be designed, not just inherited. Email is the first time that principle is implemented in machinery: a constructed protocol with regular grammar, addresses that compose, and reach across linguistic and geographic distance — Zamenhof's idea wired into a network.

ticks.name: Babbage's Analytical Engine / first computer design
ticks.constraint: calculation as requiring human mental operation
ticks.detail: Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine (designed 1837, never completed) included all the essential elements of a modern computer: an arithmetic logic unit (the 'mill'), memory (the 'store'), conditional branching, and loops. Ada Lovelace wrote the first algorithm for it. The Analytical Engine was a Victorian computer designed in brass before electricity was practical. Its incompleteness delayed computing by a century.

links.label: Science Museum: Babbage Papers — Plan of the Analytical Engine 1841
Fourmilab: Sketch of the Analytical Engine (Menabrea & Lovelace)

ticks.because: Babbage's earlier Difference Engine (1822) had specified a polynomial-evaluating mechanical computer. Jacquard's loom (1804) had used punched cards to control complex patterns. Henry's electromechanical relay (1835) opened the path to electronically controlled mechanism. The Analytical Engine combines all three — programmable, branching, with separated storage and computation. The first design for a general-purpose computer, a century before its time.

ticks.name: Memex concept (Bush) / hypertext origin
ticks.constraint: information retrieval as limited to index and search by category
ticks.detail: Vannevar Bush's 1945 article 'As We May Think' proposed the Memex — a personal information device that stored documents and allowed users to create associative 'trails' between them. The Memex was unrealized hardware but the concept of hyperlinked documents became Engelbart's research agenda and Berners-Lee's World Wide Web. Every hyperlink on the internet traces to Bush's 1945 vision.

links.label: Bush 1945 — As We May Think (The Atlantic)

ticks.because: The Harvard Mark I (1944) had demonstrated that automatic large-scale calculators were operationally feasible. Vannevar Bush's 'As We May Think' essay imagines the Memex — a device that stores books, records, and communications, with associative trails between documents. Hypertext, the personal computer, and the Web all trace conceptually to Bush's 1945 article.

ticks.name: Dartmouth conference / AI named and founded
ticks.constraint: machine intelligence as science fiction rather than a research program
ticks.detail: John McCarthy's 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence coined the term 'artificial intelligence' and launched it as a research field. McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon, and Newell attended. The optimism was spectacular (McCarthy predicted human-level AI within a generation) and the actual progress was slow — but the field was institutionalized. Every AI lab, AI ethics board, and AI company traces to Dartmouth.

links.label: McCarthy — Dartmouth Summer Research Project Proposal (Stanford)

ticks.because: Three preconditions converged in the early 1950s. Arrow-Debreu's general equilibrium proved that complex systems could be specified mathematically and proved correct. The transistor and UNIVAC made commercial computation real. The UN Charter modeled large-scale optimism about reasoned coordination. Dartmouth applied that optimism to mind itself: every aspect of intelligence, in principle, describable precisely enough for a machine to simulate.

ticks.name: LISP / functional programming
ticks.constraint: computer programs as sequences of imperative instructions
ticks.detail: John McCarthy's LISP (1958) introduced functional programming — programs as mathematical functions applied to data, with recursion rather than loops, and lists as the fundamental data structure. LISP was used for AI research for decades. Its ideas (first-class functions, closures, garbage collection, dynamic typing) influenced every subsequent language. Python, JavaScript, and Haskell all carry LISP's DNA.

links.label: ACM CACM: McCarthy, Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions (1960)
MIT DSpace: McCarthy AIM-008 (1959 LISP memo)

ticks.because: FORTRAN (1957) and the FORTRAN compiler had demonstrated that high-level programming languages were viable. McCarthy's LISP applies a different paradigm — programs as lists of symbols manipulated as data, recursion as the primary control structure, garbage collection. Functional programming as a tradition begins; AI research and symbol manipulation use LISP for decades.

ticks.name: Spacewar! / first video game
ticks.constraint: computers as purely utilitarian calculation tools
ticks.detail: Spacewar! (1962), running on MIT's PDP-1, was the first video game that was genuinely fun. It spread to every computer lab that had a PDP-1. It demonstrated that computers could be entertainment platforms, not just calculators. It inspired Nolan Bushnell to found Atari. The entire video game industry traces to MIT students spending computer time on a game in 1962.

links.label: Google Scholar: Spacewar! / first video game

ticks.because: UNIVAC I (1951) had introduced commercial computing. COBOL (1960) and the integrated circuit (1961) gave computing breadth and depth. Spacewar! on the MIT PDP-1 in 1962 is the first video game that's genuinely entertaining — two players, vector graphics, gravitational pull from a central star. Hackers playing instead of working creates the cultural template for the entire video-game industry.

ticks.name: Structured programming (Dijkstra)
ticks.constraint: programs as tangled, unmaintainable networks of goto statements
ticks.detail: Edsger Dijkstra's 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful' (1968) and subsequent work established structured programming — using only sequences, conditionals, and loops — as the discipline that made programs understandable and maintainable. Every modern programming language is structured (no arbitrary gotos). Software engineering as a discipline — the idea that programs can be systematically designed and verified — begins with Dijkstra.

links.label: Dijkstra — Go To Statement Considered Harmful (CACM 1968, Wayback)
ACM DL — Letters to the Editor: Go To Statement Considered Harmful

ticks.because: Moore's Law (1965) had committed the industry to exponentially scaling transistor counts. Engelbart's Mother of All Demos (1968) showed that software was becoming complex enough to demand new tools. ELIZA (1966) demonstrated AI's earliest conversational agent. Dijkstra's structured programming is the discipline answer — replace GOTO chains with disciplined control flow, scope variables, separate concerns. Software stops being a wild assembly and becomes engineering.

ticks.name: Xerox PARC / modern computing interface
ticks.constraint: computers as interacting through text commands only
ticks.detail: Xerox PARC's Alto computer (1973) combined the graphical user interface, the mouse, Ethernet networking, laser printing, and object-oriented programming in one research prototype. Steve Jobs saw a demo in 1979 and built the Lisa and Macintosh. Bill Gates' Windows followed. PARC's inventions define personal computing's interface — none of its inventors got rich from them.

links.label: ACM HPW: Thacker, Personal Distributed Computing — Alto/Ethernet hardware
Bitsavers: Alto: A Personal Computer System (Thacker/McCreight Dec 1974)

ticks.because: Pong (1972) proved a screen could be the medium, not just a terminal. Ethernet (Metcalfe, 1973) gave one computer a way to talk to its neighbor. Smalltalk-72 (Kay) gave the language a model where every object on screen could send and receive messages. PARC's Alto put all three together — bitmap GUI, mouse, network, object-oriented runtime — the package every personal computer since copies.

ticks.name: Linux kernel / free operating system
ticks.constraint: operating systems as proprietary, licensed products
ticks.detail: Linus Torvalds posted 'I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu)' on August 25, 1991. Linux powers 97% of the world's supercomputers, most smartphones (Android), most web servers, and essentially all cloud infrastructure. The most consequential hobby project in history. Open-source software development at scale was proved possible by Linux.

links.label: Linus Torvalds — original Usenet announcement (Internet Archive)

ticks.because: Unix (1969) had defined the modular, networked OS architecture. The IBM PC's open architecture (1981) demonstrated that hardware platforms could thrive on third-party support. The first WWW protocols (1990) created a global infrastructure for distributed collaboration. Torvalds's hobby kernel — combined with GNU's free user-space tools — becomes the reference implementation for an open-source OS that powers most servers, every Android phone, and most cloud infrastructure two decades later.

ticks.name: Hadoop / big data processing
ticks.constraint: large-scale data analysis as requiring proprietary supercomputing infrastructure
ticks.detail: Google's MapReduce paper (2004) and Doug Cutting's open-source implementation (Hadoop, 2006) enabled commodity hardware clusters to process petabytes of data. Web-scale data analysis became feasible for any organization. The big data movement, business intelligence at scale, and the training of large machine learning models all depended on distributed computing frameworks that Hadoop pioneered.

links.label: O'Reilly — A Brief History of Apache Hadoop
Pluta — A Quick History of Hadoop

ticks.because: Pre-Hadoop large-scale data analysis had required proprietary supercomputers. Hadoop (open-sourced 2006 by Doug Cutting at Yahoo, based on Google's MapReduce paper 2004) provided a free framework for distributed processing of huge datasets across commodity hardware. The first sustained-scale open-source big-data infrastructure. Foundation of the 2010s 'big data' era — companies routinely processed terabytes of data on commodity clusters. Spark (2014) eventually displaced Hadoop for many workloads, but the distributed-computing-on-commodity-hardware model persists.

ticks.name: Node.js / server-side JavaScript
ticks.constraint: JavaScript as limited to browser-side scripting
ticks.detail: Ryan Dahl's Node.js (2009) enabled JavaScript to run on servers, using event-driven, non-blocking I/O for high-concurrency applications. Full-stack JavaScript — the same language on client and server — became possible. Netflix, LinkedIn, and Uber built on Node.js. It also enabled npm (the Node Package Manager), which became the largest software package registry in the world.

links.label: TinyClouds: Ryan Dahl, Node.js JSConf.eu 2009 slides PDF
JSConf.eu: Video — Node.js by Ryan Dahl (Nov 2009)

ticks.because: GitHub's distributed version control (2008) and Django (2008) had restructured how web applications were built and deployed. Node.js applied the same shift to the runtime: V8's JavaScript engine wrapped in an event-driven I/O loop, letting developers write the server in the same language as the client — and within five years, JavaScript became the most-used backend language by GitHub commits.

ticks.name: Goat domestication
ticks.constraint: milk and fiber requiring wild herd proximity
ticks.detail: Goats were among the first domesticated animals, selected for docility in the Zagros Mountains. Their adaptability to harsh terrain meant herding cultures could thrive where cattle could not. Goat milk, meat, and hair became foundations of pastoral economies from Central Asia to West Africa. The global spread of cheese, yogurt, and cashmere textiles all trace to this tick.

links.label: PNAS — Genetic evidence of early goat domestication

ticks.because: Pottery in fired clay (9000 BC) and barley domestication in the Fertile Crescent (9000 BC) had each marked the early Holocene's agricultural upheaval. Goat domestication — selecting for docility and useful body proportions — joins the Neolithic agricultural package. Goats provide milk, meat, hides, and the ability to graze marginal terrain; pastoral economies become possible.

ticks.name: Pig domestication
ticks.constraint: meat requiring active hunting in forested terrain
ticks.detail: Pigs were domesticated independently in China and the Near East. Unlike cattle, they thrive on human food waste, making them ideal settlement companions. Pork became the protein backbone of Europe and East Asia. The pig's rapid reproduction and near-total utilization (the saying 'everything but the oink') made it perhaps the most economically efficient livestock animal in history.

links.label: Larson et al. — Ancient DNA, pig domestication, Neolithic Europe (PNAS)
Pigs in Pre-Pottery Neolithic Bestansur and Shimshara (Wiley)
Kusatman — Origins of pig domestication in Near East (UCL thesis)

ticks.because: Animal domestication (10,000 BC) had begun the long human-animal partnership. Goat domestication (8,500 BC) and the development of irrigation canals (8,000 BC) showed that early Holocene settlement was building infrastructure simultaneously. Pig domestication is the dual case — the pig thrives on human food waste, requires no pasture, and its near-total utilization (everything but the oink) makes it the most economically efficient livestock animal. Pork becomes the European and East Asian protein backbone.

ticks.name: Cattle domestication (aurochs)
ticks.constraint: heavy field labor requiring human muscle
ticks.detail: The aurochs — a massive, dangerous wild bovine — was domesticated in the Near East and independently in South Asia. Cattle enabled plowing, which unlocked heavy soils impossible to farm with digging sticks. Draft animals multiplied agricultural output by an order of magnitude. Traction agriculture is the basis of all ancient grain civilizations.

links.label: NCBI/PMC: Bollongino et al, Early history of European domestic cattle (ancient DNA)
Royal Society: mtDNA Near Eastern Neolithic origin for domestic cattle

ticks.because: Pig domestication (8000 BC) had proven that even fast-tempered species could be tamed for human settlements. Lentil domestication (8000 BC) had stabilized the protein side of the diet. Honey hunting (8000 BC) showed early humans patiently extracting calorie-dense resources from dangerous ones. Cattle domestication is the boldest of these moves — the aurochs was massive and lethal — and the prize was the highest: meat, milk, leather, and the draft power that turns agriculture into a civilization-scale operation.

ticks.name: Maize domestication (teosinte)
ticks.constraint: American caloric base requiring diverse wild foraging
ticks.detail: Maize was transformed from a scraggly wild grass (teosinte) through thousands of years of selective breeding in southern Mexico. By 1000 BC it supported the complex societies of Mesoamerica. After the Columbian Exchange, maize became a global crop — now the world's highest-volume grain by weight. The genetic transformation of teosinte into corn is one of the most dramatic domestication events in history.

links.label: PNAS — Maize was domesticated from teosinte

ticks.because: Sheep domestication (6000 BC) had proved animal selective breeding could produce specialized varieties over millennia. Cheese making (5500 BC) showed early biotechnological refinement. Maize domestication is the Mesoamerican equivalent — teosinte, a scraggly wild grass with a few hard kernels per ear, remade over thousands of years into corn with hundreds of soft starchy kernels. The agricultural foundation of every Mesoamerican civilization.

ticks.name: Olive oil production (Mediterranean)
ticks.constraint: cooking fat and light requiring animal sources
ticks.detail: Olive cultivation transformed the Mediterranean economy. Olive oil was simultaneously food, fuel (lamps), medicine, soap, and trade good. The ability to store and ship oil in amphorae created the first Mediterranean commodity trade network. Minoan, Greek, and Roman economies were deeply structured around the olive press. The Mediterranean diet and much of Western food culture trace to this tick.

links.label: Koh — Wine and Olive Oil from Early Minoan I Hilltop Fort (Academia)
World History Encyclopedia — The Olive in the Ancient Mediterranean

ticks.because: Maize domestication (5000 BC) had demonstrated that tree and grass crops could be intensified through patience. Viticulture (4000 BC) showed that fruit-based agricultural systems could anchor an economy. Beekeeping in pottery vessels (3100 BC) extended controlled biology to honey. Olive oil production becomes the Mediterranean's defining commodity — food, fuel, currency, and anointing oil all in one product. The economy of every classical Mediterranean civilization runs on oil.

ticks.name: Bronze-tipped plow (Mesopotamia)
ticks.constraint: plowing limited to soft soils
ticks.detail: The seed plow — a bronze-tipped implement that simultaneously opened a furrow and deposited seed — multiplied agricultural efficiency dramatically. Combined with animal traction, it allowed Mesopotamian grain farmers to work at scales impossible with hand tools. Surplus grain enabled professional armies, scribes, priests, and merchants: the division of labor that makes civilization possible.

links.label: ExplainThat: When Was the Plow Invented in Mesopotamia?

ticks.because: Viticulture (4000 BC) and olive-oil production (3000 BC) gave Mediterranean agriculture cash crops requiring deeper, harder soil work, and the plow itself (3000 BC) had already mechanized field preparation. The bronze tip extended what could be cultivated: heavier clays and stony soils that wooden plows could not break, expanding the agricultural frontier across the Fertile Crescent.

ticks.name: Crop rotation (ancient Mediterranean)
ticks.constraint: soil fertility requiring fallow years with no yield
ticks.detail: Greek and Roman farmers discovered that alternating legumes (which fix nitrogen) with grain crops maintained soil fertility while keeping fields productive. Medieval Europe later formalized three-field rotation. This doubled effective agricultural output without expanding land under cultivation. The nitrogen cycle was being managed empirically two millennia before it was understood chemically.
ticks.because: Plow agriculture (3500 BC) had made large-scale tillage possible, and rice domestication (7000 BC) plus cabbage (1000 BC) had widened the species pool. Ancient Mediterranean farmers alternated grains with legumes — fava beans, lentils, peas — discovering empirically that nitrogen-fixing crops restored soil that grain extraction depleted, and built the two-field system that medieval Europe later refined.

ticks.name: Horse collar (European adoption)
ticks.constraint: horse draft power limited by throat-and-girth harness
ticks.detail: The rigid horse collar, adopted from Central Asian designs, transferred pulling force to the horse's shoulders rather than its windpipe. This allowed horses to pull 50% more than oxen without choking. Combined with the wheeled heavy plow and horseshoes, the horse collar triggered an agricultural revolution in northern Europe that preceded and enabled the medieval population boom.

links.label: Brill — The Origin of the Horse Collar (Brownrigg)

ticks.because: Olive oil production (3000 BC), the bronze-tipped plow (2500 BC), Mediterranean crop rotation (600 BC), and the open-field system (800) bracket millennia of Eurasian agricultural intensification. The padded horse collar — adapted from Chinese designs — let European farmers replace oxen with horses for plowing and hauling: horses pulled faster, worked longer, and could be re-harnessed quickly between fields, and tripled effective draft power per farm.

ticks.name: Three-field system widespread adoption
ticks.constraint: arable land requiring one-third to lie fallow annually
ticks.detail: Medieval Europe shifted from two-field to three-field rotation: one field winter grain, one spring grain, one fallow. This increased the proportion of land under cultivation from 50% to 67% and diversified crops, reducing famine risk. The medieval population of Europe doubled between 1000-1300 AD, and this agricultural intensification was the primary cause.

links.label: Bibliotheca Augustana: Capitulare de villis (Charlemagne, c.795)

ticks.because: The horse collar's European adoption (900) and the panemone windmill in Persia (900) demonstrated that medieval-era agricultural technology was systematizing. Three-field crop rotation (1000) — one field winter wheat, one spring barley, one fallow — increases yield by fifty percent over the older two-field system. European food production rises substantially; population growth and urbanization follow.

ticks.name: Guano trade / first chemical fertilizer
ticks.constraint: soil nutrient replacement requiring fallow or manure
ticks.detail: Peruvian seabird guano — concentrated nitrogen and phosphorus — was imported to Europe in extraordinary quantities after 1840. It was the 19th century's fertilizer revolution, temporarily solving the soil depletion that threatened European agriculture. The guano boom funded Peru's economy and triggered wars. It also revealed that food production was fundamentally a nitrogen problem, pointing directly toward Haber-Bosch.
ticks.because: Liebig's mineral theory of plant nutrition (1840), Denison's corn sheller (1839), and the daguerreotype (1839) bracket a moment when both agricultural chemistry and industrial mechanization were intensifying. The Peruvian guano trade — Pacific seabird droppings shipped to Europe and the US as concentrated nitrogen and phosphorus — gave 19th-century farming its first global commodity fertilizer, supported the agricultural intensification that fed industrial cities, and triggered the Guano Islands Act enabling US territorial claims.

ticks.name: Superphosphate fertilizer (Lawes)
ticks.constraint: soil phosphorus depletion as unreversible without organic inputs
ticks.detail: John Bennet Lawes treated mineral phosphate with sulfuric acid to create soluble superphosphate — the first manufactured chemical fertilizer. This began the modern agrochemical industry. Lawes also founded the Rothamsted Experimental Station, which pioneered agricultural field trials and is the longest-running scientific experiment in history (still ongoing since 1843).

links.label: Wikisource — Lawes biography (Dictionary of National Biography 1901)
Harpenden History — Sir John Bennet Lawes

ticks.because: Liebig's mineral theory of plant nutrition (1840) and the Peruvian guano trade (1840) established that soil fertility could be replenished through mineral inputs. John Bennet Lawes's superphosphate fertilizer (1842) — produced by treating bones or rock phosphate with sulfuric acid to make phosphorus water-soluble and plant-available — gave 19th-century agriculture its first synthetic phosphorus fertilizer, and started the Rothamsted experimental station that founded modern agricultural science.

ticks.name: Tractor displaces draft animals (mass adoption)
ticks.constraint: farm power requiring land devoted to feeding draft animals
ticks.detail: In 1920, one in four US farm acres fed horses and mules. As tractors became affordable, that land became food production. One farmer with a tractor could work ten times the acreage. Between 1920-1960, US agricultural labor fell from 30% of the workforce to 10% while output doubled. The rural-to-urban migration this enabled built the 20th-century industrial labor force.

links.label: Model T Ford Club: Fordson Tractor PDF (1921 catalog)
HCFI Library: 1921 Ford and Fordson Farm Tractor

ticks.because: Internal combustion (1885) had powered cars from 1900. Tractor adoption was slow until Ford's Fordson (1917) brought it under $400. By 1921, US tractor sales were a mass market. In 1920, one in four US farm acres fed horses and mules; by 1960 the number was approximately zero. One farmer with a tractor could work ten times the acreage.
