Between 1920 and 1960, US agricultural labor fell from 30% of the workforce to 10% while output doubled.

ticks.name: Green Revolution begins (Borlaug wheat)
ticks.constraint: wheat yield limited by plant height (lodging)
ticks.detail: Norman Borlaug bred semi-dwarf wheat varieties that could support heavy grain heads without falling over. Combined with fertilizers and irrigation, yields tripled in a decade. The Green Revolution prevented the famines predicted for Asia in the 1960s-70s. Borlaug is credited with saving a billion lives. He also initiated the debate about industrial agriculture's long-term soil and water costs.
ticks.because: Haber-Bosch (1909) had made nitrogen fertilizer essentially limitless. Mendel's rediscovered genetics gave breeders a method. Borlaug's semi-dwarf wheat varieties at CIMMYT (1944 onward) could carry heavy grain heads on short stems without lodging. Combined with fertilizer and irrigation, yields tripled in a decade. The famines predicted for 1960s Asia did not arrive. Borlaug's Nobel Peace Prize citation credits him with saving a billion lives.

ticks.name: First commercial pesticides (DDT era begins)
ticks.constraint: crop losses from insect pests as uncontrollable
ticks.detail: DDT and organochlorine pesticides dramatically reduced agricultural pest losses. Crop protection chemistry enabled the yield increases of the Green Revolution. DDT also nearly eliminated malaria in several countries. Rachel Carson's 1962 Silent Spring documented the ecological costs — a tick whose negative externalities generated the environmental movement.

links.label: Nobel Prize — Paul Müller biographical (DDT discovery)

ticks.because: Electric fences for livestock (1938) and the industrial-scale soybean processing of the 1940s bracket a period when agricultural production was being intensified in every dimension. DDT — its insecticidal action discovered by Müller in 1939 — became commercially available in 1944 and triggered the era of synthetic pesticides, ending insect-driven crop loss as a major risk and beginning the public-health era of vector control until Silent Spring forced the reckoning.

ticks.name: Precision agriculture / GPS-guided farming
ticks.constraint: field treatment as uniform across variable soil conditions
ticks.detail: GPS-guided tractors with yield monitors and variable-rate technology allowed farmers to treat different zones of a field differently — applying more fertilizer where soil was poor, less where it was rich. Precision agriculture reduced input costs while increasing yields. It also generated the first wave of agricultural data, foreshadowing AI-optimized farming.

links.label: Google Scholar: Precision agriculture / GPS-guided farming

ticks.because: GPS Full Operational Capability (1995) and the Flavr Savr GM tomato (1994) bracket a moment when both location data and crop genetics were becoming programmable inputs. GPS-guided tractors with variable-rate seeders and sprayers turned the field from a uniform unit into a 10cm-resolution grid, treating each square meter according to its own measured needs.

ticks.name: Shamanism / first religious specialists
ticks.constraint: spiritual mediation as open to any group member
ticks.detail: Archaeological evidence of shamanic practices — ritual costume, animal imagery, trance-inducing substances — appears across Paleolithic cultures globally. The shaman as intermediary between human and spirit worlds created the first religious specialization. This division of labor — some humans manage relations with the sacred — is the template for priesthood, prophecy, and religious authority in every civilization.

links.label: Steif — Upper Paleolithic cave art and shamanism (Michigan)

ticks.because: Burial ritual (40,000 BC) was the first evidence that early humans treated certain events as sacred. Animism (30,000 BC) provided the framework — a world filled with spirits, intentions, moral significance. Venus figurines made the sacred portable. Shamanism is the moment a community designates one of its members to manage relations with that sacred order — religious specialization, the template for every priesthood since.

ticks.name: Temple as economic institution (Mesopotamia)
ticks.constraint: redistribution requiring a secular central authority
ticks.detail: The Sumerian temple was simultaneously house of the god, granary, workshop, school, and bank. Priests managed land, organized labor, issued credit, and maintained weights and measures. Religion was not separate from the economy — it was its organizing structure. The temple-economy model spread across the ancient Near East and directly shaped early state formation.

links.label: Academia: Storage Practices and Temple Economy in 3rd Millennium BC Mesopotamia
Toledo Museum: Sumerian Tax Tablet for Temple of Dungi

ticks.because: Shamanism (30,000 BC) had established religious specialization. Proto-cuneiform tokens (3200 BC), proto-cuneiform administrative writing (3400 BC), and Sumerian literature (3200 BC) provided record-keeping infrastructure. The temple synthesizes them — sacred authority combined with administrative literacy and durable accounting, becoming the first institution that holds wealth, employs labor, and outlasts any individual ruler.

ticks.name: Afterlife theology (Egyptian Book of the Dead precursor)
ticks.constraint: death as simply the end of the person
ticks.detail: Egyptian elaboration of afterlife theology — judgment of the soul, the weighing of the heart against a feather, eternal reward or punishment — gave moral structure to human life. Every monotheistic tradition's heaven/hell theology is downstream of Egyptian afterlife concepts. The ethical consequences of eternal judgment transformed how societies conceptualized justice and personal morality.

links.label: British Museum — Book of the Dead
Met Museum — The Egyptian Book of the Dead

ticks.because: Cuneiform writing (3400 BC) and Egyptian phonetic hieroglyphics (3100 BC) gave priestly classes the means to record complex doctrine. Sumerian numbers (3200 BC) made temple economies tractable; the temple itself (3000 BC) served as durable institution. Afterlife theology is the corresponding metaphysical system — a coherent set of practices and texts (later collected as the Book of the Dead) for navigating what comes after, written down rather than passed orally.

ticks.name: Vedic religion / Brahmin priestly class
ticks.constraint: sacrificial ritual as open to any participant
ticks.detail: The Vedas codified ritual sacrifice as requiring specialist knowledge — Sanskrit pronunciation, precise timing, correct procedure. Only trained Brahmin priests could perform valid rituals. This created hereditary religious specialists with unique social power. The caste system's foundations are inseparable from this ritual specialization. Vedic religion also preserved some of the oldest religious poetry in human history.
ticks.because: Egyptian afterlife theology — Maat, the Book of the Dead (1550 BC) — and the Atra-Hasis epic (1646 BC) had already turned ritual into a specialist's craft requiring textual authority. Vedic religion took that move further: sacrificial ritual was not just ritual but mantra and Veda, and only Brahmins could perform it correctly — locking in a priestly caste that ordered the entire social structure.

ticks.name: Resurrection theology (Christianity)
ticks.constraint: death as the permanent defeat of the individual
ticks.detail: The claim that Jesus physically rose from the dead transformed a small Jewish sect into a world religion. Resurrection theology offered personal triumph over death to every believer, regardless of social status. This democratic promise — available to slaves and emperors alike — explains Christianity's unusual spread across social classes. The afterlife as personal continuation, not just ancestral memory, was theologically novel.

links.label: SATS: Jesus' Resurrection and the Resurrected Body — analysis of 1 Cor 15 PDF

ticks.because: Phoenician alphabetic writing (1050 BC) had just made narrative scripture broadly transmissible, and Akhenaten's monotheism (1350 BC) plus Vedic-era Brahmanism (1500 BC) had each tried to centralize the divine. Christian resurrection theology took the next step: the individual's bodily continuation past death, attached to a specific historical person — and made the afterlife a personal hope rather than a clan-or-pharaoh privilege.

ticks.name: Council of Nicaea / creedal orthodoxy
ticks.constraint: Christian doctrine as locally variable and contested
ticks.detail: The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) resolved the Arian controversy by defining the Trinity in the Nicene Creed — Jesus as consubstantial with the Father. This created the template for all subsequent ecumenical councils: disputed doctrine → assembly → binding creed → heresy defined. The institutional mechanism for managing religious dissent that the Catholic Church used for 1,500 years was invented here.

links.label: Catholic Encyclopedia — First Council of Nicaea
Wikipedia: Council of Nicaea / creedal orthodoxy

ticks.because: Resurrection theology (30 AD) gave Christianity its core doctrine, but three centuries of theological debate had produced contested local orthodoxies. The Donatist schism (311) was one such fracture. The Council of Nicaea (325) — convened by Constantine — produced the Nicene Creed, the first ecumenical doctrinal statement binding on all of Christendom, defined the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father against Arianism, and started the model of ecumenical councils as the highest authority of Catholic and Orthodox Christianity.

ticks.name: Hajj / pilgrimage as religious institution
ticks.constraint: divine encounter requiring local shrine or specialist
ticks.detail: The Islamic obligation of Hajj — pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime for those able — created the world's first mass religious gathering infrastructure. At its peak the Hajj drew 2-3 million pilgrims annually. It also functioned as a pan-Islamic communication network, trade fair, and political forum, connecting scholars and leaders across the Muslim world long before print or telegraph.
ticks.because: The Council of Nicaea's establishment of Christian creedal orthodoxy (325) gave one Abrahamic tradition a centralized doctrinal framework. The institutionalization of the Hajj — Muhammad's reformulation of pre-Islamic Arabian pilgrimage practices around the Kaaba in Mecca, beginning with his Farewell Pilgrimage in 632 — gave Islam its central recurring ritual, made Mecca the geographic anchor of the Muslim umma, and created the largest annual recurring religious gathering in human history.

ticks.name: Great Schism (Eastern/Western Christianity)
ticks.constraint: Christianity as a unified institutional church
ticks.detail: The mutual excommunication of the Pope and Patriarch of Constantinople formalized the split between Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christianity. The theological disputes (filioque, papal supremacy) masked deeper political and cultural divergences. The Eastern Orthodox tradition preserved Greek learning and shaped Byzantine, Russian, and Balkan civilization on a fundamentally different trajectory from the Latin West.

links.label: Carleton: Account of the Embassy of Humbert of Silva Candida 1054 (PDF)
Fordham IHSP Medieval: Michael Kerularios Letter to Peter of Antioch (1054)

ticks.because: Muhammad's Hijra (622), the Diamond Sutra's printing (868), and Abd al-Rahman III's Caliphate of Córdoba (929) bracket centuries when Eurasian religious traditions were institutionalizing into stable competing communions. The Great Schism of 1054 — mutual excommunications between Pope Leo IX's legate and Patriarch Michael Cerularius — formalized the centuries-long drift between Latin and Greek Christianity, and split Christendom into Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions that have not reunited since.

ticks.name: First Crusade / religiously justified war
ticks.constraint: war as requiring secular political justification
ticks.detail: Pope Urban II's call for crusade created the template for holy war — violence religiously mandated and spiritually rewarded. This concept transformed the relationship between Christianity and political violence. The military orders (Templars, Hospitallers) were entirely novel institutions. The crusading framework also transmitted Islamic philosophy, medicine, and mathematics to Europe during and after the campaigns.

links.label: Internet Medieval Sourcebook (Fordham) — Urban II's call for crusade

ticks.because: The Great Schism between Eastern and Western Christianity (1054) and Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita philosophy (1077) demonstrated that eleventh-century religious authority was being doctrinally restructured. Pope Urban II's call for crusade in 1095 creates the template for holy war — violence as religious obligation, divine indulgence for participating soldiers. The Crusades shape Christian-Muslim relations and Western military culture for the next thousand years.

ticks.name: Church of England / national church
ticks.constraint: Christian church authority as transnational and Roman
ticks.detail: Henry VIII's break with Rome created the first major national church — a Christianity loyal to a sovereign rather than the Pope. The Anglican model was exported to every British colony. More importantly, it established that religion could be a matter of national rather than universal jurisdiction, a precondition for the eventual separation of church and state.
ticks.because: Luther's 95 Theses (1517) and Tyndale's English New Testament (1526) demonstrated that vernacular scripture and theological argument could split Western Christendom. Henry VIII's Acts of Supremacy made the King the supreme head of the Church of England — the first national church to break with Rome on jurisdictional rather than purely theological grounds, and the model for state-church arrangements across Europe.

ticks.name: Darwin vs. Genesis / evolution challenges creation
ticks.constraint: natural theology as compatible with biology
ticks.detail: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection directly contradicted the literal reading of Genesis and, more deeply, the argument from design (nature's complexity as evidence of God). The ensuing conflict transformed Protestant Christianity, producing the fundamentalism/modernism split that still defines American religious politics. Evolution is the single biggest scientific challenge to religious cosmology in history.

links.label: Darwin Online — On the Origin of Species

ticks.because: The Millerite movement's failed apocalyptic predictions (1844) demonstrated that literal scriptural prediction could fail empirically, and the Mormon polygamy announcement (1852) showed religious authority making claims that secular law would soon contest. Darwin's Origin of Species (1859) made the explicit challenge to Genesis: species arose through natural selection, not separate creation, and the design argument no longer required God as the designer.

ticks.name: The Fundamentals / Christian fundamentalism
ticks.constraint: Protestant accommodation of biblical criticism
ticks.detail: A series of essays funded by oil millionaires defining non-negotiable Christian doctrines: biblical inerrancy, the virgin birth, physical resurrection, substitutionary atonement. This formalized Christian fundamentalism as a conscious movement resistant to modernism. The creation-evolution debate, abortion politics, and American evangelical political power all trace to the movement crystallized in The Fundamentals.

links.label: Christianity Today — Who Were the Fundamentalists?
Bible Notes — The Fundamentals: A Testimony to the Truth (Torrey ed.)

ticks.because: Vatican I's papal infallibility (1869) had set the Catholic line against modernist accommodation, and the Azusa Street Revival (1906) demonstrated that a new Pentecostal Christianity was forming below the denominational level. The Fundamentals — twelve volumes published 1910–1915 — gave conservative Protestantism a parallel hard line: biblical inerrancy, virgin birth, substitutionary atonement — and named Christian fundamentalism as a movement.

ticks.name: State of Israel / religious nationalism
ticks.constraint: Jewish diaspora as politically permanent
ticks.detail: The founding of Israel combined secular Zionism with deep religious symbolism — the return to the biblical homeland. It created a modern state defined by ethnic-religious identity, a model subsequently influential across the Middle East. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict embedded religious claims into a territorial dispute that has shaped global geopolitics for 75 years.

links.label: Israel State Archives: Ben-Gurion reads Israel's Declaration of Independence
JTA: Full Text of Israel's Proclamation of Independence (May 1948)

ticks.because: Saussure's general linguistics (1916), the OED's completion (1928), and the Nuremberg Trials' simultaneous interpretation system (1945) bracket the long 20th-century moment when language, identity, and human-rights infrastructure were being formalized. The 1948 establishment of the State of Israel — UN partition of Palestine, Israeli declaration of independence, the immediate Arab-Israeli war — gave political Zionism its territorial expression, and made religious nationalism a defining feature of post-war Middle Eastern politics.

ticks.name: Cogito ergo sum (Descartes)
ticks.constraint: certainty requiring sensory confirmation
ticks.detail: Descartes' radical skepticism — doubting everything until reaching the one undeniable fact of his own thinking — established consciousness as the foundation of knowledge. The mind-body problem, the hard problem of consciousness, and every subsequent epistemology is in dialogue with this moment. The cogito also made the individual thinking self the starting point of philosophy, displacing God and tradition.

links.label: Descartes — Discourse on the Method (Project Gutenberg)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Descartes' Epistemology

ticks.because: Bacon's Great Instauration (1620) had argued for organized scientific knowledge production. Descartes's Cartesian coordinates (1637) had reframed geometry algebraically. The cogito is the philosophical correlate — a methodological doubt down to bedrock, finding the thinking self as the one undeniable foundation. Modern epistemology and the dualism of mind and body both descend from this move.

ticks.name: Husserl's phenomenology
ticks.constraint: consciousness as transparent to introspection
ticks.detail: Husserl's phenomenological method — 'bracketing' assumptions to describe the pure structure of experience — created a new philosophical tradition. Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, Sartre, and Levinas all worked within the phenomenological framework. Phenomenology also influenced cognitive science, anthropology, and the design of human-computer interfaces through the concept of embodied cognition.

links.label: PhilPapers: Logical Investigations Vols I & II (PDF)

ticks.because: Cantor's set theory (1874) had pushed mathematics toward radical foundations. Nietzsche's death of God (1882) had questioned Western metaphysics directly. James's defense of faith without evidence (1896) extended the move into experience itself. Husserl's phenomenology brackets metaphysical assumptions to describe the structure of conscious experience — perception, memory, time-awareness — as it presents itself. The continental tradition's foundational method.

ticks.name: Wittgenstein's Tractatus / logical atomism
ticks.constraint: philosophy as capable of solving all meaningful questions
ticks.detail: The Tractatus argued that language pictures facts about the world, and that most traditional philosophical problems arise from language misuse — they are not false but meaningless. 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.' This helped found logical positivism and the Vienna Circle. Wittgenstein later repudiated the Tractatus in the Philosophical Investigations, founding a second philosophical tradition.
ticks.because: Weber's Protestant Ethic (1905) and the broader 1921 publication of Wittgenstein's Tractatus on the limits of language had each addressed how meaning systems function. The Tractatus's logical atomism — the world is a set of facts, language pictures facts, what cannot be said clearly should be passed over in silence — sets the foundational program for analytic philosophy. The young Wittgenstein's seven propositions reorder twentieth-century philosophy of language.

ticks.name: Philosophical Investigations (Wittgenstein)
ticks.constraint: meaning as a property of words independent of use
ticks.detail: Wittgenstein's late work argued that meaning is use — words gain meaning from their role in 'language games' embedded in 'forms of life.' There is no private language; no inner meaning that words point to. This demolished the Cartesian picture of the mind as a private theater. Ordinary language philosophy, speech act theory, and philosophy of mind were all transformed.

links.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Ludwig Wittgenstein

ticks.because: Popper's falsificationism (1934) and Quine's Two Dogmas of Empiricism (1951) had each undermined the logical-positivist project Wittgenstein himself had founded. Operations research (1945) had shown that rigor could be produced without metaphysical foundations. The late Wittgenstein turns sharply — meaning is use, language games are embedded in forms of life, philosophical confusion comes from pulling words out of their working contexts. Ordinary-language philosophy and pragmatist linguistics begin here.

ticks.name: Bolshevik Revolution / Soviet state
ticks.constraint: industrial capitalism as the only path to modernity
ticks.detail: Lenin's seizure of power created the first Marxist state. For 70 years, the Soviet model — state ownership, central planning, one-party rule — competed with liberal democracy for the allegiance of decolonizing nations. The Cold War, the Non-Aligned Movement, and virtually all 20th-century political history are responses to 1917. The failure of the Soviet model in 1991 was as significant as its creation.

links.label: Marxists.org: Decree on Transfer of Power to the Soviets (1917)
Fordham Internet Modern History Sourcebook: Lenin's Call to Power, Oct 24, 1917

ticks.because: WWI (1914-17) had broken the Tsarist economy and the army's discipline. The February Revolution (March 1917) replaced the Tsar with a Provisional Government that kept Russia in the war. Lenin returned from Swiss exile (April 1917, via German train) and moved the Bolsheviks toward armed insurrection. October 25, 1917 (Old Style): the Winter Palace seized, Lenin's government installed. The world's first self-described communist state. Whatever the trajectory of the next 74 years, October 1917 set the political agenda of the twentieth century.

ticks.name: 19th Amendment / women's suffrage (US)
ticks.constraint: political citizenship as male by default in the US
ticks.detail: After 72 years of organized advocacy since Seneca Falls, the 19th Amendment granted women the right to vote. Combined with similar movements in Europe, this doubled the voting population of democracies. The feminization of the electorate permanently shifted policy priorities — social welfare, education, and healthcare became more central to democratic politics. Women's suffrage is the largest expansion of democratic participation in US history.

links.label: National Archives: 19th Amendment to US Constitution (1919/1920)

ticks.because: The Seneca Falls Convention (1848) had launched organized US suffrage advocacy. Seventy-two years of lobbying, marches, hunger strikes, and a state-by-state campaign produced the 19th Amendment (ratified August 18, 1920). Combined with similar movements in the UK (1918, 1928) and across Europe, women's suffrage doubled the voting population of democracies. The political demand cycle and the legislative agenda rebalanced — child welfare, education, public health became campaign issues.

ticks.name: Montgomery Bus Boycott / Civil Rights Movement
ticks.constraint: Jim Crow segregation as a fixed feature of Southern life
ticks.detail: Rosa Parks's arrest and the subsequent 381-day boycott — organized through Black churches and the newly formed MIA with MLK as spokesman — proved that nonviolent mass action could defeat legal segregation economically. The boycott's success launched the Civil Rights Movement as a national force. The strategic toolkit (boycotts, sit-ins, marches, legal challenges) was developed and proven here.

links.label: National Park Service — Montgomery Bus Boycott
Library of Congress — Civil Rights History Project

ticks.because: Brown v. Board (May 1954) had made segregated education unconstitutional in principle. Implementation was slow. Rosa Parks's arrest on December 1, 1955 (coordinated with the local NAACP) launched a 381-day boycott of Montgomery's bus system. Black ridership was 75% of the customer base; the bus company nearly went bankrupt. Browder v. Gayle (December 1956) ended bus segregation in Montgomery. Martin Luther King Jr. became a national figure. The Civil Rights Movement's modern phase begins here.

ticks.name: Prague Spring / limits of Soviet reform
ticks.constraint: the belief that Soviet-style communism could reform from within
ticks.detail: Alexander Dubček's 'socialism with a human face' — political liberalization within a communist framework — was crushed by Soviet tanks in August 1968. The Brezhnev Doctrine declared that the USSR would intervene against any socialist state that threatened the bloc. This ended the reformist strain of Eastern European communism. Dissidents concluded that the system could not be reformed, only endured or overthrown — a conclusion that led to Solidarity and 1989.

links.label: National Security Archive: The Prague Spring '68
Wilson Center Digital Archive: Letter from Czech Politicians to Brezhnev (Aug 1968)

ticks.because: Khrushchev's de-Stalinization (1956) and Kádár's Hungarian compromise had suggested communism could liberalize within the Bloc. Dubček's Action Programme (April 1968) — 'socialism with a human face' — pushed press freedom, parliamentary democracy, market reforms, and federalization within Czechoslovakia. Soviet tanks rolled in on August 21, 1968. The Brezhnev Doctrine declared the USSR would intervene against any reform threatening communist rule. Reform from within the Bloc was now closed.

ticks.name: Woodstock / counterculture as mainstream
ticks.constraint: youth culture as a demographic segment to be marketed to
ticks.detail: Woodstock's 400,000 attendees demonstrated that the counterculture had mass scale. More importantly, the event crystallized a generational identity that would transform American politics, culture, and consumer markets. The marketing of rebellion, the commodification of authenticity, and the boomer generation's outsized cultural influence all trace to the brief moment when the counterculture believed it was the culture.

links.label: Smithsonian: Woodstock Festival, Bethel NY 1969 (Lisa Law photographs)
Aperture archive: Woodstock Music Festival at Bethel, NY 1969

ticks.because: Mid-1960s youth culture — civil rights, anti-war, free love, psychedelics — had been a contested subset of American identity. Woodstock (August 15-18, 1969, Bethel NY) drew 400,000 attendees to a dairy farm for three days of music, peaceful coexistence, and almost no police presence. The Newsweek and Life cover stories crystallized a generational identity. The counterculture became mainstream culture — at least as a marketing target. The Altamont Free Concert (December 1969) and the violence at the Hells Angels-managed security suggested the limits of the model.

ticks.name: Tiananmen Square / limits of Chinese liberalization
ticks.constraint: economic and political liberalization as necessarily linked
ticks.detail: The Chinese Communist Party's violent suppression of the Tiananmen protests proved that rapid economic growth could proceed without political democratization. The 'China model' — authoritarian capitalism — became the alternative to the Western assumption that markets require liberal democracy. Every subsequent debate about China's political future is framed by the choice made in June 1989.

links.label: Wikipedia: Tiananmen Square / limits of Chinese liberalization

ticks.because: Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms (1978 onward) had grown the Chinese economy at 10% a year. Western and Chinese intellectuals assumed political liberalization would follow. The student protests in Tiananmen Square (April-June 1989) tested the assumption. The People's Liberation Army's June 4 crackdown ended it. The 'China model' — authoritarian capitalism with Leninist political control — became the durable alternative to liberal democracy. Three decades of GDP growth without political opening followed.

ticks.name: Behaviorism (Watson's manifesto)
ticks.constraint: psychology requiring any reference to mental states
ticks.detail: John Watson's manifesto 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It' proposed that psychology should study only observable behavior — stimulus and response — and abandon all reference to consciousness, thought, or emotion. Behaviorism dominated academic psychology for 40 years. Skinner's operant conditioning, behavior therapy, and the design of behavioral reinforcement systems (slot machines, social media) all derive from Watson's radical proposal.

links.label: Classics in the History of Psychology: Watson (1913) 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It'
APA PsycNET record: Psychology as the behaviorist views it

ticks.because: Wundt's experimental psychology (1879) had treated introspection as the method. Freud's unconscious (1900) was claimed to drive everything. Watson's 1913 manifesto rejected both: psychology should study only observable behavior — stimulus and response — and abandon all reference to consciousness. Behaviorism dominated US academic psychology for forty years. Skinner's operant conditioning, behavior therapy, and the entire stimulus-response training of pets and children all descend from this manifesto.

ticks.name: Craik / computational theory of mind
ticks.constraint: thinking as requiring a biological substrate
ticks.detail: Kenneth Craik's 1943 book proposed that the mind works by constructing internal models of external reality — symbolic representations that can be manipulated. This was the first computational theory of mind, proposed before modern computers. Cognitive science, AI, and the information-processing model of human cognition all trace to Craik's insight that thinking might be substrate-independent symbol manipulation.

links.label: Google Books: Craik, The Nature of Explanation (1943)
Cambridge Philosophy: Review of Craik's Nature of Explanation (1944)

ticks.because: Behaviorism (1913) had said the mind shouldn't be modeled at all. Craik's The Nature of Explanation (1943) proposed the opposite: the mind works by constructing internal models of external reality — symbolic representations that can be manipulated to predict outcomes before acting. The first computational theory of mind, proposed before computers existed in working form. Cognitive science, AI, and information-processing models of cognition all start here.

ticks.name: Dartmouth Workshop / AI as a field
ticks.constraint: machine intelligence as science fiction rather than research program
ticks.detail: The 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project, organized by McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon, and Simon, coined the term 'artificial intelligence' and defined it as a legitimate field of scientific inquiry. The founding assumption — that every aspect of learning and intelligence can in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it — structured AI research for the next 70 years.

links.label: McCarthy et al. 1955 — Dartmouth proposal (Stanford archive)

ticks.because: Arrow-Debreu's existence proof showed that economic agents could be modeled rigorously. The cognitive revolution (Miller, Chomsky) showed that mind could too. The UN Charter's commitment to formalized international order set the cultural mood. Dartmouth combined them — declaring that intelligence was a research target, not a metaphor.

ticks.name: Cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger)
ticks.constraint: behavior as driven by rational assessment of evidence
ticks.detail: Leon Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance showed that people change their beliefs to match their behavior, not the reverse. When actions conflict with beliefs, we reinterpret beliefs rather than change actions. This inverted the assumption that beliefs cause behavior. Marketing, political persuasion, cult dynamics, and the psychology of self-deception are all illuminated by this tick.

links.label: Festinger, A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance (1957) — Internet Archive PDF
De Gruyter: A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance front matter (Stanford UP, 1957)

ticks.because: George Miller's working-memory paper (1956) and the Dartmouth AI workshop (1956) bracket a year when cognition was being reconceived as an information-processing system with measurable limits. Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory — people change beliefs to resolve internal contradiction, even when contradicted by evidence — gave social psychology a mechanism explaining why people do not update on facts, and reordered persuasion, marketing, and political communication.

ticks.name: Terror Management Theory (Becker/Greenberg)
ticks.constraint: culture as merely adaptive or aesthetically motivated
ticks.detail: Ernest Becker's Denial of Death (1974) and subsequent experimental work by Greenberg, Pyszczynski, and Solomon proposed that awareness of death is the root of human symbolic culture. Cultural worldviews, self-esteem, and in-group/out-group dynamics all function to manage death anxiety. Terror Management Theory explains nationalism, religious fundamentalism, and political tribalism as mortality salience effects — a profoundly unifying theory of human culture.

links.label: Internet Archive: Becker, The Denial of Death (1973)
Solomon, Greenberg & Pyszczynski: The Worm at the Core (2015) PDF

ticks.because: Cultural anthropology had treated culture as adaptive or aesthetic. Ernest Becker's Pulitzer-winning Denial of Death (1973) argued that culture is fundamentally a response to mortality awareness — we build symbolic immortality projects to deny our biological end. Greenberg, Pyszczynski, and Solomon (from 1986) operationalized the claim experimentally: subjects reminded of their mortality (mortality-salience manipulation) defend their cultural worldview more strongly. One of the most replicated paradigms in social psychology.

ticks.name: Declaration of Independence / rights as natural
ticks.constraint: rights as granted by rulers rather than inherent
ticks.detail: 'All men are created equal, endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights' — the declaration that rights pre-exist government and governments are instituted to protect them, not grant them. This Lockean formulation transformed political philosophy into constitutional design. Every subsequent human rights declaration, constitutional court, and civil liberties argument invokes this framework.

links.label: National Archives: Declaration of Independence — Transcription
Library of Congress Research Guide: Declaration of Independence

ticks.because: Hume's problem of induction (1748), L'Épée's school for sign language (1755), and Johnson's Dictionary (1755) bracket the mid-18th-century moment when both philosophy and language were being systematized in ways that bore on political theory. The 1776 Declaration of Independence — Jefferson's appeal to 'self-evident' truths and 'unalienable rights' — gave the American Revolution its founding philosophical claim, and started the natural-rights tradition that the French Revolution and every later democratic movement drew on.

ticks.name: Napoleonic Code
ticks.constraint: French civil law as feudal, regional, and contradictory
ticks.detail: Napoleon's civil code unified French law on Enlightenment principles: legal equality, property rights, freedom of contract, secular courts. Exported across conquered Europe and adopted voluntarily in Latin America, the Middle East, and Africa, the Napoleonic Code structured legal systems for 200 years. It is one of the most influential legal documents in history, second only to Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis in global reach.

links.label: Gallica/BnF: Code civil des français — édition originale 1804

ticks.because: The US Constitution (1787), the US Bill of Rights (1789), and the Patent Act of 1790 demonstrated that Enlightenment principles could be codified into systematic law. Napoleon's civil code applies the same approach to French law — secularism, equality before the law, property rights, religious tolerance. Most of continental Europe and Latin America inherits the Napoleonic Code's structure.

ticks.name: Lieber Code / laws of war
ticks.constraint: military conduct as entirely at commanders' discretion
ticks.detail: Francis Lieber's instructions for Union Army conduct became the first codification of the laws of armed conflict. It influenced the Hague Conventions, the Geneva Conventions, and ultimately the International Criminal Court. The idea that there are laws governing how wars may be fought — not just whether they may be started — is Lieber's lasting contribution. War crimes as a legal category begins here.
ticks.because: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) and the broader 1863 cluster of international humanitarian law instances demonstrated that nineteenth-century governments were codifying principled limits on power. The Repeal of the Corn Laws (1846) had earlier shown that British policy could shift on systematic argument. The Lieber Code — Francis Lieber's instructions for Union Army conduct — is the first modern codification of laws of war, becoming the precursor to the Hague Conventions and Geneva Conventions.

ticks.name: Nuremberg Principles / individual criminal responsibility
ticks.constraint: international law as binding only on states, not individuals
ticks.detail: The Nuremberg trials established that individuals — including heads of state and military commanders — could be held criminally responsible for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and crimes against peace. 'Following orders' was not a defense. This created the foundation for all subsequent international criminal law: the Yugoslav Tribunal, Rwanda Tribunal, and the International Criminal Court.

links.label: UN International Law Commission: Formulation of the Nürnberg Principles
UN ILC: Principles of International Law Recognized in the Nürnberg Charter (1950 PDF)

ticks.because: Nuremberg (1945-46) had tried specific defendants. The principles' codification by the UN International Law Commission (1950) made the legal theory portable — heads of state and military commanders could be held criminally responsible for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and crimes against peace. Following orders was not a defense. Every subsequent war-crimes tribunal and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998) builds on this codification.

ticks.name: Miranda rights / right to silence
ticks.constraint: police interrogation as constrained only by torture prohibition
ticks.detail: Miranda v. Arizona required police to inform suspects of their right to remain silent and to have counsel before interrogation. This transformed criminal procedure — not just in the US but as an international standard. The Miranda warning is perhaps the most recognizable legal formula in the world, embedded in popular culture through 50 years of police procedural fiction.

links.label: Library of Congress: Miranda v. Arizona Supreme Court opinion (PDF)
National Archives: Miranda v Arizona opinion PDF

ticks.because: Amnesty International's founding (1961), Griswold v. Connecticut's establishment of marital privacy (1965), and Miranda's confession-law upheaval (1966) bracket the 1960s moment when both international and domestic law were extending individual-rights protections. The Miranda decision — requiring police to inform suspects of their rights to silence and counsel before custodial interrogation — extended the Fifth Amendment's protection beyond the courtroom, and reordered American criminal procedure.

ticks.name: Spontaneous generation disproven (Redi)
ticks.constraint: living organisms as capable of arising from non-living matter
ticks.detail: Francesco Redi's controlled experiments with maggots and meat — comparing covered vs. uncovered samples — disproved the ancient theory that life could spontaneously generate from non-living matter. Pasteur's later experiments extended this to microorganisms. The disproof of spontaneous generation forced the question: if life cannot arise spontaneously, how did the first life begin? The origin of life problem is the child of this tick.

links.label: NCBI PMC — Francesco Redi and spontaneous generation

ticks.because: Hippocratic naturalism (400 BC) had argued that disease had natural causes. Galen's authoritative synthesis (130-200 AD) made medicine systematic but also dogmatic for fourteen centuries. Avicenna's Canon (1025) introduced clinical trials. Redi's covered-versus-uncovered meat experiment is the moment those threads converge into a controlled experiment — and into the rule that life cannot arise from non-life, which forces the origin question forever after.

ticks.name: Mendel's laws of heredity
ticks.constraint: inheritance as blending and therefore always averaging
ticks.detail: Gregor Mendel's pea experiments revealed that traits are inherited as discrete units (what we now call genes) — dominant and recessive — not as blends. This explained why offspring don't simply average their parents' traits. Mendel's work was ignored until 1900, when it was rediscovered simultaneously in three countries. The discrete particle model of inheritance, combined with Darwin's natural selection, completed the Modern Evolutionary Synthesis.

links.label: Mendel, Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden (1866) — Deutsches Textarchiv
Bauhaus-Universität Weimar: Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden metadata

ticks.because: Broca's area (1861) had localized language in specific brain tissue; Pasteur and Koch's germ theory (1861) had identified specific causal agents for disease. Lister's antiseptic surgery (1865) demonstrated that controlled procedures could change outcomes systematically. Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) had laid out the variation-selection mechanism. Mendel's pea experiments — published 1866, ignored for thirty-four years — provide the missing piece: variation is inherited as discrete units in predictable ratios.

ticks.name: Punctuated equilibrium (Gould/Eldredge)
ticks.constraint: evolution as proceeding by uniformly gradual change
ticks.detail: Stephen Jay Gould and Niles Eldredge proposed that most species remain stable for long periods and change rapidly in brief bursts — punctuated equilibrium rather than gradualism. This fit the fossil record better than Darwin's insistence on uniform gradual change. The debate transformed evolutionary biology and introduced the concepts of mass extinction as evolutionary driver and species selection as a level of evolution distinct from individual selection.
ticks.because: Reverse transcriptase (1970) and oncogene discovery (1970) had recently destabilized assumptions about how genetic information flows. Gould and Eldredge make the analogous move for evolution — long stable periods punctuated by rapid speciation, rather than gradualism throughout. The fossil record's apparent jumps stop being a problem and become the prediction.

ticks.name: Marathon / Persian repulsion and Athenian confidence
ticks.constraint: Greek city-states as inevitably subordinate to Persian imperial power
ticks.detail: The Athenian hoplite victory at Marathon — heavily outnumbered citizen soldiers defeating professional Persian infantry — proved that Greek civic armies could defeat imperial forces. It gave Athens the confidence and credibility to lead Greek resistance at Salamis and Plataea. Without Marathon, Athens likely becomes a Persian satrapy. The Golden Age of Greek philosophy, drama, and democracy are contingent on this battle.

links.label: Wikipedia: Marathon / Persian repulsion and Athenian confidence

ticks.because: The phalanx formation (500 BC) gave Greek hoplites a tactical structure that maximized disciplined infantry power. The Battle of Marathon (490 BC) demonstrated the decisive result. The Olympic Games (776 BC) had built the cultural infrastructure of pan-Hellenic identity that turned a tactical victory into civilizational confidence. Marathon as collective memory is what fuels Athenian democratic confidence and the explosive cultural production of the next century.

ticks.name: Longbow at Crécy / infantry defeats cavalry
ticks.constraint: armored cavalry as tactically dominant on the medieval battlefield
ticks.detail: English longbowmen destroyed the flower of French chivalry at Crécy. The longbow — requiring years of training, capable of 15 aimed shots per minute, penetrating plate armor at 100 meters — made mounted knights vulnerable to disciplined infantry. Crécy began the 150-year transition from cavalry to infantry dominance. Combined with later gunpowder weapons, it ended the social and military primacy of the feudal knight.

links.label: Erenow: Froissart, The Battle of Crécy 26 August 1346
Bloomsbury Primary Source 4.4: Froissart on Crécy (PDF)

ticks.because: The Mongol invasions' mobile warfare doctrine (1241) and the Mongol conquest of Song China (1279) demonstrated that medieval military superiority could be tactically rather than chivalrously determined. The English longbowmen at Crécy in 1346 — destroying mounted French chivalry from long range — apply the same logic in Western Europe. The era of armored cavalry as decisive battlefield force begins to end; gunpowder eventually completes the transition.

ticks.name: Battle of the Somme / industrial slaughter
ticks.constraint: infantry assault as a viable offensive tactic in the industrial age
ticks.detail: 60,000 British casualties on the first day (July 1, 1916), 1.5 million total on all sides over five months — for no strategic gain. The Somme made the futility of frontal assault against entrenched machine guns undeniable. It drove the development of tanks, combined arms tactics, and eventually the blitzkrieg doctrine. It also permanently changed the British public's relationship to military authority and sacrifice.

links.label: Imperial War Museums — Battle of the Somme

ticks.because: Poison gas at Ypres (1915) and the modern flamethrower (1915) had already demonstrated that industrial chemistry was now a battlefield force multiplier, and the previous year's trenches had stalemated the Western Front. The Somme — 1.2 million casualties for a few miles of mud — definitively showed that infantry assault against entrenched machine guns was not a viable offensive tactic, and forced the doctrinal rethink that produced 1918 combined-arms operations.

ticks.name: Battle of Britain / air power as decisive
ticks.constraint: national defense requiring territorial ground forces
ticks.detail: The Luftwaffe's failure to achieve air superiority over Britain — prevented by RAF Fighter Command, radar, and the production miracle of Spitfires and Hurricanes — was the first major campaign decided primarily by air forces. It proved that air superiority was a precondition for any successful invasion. Every major military power reorganized its doctrine around this lesson. Strategic airpower as the dominant arm of modern warfare begins here.

links.label: UK National Archives blog: Air Vice-Marshal Keith Park's Battle of Britain report
London Gazette dispatch: The Battle of Britain (Dowding)
Teaching American History: Churchill 'Every Man to His Post' (1940)

ticks.because: Stormtrooper tactics (1918) had taught that maneuver could break attritional warfare. Blitzkrieg in Poland and France (1939) demonstrated air-ground integration. Magnetic mines (1939) showed that the WWII technological pace was unprecedented. The Battle of Britain is the first major battle decided by air power alone — RAF radar, Hurricanes and Spitfires, ground control. The Luftwaffe's failure ends invasion plans and proves that air superiority is now strategic.

ticks.name: Gulf War / precision-guided munitions era
ticks.constraint: air strikes as requiring saturation bombing to destroy targets
ticks.detail: Operation Desert Storm demonstrated that precision-guided munitions (laser-guided and GPS-guided bombs) could destroy specific buildings, bridges, and vehicles rather than city blocks. The 43-day air campaign destroyed Iraqi military capability with minimal coalition casualties. This transformed military doctrine globally — every military power subsequently invested in precision munitions. The era of carpet bombing was over.

links.label: Wikipedia: Gulf War / precision-guided munitions era

ticks.because: The Falklands War (1982) had taught precision strike at sea. Network-centric warfare's emergence (also 1991) demonstrated that information could reorder combat structure. The Gulf War combines all of it — laser-guided bombs, GPS-aided navigation, F-117s with hours-old satellite intelligence. Industrial-age combat ends; precision-guided combat as we know it begins.

ticks.name: First corporate dividend (Dutch East India Co.)
ticks.constraint: investor returns requiring company liquidation
ticks.detail: The VOC paid its first dividend in 1602 — distributing profits to shareholders while continuing operations. This innovation separated investment return from company dissolution, making permanent corporate entities viable. Investors could benefit from ongoing operations without demanding their capital back. Every dividend-paying corporation in the world descends from this structural innovation.

links.label: World's First Stock Exchange: What was the return on VOC shares?
OSAM: Dividend History — VOC and the first dividends

ticks.because: The Dutch East India Company's joint-stock founding (1602) and its annual dividend mechanism (1602) established the institutional substrate. The first actual dividend distribution — VOC profits split among shareholders — closes the loop on what a corporation does. Modern shareholder capitalism's defining transaction has its precedent.

ticks.name: National debt as perpetual (British model)
ticks.constraint: government borrowing requiring repayment within the ruler's lifetime
ticks.detail: The Bank of England's innovation was the consolidation of government debt into perpetual annuities (Consols) — bonds paying interest forever with no repayment date. Investors were content to hold perpetual debt because the secondary market made it liquid. This allowed Britain to borrow at lower rates than France for 150 years, funding the Royal Navy and winning the imperial competition. Deficit spending as a permanent feature of government finance begins here.

links.label: Centre for Financial History (Cambridge): A Very Short History of the National Debt (Needham, PDF)
NBER: The Origins of National Debt — Financing the War of the Spanish Succession (Neal, PDF)
CEPR DP12304: Managing the UK National Debt 1694-2017

ticks.because: Lloyd's of London's insurance market (1688) had earlier demonstrated that risk could be priced and pooled at institutional scale. The Bank of England's 1694 founding includes the perpetual-debt innovation — government borrowing without specified repayment date, with interest payments funded from dedicated tax streams. Modern public finance begins; British eighteenth-century military success is partly underwritten by superior debt access.

ticks.name: SEC established / securities regulation
ticks.constraint: securities markets as operating without disclosure requirements
ticks.detail: The Securities and Exchange Commission (1934) required companies to disclose financial information and prohibited insider trading and market manipulation. This transformed stock markets from gentleman's gambling clubs to (relatively) trustworthy institutions for capital allocation. The post-WWII expansion of retail investment in equities — the 401(k) era — required the trust that the SEC's disclosure regime built.

links.label: Investopedia: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934

ticks.because: Smoot-Hawley (1930), Glass-Steagall (1933), and Tarski's undefinability theorem (1933) bracket a year when US legal and economic institutions were being radically restructured after the Crash. The SEC — established by the 1934 Securities Exchange Act — gave US financial markets their first federal disclosure-and-anti-fraud regulator, required public companies to file periodic reports, and made the modern public-equity capital market possible by reducing information asymmetry.

ticks.name: OPEC oil embargo and price shock
ticks.constraint: energy prices as determined by consuming-nation governments
ticks.detail: The 1973 Arab oil embargo quadrupled oil prices in months, causing recessions across the industrialized world. It demonstrated that commodities cartel pricing could restructure global economies, ended cheap-energy-fueled postwar growth, and triggered both energy conservation and alternative energy research. The petrodollar system (oil priced in dollars) became a pillar of American monetary hegemony.

links.label: CSIS: The Arab Oil Embargo — 40 Years Later

ticks.because: Nixon's closing of the gold window (1971) ended Bretton Woods and floated the dollar — making oil priced in dollars a lever the producers, not the consumers, could now pull. Once exchange rates were market-set rather than treaty-set, OPEC could quadruple prices in months and the consuming world had no fixed dollar to defend against.

ticks.name: 401(k) defined contribution retirement
ticks.constraint: retirement security requiring employer pension or government provision
ticks.detail: A provision of the 1978 Revenue Act allowed employees to defer wages into tax-advantaged accounts. The 401(k) shifted retirement risk from employers and governments to individual workers. It also created a massive new pool of equity investment (workers buying index funds), fueling the 1980s-90s bull market. The financialization of retirement made middle-class Americans stakeholders in stock market performance and created powerful political constituencies for low capital gains taxes.

links.label: TIME: A Brief History of the 401(k)
Business Insider: Where Did 401(k)s Come From?

ticks.because: Index funds (1975), public-key cryptography (1976), and the Apple I and Altair 8800 (1975–1976) bracket a moment when low-cost computation was making individual financial management feasible. The 1978 Revenue Act's section 401(k) shifted retirement saving from defined-benefit pensions to defined-contribution accounts — moving market risk from the employer to the household, and making the stock market a household concern.

ticks.name: iPhone App Store / platform economy
ticks.constraint: software distribution requiring physical retail or direct download
ticks.detail: The App Store model — Apple as platform taking 30% of every transaction, setting rules for what apps could exist, controlling access to a billion users — created a new kind of market. Platform economics, where the platform takes rent from every transaction, became the dominant business model of the 2010s. Uber, Airbnb, Spotify, and TikTok are all App Store descendants structurally.

links.label: Apple Newsroom: iPhone 3G on Sale Tomorrow / App Store launch (July 10, 2008)
Macworld: Apple opens iTunes App Store
Computerworld: Apple's iPhone App Store opens for business

ticks.because: The 2008 financial crisis and the App Store model launched in the iPhone SDK (2008) mark when Apple's platform shifted from a closed device to an open-developer economy. The App Store — curated, frictionless, with a 70/30 revenue split — gave every developer global software distribution and built the $500B/year mobile-app economy on top of it, restructuring the software industry around platform-mediated discovery and payment.

ticks.name: Venus figurines / portable art tradition
ticks.constraint: art as site-specific and immovable
ticks.detail: Venus figurines — small carved female forms found across a 20,000km arc from Spain to Siberia — are the oldest portable art tradition. They suggest either trade networks connecting distant cultures or parallel symbolic development. The symbolic preoccupation with fertility and the female form across 25,000 years of prehistory reveals something about the deep structure of human symbolic thought.

links.label: Smithsonian: Carved Ivory Venus from Hohle Fels Cave
Smithsonian 3D: Venus Figurine from Hohle Fels Cave

ticks.because: Cave paintings made art bound to place. Bone flutes added time. Painted ritual masks added upheaval. Venus figurines collapse all three into something a hand could carry — symbolic art uncoupled from a specific cave or ceremony, traveling the trade network of an entire continent.

ticks.name: Greek tragedy as art form (Sophocles/Euripides)
ticks.constraint: theatrical performance as purely ritual or celebratory
ticks.detail: Greek tragedy — Sophocles's Oedipus Rex, Euripides's Medea — invented the dramatic exploration of human suffering and moral complexity. The tragic form: a protagonist of stature making choices that lead to catastrophe despite their virtues. This is the template for Shakespeare, for opera, for film drama. Aristotle's analysis of tragedy in the Poetics defined drama theory for 2,000 years.
ticks.because: Greek tragedy's earliest emergence (470 BC, Aeschylus) and Pindar's victory odes (476 BC) established the era's poetic ambitions. Sophocles's Oedipus Rex and Euripides's Medea give the form its full development — psychological complexity, moral ambiguity, the limits of human knowledge as subjects. Western theater's foundational works; their formal architecture shapes drama for the next twenty-five hundred years.

ticks.name: Polyphonic music (Notre Dame school)
ticks.constraint: music as a single melodic line
ticks.detail: The Notre Dame school of polyphony (Léonin, Pérotin) developed sustained multi-voice music notation in the 12th-13th centuries. Multiple independent melodic lines moving simultaneously required written scores — improvisation couldn't coordinate polyphonic complexity. Polyphony unlocked the entire Western classical tradition: counterpoint, harmony, orchestration, and opera all require multiple simultaneous voices.

links.label: Cambridge History of Medieval Music: Notre Dame (Ch. 27)

ticks.because: Western music since antiquity had been monophonic — a single melodic line, with parallel doubling at most. Léonin and Pérotin at Notre Dame (1170-1200) developed sustained two-, three-, and four-voice polyphony with measurable rhythm. Multiple independent melodic lines required written scores; improvisation couldn't coordinate the complexity. Western music's distinctive history — counterpoint, harmony, sonata form — descends from Notre Dame's choir lofts.

ticks.name: Shakespeare's Globe Theatre / commercial drama
ticks.constraint: theater as either court entertainment or religious ceremony
ticks.detail: The Globe (built 1599) was a commercial theater — Shakespeare's plays written for paying audiences of all classes, performed in daylight, with a diverse cast. This created the commercial entertainment industry. Drama as a business rather than a ritual or patronage service. Television, Hollywood, and streaming are all commercial drama at scale — linear descendants of the Globe's business model.

links.label: Shakespeare Documented (Folger): Lease for the site of the Globe Playhouse (1599)

ticks.because: Dürer's mass-distributed woodcuts (1498), Vasari's Lives of the Artists (1550), and the Cumberland graphite deposit's pencil enablement (1565) demonstrated that late-Renaissance European art was building commercial and critical infrastructure. The Globe Theatre — built 1599 — is the same logic for drama: commercial, audience-funded, sustaining sophisticated playwrights including Shakespeare himself. Modern commercial theater begins.

ticks.name: Novel as dominant literary form (Richardson/Fielding)
ticks.constraint: extended narrative requiring epic or historical framework
ticks.detail: Samuel Richardson's Pamela (1740) and Henry Fielding's Tom Jones (1749) established the novel — extended prose fiction about ordinary contemporary people — as a literary form. The novel made psychological interiority (inner life, consciousness, motivation) the subject of art for the first time. Every subsequent form of psychological fiction, from Tolstoy to Proust to contemporary literary fiction, descends from Richardson and Fielding.

links.label: Britannica — Novel: rise of the novel
Wikipedia: Novel as dominant literary form (Richardson/Fielding)

ticks.because: The Daily Courant (1702) had created a market for accessible English prose. The Venice opera house (1637) and Stradivari's violins (1700) demonstrated that mass-market and craft-luxury cultural production could coexist. Richardson's Pamela (1740) and Fielding's Tom Jones (1749) establish the novel as the dominant literary form — accessible to the middle class, narrative-driven, psychological. The form runs the next two centuries of literary culture.

ticks.name: Photography frees painting from representation
ticks.constraint: art's prestige dependent on verisimilitude
ticks.detail: Once photographs could capture appearances with mechanical precision, painting's social function as documentary record was superseded. This freed painting to be what photography couldn't be: interpretation, emotion, abstraction. Impressionism, Expressionism, Cubism, Abstraction — the entire history of modern art is the story of painting discovering what it can do that photography cannot.

links.label: Met Museum: Daguerre and the Invention of Photography
Met Museum Heilbrunn Timeline: The Daguerreian Age in France 1839–55

ticks.because: The Gothic novel (1764) had legitimized fictional and psychological subjects for serious literature. Daguerre's photography (1839) provided the mechanical means. Gas lighting in theaters (Lyceum, 1817) had reordered visual production for performance. Once photographs could capture appearances mechanically, painting's documentary function dissolves — Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, abstraction, and the entire modern art tradition emerge from this liberation.

ticks.name: Rite of Spring premiere / modernism in music
ticks.constraint: Western harmony as the necessary basis for serious music
ticks.detail: Stravinsky's Rite of Spring premiered in Paris on May 29, 1913, causing a riot. Its irregular rhythms, dissonance, and rejection of tonal resolution were genuinely new. Within 20 years, Schoenberg's twelve-tone method eliminated tonality entirely. Jazz, rock, electronic music, and contemporary classical music are all, in different ways, working out the implications of 1913.

links.label: NYT TimesMachine: Russian Dancer's Latest Offering — The Consecration of Spring (June 8, 1913)
HAL: Buch, The Scandal at Le Sacre — Games of Distinction

ticks.because: The Armory Show (1913) had brought European modernism to America. Stravinsky's Rite of Spring premiere on May 29, 1913 — the riotous Paris reception — confirms that modernism could provoke and survive scandal in music. Tonality's collapse, primitive rhythmic complexity, and the post-Romantic break all become culturally legitimized after the Rite.

ticks.name: The Jazz Singer / sound film
ticks.constraint: cinema as a silent visual medium
ticks.detail: The Jazz Singer (1927) demonstrated that synchronized sound film was commercially viable, making silent film obsolete within three years. The addition of dialogue transformed cinema from a visual art form into a combined verbal-visual medium. Acting styles, narrative possibilities, and the entire grammar of film changed. Hollywood's global cultural dominance — soft power through storytelling — required synchronized sound.

links.label: Library of Congress — National Film Registry: The Jazz Singer
Wikipedia: The Jazz Singer / sound film

ticks.because: The Waste Land's modernist poetry (1922) and the Surrealism manifesto (1924) demonstrated that interwar art was being radically reorganized. The Jazz Singer in 1927 makes synchronized-sound film commercially viable — Al Jolson's 'You ain't heard nothing yet' as both promise and prediction. Silent film ends within five years; the talkie restructures Hollywood.

ticks.name: Elvis on Ed Sullivan / rock and roll mainstream
ticks.constraint: popular music as safe, decorous, and intergenerational
ticks.detail: Elvis Presley's Ed Sullivan appearances (1956-57, watched by 60 million) introduced Black American R&B performance style to white mass media audiences. Rock and roll's physicality, sexual energy, and generational exclusivity created youth culture as a distinct market and social force. The music industry, youth fashion, and the concept of the generation gap all crystallized in Elvis's pelvis.

links.label: History.com: Elvis Presley first appearance on Ed Sullivan, Sept 9, 1956
EdSullivan.com: Elvis on The Ed Sullivan Show 1956

ticks.because: Magnetic tape recording (1948) gave the recording studio its production tool. Rock and roll's emergence as a market category (1955) had created the genre. Elvis's Ed Sullivan appearances in 1956-57 — sixty million viewers, broadcast television's reach — bring rock and roll into respectable American living rooms. The cultural mainstream incorporates the new music; teenage consumer power is established.

ticks.name: Hip-hop invented (South Bronx)
ticks.constraint: music creation requiring instruments and recording budgets
ticks.detail: DJ Kool Herc's use of two turntables to extend the percussion break in records created hip-hop's foundational technique in 1973. By 1975 the culture had its four elements: DJing, MCing, breakdancing, graffiti. Hip-hop enabled music creation from poverty — two turntables and a microphone. It became the most globally influential musical form since rock and roll, restructuring popular music, fashion, language, and politics.

links.label: Smithsonian Magazine: How Hip-Hop Was Born 50 Years Ago
NY Magazine: 1520 Sedgwick — birth of hip-hop

ticks.because: Earth Day's environmental art (1970) had legitimized art as activist intervention; Atari's Pong (1972) had made interactive electronic media a mass medium. Hip-hop combines both — a culture invented from poverty using two turntables and a microphone, treating recorded music as raw material to be remixed live. The four elements (DJing, MCing, breaking, graffiti) become the most globally influential popular form of the next half-century.

ticks.name: Difference Engine (Babbage concept)
ticks.constraint: mathematical tables as requiring error-prone human calculation
ticks.detail: Charles Babbage's design for a mechanical calculator — gears, wheels, and columns of digits — was never completed in his lifetime but established the conceptual architecture of programmable computation. Ada Lovelace's notes on the Analytical Engine contained the first algorithm and the first recognition that such machines could manipulate symbols, not just numbers. The conceptual framework preceded the technology by a century.

links.label: Computer History Museum — Babbage's Difference Engine

ticks.because: The sundial (1600 BC), Archimedes (250 BC), and Eratosthenes (250 BC) showed that mechanical or geometric devices could compute physical quantities. Galileo's kinematics (1589) made motion mathematical. Babbage's Difference Engine is the conceptual leap — a fully mechanical machine designed to compute arbitrary polynomial values, the first explicit attempt to mechanize mathematical labor itself.

ticks.name: Enigma breaking / cryptanalysis as weapon
ticks.constraint: encrypted communications as effectively secure against non-holders
ticks.detail: Alan Turing's work at Bletchley Park on breaking the Enigma cipher (with Rejewski's earlier Polish work) shortened WWII by an estimated 2-4 years. More importantly, it demonstrated that mechanical encryption could be mechanically broken — that there were systematic vulnerabilities in systems thought unbreakable. This insight drove both cryptography and computing research throughout the Cold War.

links.label: US National Archives: Turing's Treatise on the Enigma (PDF)
AndrewHodges/Turing.org.uk: Turing's report on the Enigma, 1940
Codes and Ciphers: Bletchley Park translated Enigma manual (PDF)

ticks.because: The Church-Turing thesis (1936) had defined what computation was and what it could in principle do. Bletchley Park applies the theory to wartime cryptanalysis — the bombe and Colossus break Enigma and Lorenz, shortening WWII by an estimated two years. Code-breaking becomes a strategic weapon, and the concept of the computer as a strategic asset is born.

ticks.name: TCP/IP standardized (ARPANET transition)
ticks.constraint: computer networks as requiring compatible hardware to communicate
ticks.detail: On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP as its standard protocol — the moment the modern internet was born. TCP/IP's layered architecture allowed any hardware to communicate with any other hardware, provided both spoke the protocol. The internet's extraordinary diversity of devices, applications, and uses all depend on this protocol agnosticism.

links.label: Internet Society — A Brief History of the Internet

ticks.because: ARPANET's first message (1969) had established the network. The IBM PC's open architecture (1981) and SMTP for email (1982) demonstrated that open standards could underwrite massive ecosystems. The January 1, 1983 ARPANET transition to TCP/IP — Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn's protocol — is the moment the internet's universal addressing and routing scheme becomes operational. Every IP address since flows from this Flag Day.

ticks.name: First website goes live (CERN)
ticks.constraint: internet content as accessible only by direct address
ticks.detail: Tim Berners-Lee's first website — explaining the World Wide Web project itself — went live at CERN on August 6, 1991. The combination of HTML (markup), HTTP (protocol), and URLs (addresses) created a universal surface for publishing and linking. Within 5 years, the web was the primary metaphor for the internet. Within 10, it had transformed commerce, media, and social life.

links.label: CERN: The birth of the Web

ticks.because: Berners-Lee's WWW proposal (1989), Unicode (1991), and Linux (1991) had each provided the substrate. The first website is the canonical demonstration — explaining what the Web is, on the Web itself. Documentation and instance combined; the bootstrap tick.

ticks.name: Electron discovered (J.J. Thomson)
ticks.constraint: atoms as the smallest indivisible particles
ticks.detail: Thomson's cathode ray experiments revealed a particle 2,000 times lighter than hydrogen — the electron. The atom had structure. This opened a new scale of physical reality. Within 30 years: the nuclear model, quantum mechanics, and quantum electrodynamics. The electron is the particle that makes chemistry, materials science, and all electronic technology possible to understand and engineer.

links.label: Wikisource: Thomson, Cathode Rays (Phil Mag Oct 1897)

ticks.because: Maxwell's demon (1873) had connected information and thermodynamics. Michelson-Morley (1887) had eliminated the ether. Röntgen's X-rays (1895) demonstrated that matter contained invisible structure. Thomson's cathode-ray tube experiments reveal a particle two thousand times lighter than hydrogen — the electron. Atoms are no longer fundamental, and twentieth-century physics has its first elementary particle.

ticks.name: Eddington's eclipse observation / general relativity confirmed
ticks.constraint: Newton's gravity as the definitive theory of gravitation
ticks.detail: Arthur Eddington's measurement of starlight bending around the sun during a solar eclipse confirmed Einstein's prediction from general relativity. Overnight, Einstein became the world's most famous scientist. More importantly, the confirmation that massive objects curve spacetime replaced Newtonian gravity as the correct description of the universe. GPS satellites require general relativistic corrections to give accurate positions.
ticks.because: Einstein's general relativity (1915) and its 1916 formal exposition had made the theoretical claim. Eddington's measurement of starlight bending around the sun during the May 29, 1919 solar eclipse confirms the prediction with the full ceremony of a postwar international expedition. General relativity becomes physics-establishment orthodoxy; Einstein becomes a global celebrity.

ticks.name: Electroweak unification (Weinberg/Salam/Glashow)
ticks.constraint: electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force as unrelated
ticks.detail: The electroweak theory showed that electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force (responsible for radioactive decay) are aspects of a single electroweak force at high energies. This was the first fundamental unification since Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism. The Nobel-winning theory predicted the W and Z bosons, discovered at CERN in 1983. It is the template for all grand unified theories.

links.label: CERN Courier: Birth of a symmetry (Weinberg 1967 paper)

ticks.because: Plate tectonics (1965) and the cosmic microwave background (1965) had each closed an open question with a unified theoretical answer. Moore's law (1965) and DRAM (1966) showed that engineering precision was scaling exponentially. Weinberg, Salam, and Glashow apply the same unification mood to particle physics — electromagnetism and the weak force become two sides of one symmetry, predicting the W and Z bosons that 1983 confirms.

ticks.name: Accelerating universe / dark energy discovered
ticks.constraint: the expansion of the universe as slowing due to gravity
ticks.detail: Two teams measuring distant supernovae discovered that the universe's expansion is accelerating — something is pushing space apart. This 'dark energy' (comprising ~68% of the universe's energy content) has no explanation in the Standard Model. It is the largest unexplained phenomenon in physics. The discovery fundamentally changed cosmology: the universe will expand forever, and most of it is made of something we do not understand.

links.label: IOPscience: Riess et al, Observational Evidence from Supernovae for an Accelerating Universe (1998)

ticks.because: Hubble's deep-field images at billions of light-years gave cosmology a meter that could measure expansion at the largest scales. Bose-Einstein condensates the same decade confirmed quantum mechanics still ruled at the smallest. Together they made the dark-energy surprise believable: a result this strange could only stand on instruments this trustworthy.

ticks.name: First direct gravitational wave detection (LIGO)
ticks.constraint: gravitational waves as theoretically predicted but undetectable
ticks.detail: LIGO detected gravitational waves from two merging black holes 1.3 billion light years away — a signal that stretched and compressed the 4km detector by 1/1000th the width of a proton. This opened a new observational window on the universe: astronomy by listening to spacetime ripples rather than seeing electromagnetic radiation. Neutron star mergers, black hole populations, and tests of general relativity in extreme conditions are now accessible.

links.label: Physical Review Letters 2016 — Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger

ticks.because: LIGO's gravitational wave detection (2015), the broader gravitational wave astronomy opening (2015), and the direct LIGO observation are facets of the same single tick. Gravitational wave astronomy as an observational discipline opens; multi-messenger astronomy follows when neutron star mergers are observed simultaneously in EM and gravitational signals.

ticks.name: Sumerian number system (sexagesimal)
ticks.constraint: counting beyond small numbers without a positional system
ticks.detail: The Sumerian base-60 system — with its positional notation and concept of zero as a placeholder — is the ancestor of our clock (60 seconds, 60 minutes) and circle (360 degrees). It enabled the astronomical calculations that powered Babylonian science. A positional number system is a cognitive prosthetic that makes complex arithmetic possible — you cannot do long division with Roman numerals.

links.label: Springer/Archive for History of Exact Sciences: 'The sixty system of Sumer' (Seidenberg, 1965)
Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative: Sexagesimal place value notation in 3rd millennium BC

ticks.because: Cuneiform was a spreadsheet before it was a story. A spreadsheet without a positional number system is a list of marks; with one, it becomes a calculator. Sumerian merchants needed to multiply and divide on clay — sexagesimal positional notation, with zero as a placeholder, made that possible.

ticks.name: Library of Alexandria / knowledge aggregation
ticks.constraint: knowledge as geographically trapped in its place of origin
ticks.detail: The Library of Alexandria — at its height containing 700,000 scrolls — was the first systematic attempt to collect all human knowledge in one place. Ptolemaic policy required all ships entering Alexandria to surrender their books for copying. The model of the universal library — aggregate everything, make it accessible — is the ancestor of Google Books, Wikipedia, and the internet itself.

links.label: Edinburgh: Erskine, Culture and Power in Ptolemaic Egypt — Library of Alexandria
Wikipedia: Library of Alexandria / knowledge aggregation

ticks.because: Pāṇini's Sanskrit grammar (500 BC), the Library of Alexandria's founding (300 BC), and the Erya — the first Chinese dictionary (300 BC) — bracket a Eurasian moment when systematic knowledge was being collected, organized, and indexed for the first time. The Alexandria library at its peak held perhaps 400,000 scrolls, and gave the Hellenistic and later Roman world a single repository where Greek, Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Indian learning could be cross-referenced.

ticks.name: Wycliffe Bible / vernacular scripture
ticks.constraint: Christian scripture accessible only in Latin
ticks.detail: John Wycliffe's English translation of the Bible (1382) gave English speakers direct access to scripture without priestly mediation. It was immediately declared heretical — the Church understood what was at stake. Tyndale's English Bible (1526) and Luther's German Bible (1534) completed the democratization of scripture. Vernacular translation directly enabled the Reformation.
ticks.because: The Diamond Sutra (868 AD) had shown that printing technology and spiritual texts could combine for free distribution. Arabic as the language of science (1000 AD) and the Toledo School (1125) had established translation as a high-stakes intellectual practice. Guido's musical staff (1025) proved that vernacular notations could carry sophisticated content. Ibn Manzur's Lisan al-Arab (1290) and Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah (1377) showed that vernacular scholarship could match Latin scholarship's rigor. Wycliffe's English Bible is the application of all these threads to scripture — and the Church's heresy declaration confirms what's at stake.
